issues.title: [Linux desktop] Cannot send any message on 26.1103.32239 (Enter / Send button no-op); reverting to 26.1027.51404 fixes it

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

issues.body:
## Summary

On the Linux desktop app, build **26.1103.32239** cannot send messages: the composer accepts typing, but pressing Enter does nothing and the Send button does nothing. It affects **every** thread, including a brand-new empty chat. Fully quitting and relaunching does not help. Reverting to **26.1027.51404** fixes it immediately.

## Environment

- Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS, kernel `7.0.0-43-generic`, X11
- Codex desktop (`chatgpt` deb, `https://persistent.oaistatic.com/codex-app-prod/linux/deb`)
  - broken build: `26.1103.32239`
  - working build: `26.1027.51404`
- Same machine / same account: `codex-cli 0.149.0` works fine (`codex login status` → `Logged in using ChatGPT`)

## Steps to reproduce

1. Update the desktop app from `26.1027.51404` to `26.1103.32239` via apt.
2. Restart the app (the new build only takes effect after a restart of the Electron process).
3. Open any thread — an existing one or a brand-new empty chat.
4. Type some text, then press Enter, and/or click the Send button.

## Actual

Nothing is sent. No user message appears in the transcript, no turn starts, no error is shown, and the composer keeps the text. Restarting the app does not change anything.

## Expected

The message is submitted and a turn starts.

## Evidence from the local app-server log (`~/.codex/logs_2.sqlite`)

The client build is recorded on every RPC, which makes the boundary exact:

| window | `app_server.client_version` | behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| ≤ 09:33:09 | `26.1027.51404` | normal, UI issues `turn/start` RPCs (01:20:21, 09:32:07, 09:33:05) |
| 09:33:28 → 12:15:41 | `26.1103.32239` | **broken**: zero user-initiated submissions over 2h42m of continuous use |

Supporting observations inside the broken window:

- The app-server was healthy the whole time: Responses WebSocket upgrades returned `status=101`, backend HTTP calls returned `200`, and a goal-mode turn ran continuously for 27 minutes. So this is not a connectivity/auth failure.
- In a thread that already had an active turn, pressing Enter did emit `turn/steer` and the server answered `response.interrupt.accepted`, but nothing changed in the UI.
- In an idle or brand-new thread, **nothing at all reached the app-server** — the submit was swallowed client-side before any RPC.

## Ruled out

- **Auth**: `codex login status` → `Logged in using ChatGPT`; requests carry a valid token.
- **Backend / network**: WebSocket `101` and HTTP `200` to `chatgpt.com` throughout; the CLI works on the same account and network.
- **Proxy**: both builds run behind the same proxy (mihomo TUN + mixed port); no proxy config changed between them.
- **Corrupted local state**: the thread store, config and auth files were untouched across the upgrade/downgrade; the same state works on the old build.

## Workaround (verified)

Downgrade and pin the previous build — sending works again immediately, same account and same local state:

```sh
sudo apt install --allow-downgrades /var/cache/apt/archives/chatgpt_26.1027.51404_amd64.deb
sudo apt-mark hold chatgpt   # otherwise apt puts 26.1103.32239 back
```

## Notes

- `apt-cache policy chatgpt` only offers `26.1103.32239` from the repo, so a fresh install has no way to get a working build without the cached `.deb`.
- Happy to attach more logs, capture a renderer trace with `--remote-debugging-port`, or test a fixed build.

issues.body:
Env: Codex desktop 26.1029.7803.0 (Microsoft Store), Windows 11 Pro 26200, app-server 0.166.0

Steps:
1. Open the side terminal next to a thread.
2. Run a full-screen TUI with a long session (e.g. Claude Code with a long transcript).
3. Switch to another thread, then switch back.

Expected: Terminal reappears instantly.
Actual: UI freezes for several seconds. Hiding the side terminal before switching makes the lag disappear.

Suspected cause: Terminal gets resized (0 -> real width) or remounted on thread switch, sending a resize to the PTY; the TUI redraws its entire scrollback, and xterm re-parses it. Desktop log shows repeated "ResizeObserver loop completed" errors.
Suggestion: Keep hidden terminals mounted and skip PTY resize while hidden (like VS Code does), or debounce resize until visible.

issues.body:
## Summary

The new-chat Work composer shows **Full access**, but the resulting conversation's execution context reports **workspace-write with restricted network access**. The user reports that the Full access control is visible only before starting the chat and then disappears, leaving no visible in-thread way to inspect or correct the selected mode.

A harmless, explicitly authorized SSH check fails at the first jump-host TCP connection, before SSH authentication. Fully restarting the ChatGPT desktop app did not change the result. Returning to the same conversation through the web interface also produced the same result from its local command runner.

## Environment

- ChatGPT desktop on Windows; Work mode.
- Desktop app version **26.1103.32239**, reported by the user from the app's version display. The assistant did not independently inspect the About dialog.
- ChatGPT Pro.
- Observed November 6, 2026, America/Chicago (November 7 UTC).
- Local PowerShell **7.6.9** and **OpenSSH_for_Windows_9.5p2, LibreSSL 3.8.2**, confirmed by command execution.
- Exact Windows OS build was not collected.

## Reproduction and observations

1. Start a Work chat with Full access selected in the new-chat composer. A user-supplied screenshot shows Work and the orange Full access indicator.
2. Authorize a read-only SSH check using an existing key, pinned known-hosts file, strict host checking, BatchMode, IdentitiesOnly, and bounded connection timeouts.
3. Run a marker-only remote command over an existing jump-host route.
4. The SSH child process returns **255**, with the private addresses redacted here:

```text
ssh: connect to host <existing-jump-host> port 22: Permission denied
Connection closed by UNKNOWN port 65535
```

5. The user reports that the Full access control disappears after chat creation.
6. Fully restart the desktop app and retry the same connection: same SSH exit 255 and error.
7. Open the conversation in the web version and retry through the available local executor: same SSH exit 255 and error.

The enclosing Python command completed successfully and printed the SSH child's exit code; **255 is the SSH process's exit code**, not the wrapper's.

## Effective permissions supplied to the execution session

The session reports:

- sandbox mode: workspace-write
- network access: restricted
- approval policy: granular
- sandbox/rule/skill approval categories: automatically rejected rather than prompting
- a managed filesystem permission profile

These observations do not match the user's Full access selection. The source of the managed restriction has not been identified.

## Expected behavior

The selected access mode should either be reflected in the command runner's effective permissions, or the UI should clearly explain the overriding restriction, its source, and the supported way to resolve it. The current chat's permission control should remain accessible.

## Actual behavior and impact

Local PowerShell works, but authorized remote development is blocked before authentication. The visible Full access selection and effective execution permissions appear inconsistent, and the permission control is unavailable after chat creation according to the user.

We did not modify SSH server policy, disable host checking, expose private keys, change application security settings, or attempt an alternate transport to bypass the restriction.

## Diagnostic limits

- This is a report of observed behavior, not a confirmed root cause.
- No successful fresh connection from an ordinary unsandboxed terminal was established in this receiving session.
- The failure does not establish whether remote hosts or SSH credentials would work from an authorized environment.
- We did not collect a native socket error code, test HTTPS/DNS, or inspect network environment flags in this reproduction.
- A separate dot session reported restricted network access and stopped before attempting SSH; that is a reported permission observation, not an independent connection test.
- Switching to the web UI reused the available command runner; this does not prove a distinct web execution backend has the same defect.

## Related reports

- #57671 — Windows / ChatGPT Work TCP connections blocked despite Full access.
- #59528 — Full access control disappears and effective permissions remain restricted, reported on macOS.

Please consolidate with an existing issue if appropriate, and identify whether version 26.1103.32239 has a permission-propagation defect or is subject to an overriding managed policy. A supported recovery path or confirmed fixed version would be helpful.

Private host addresses, local usernames, filesystem paths, credentials, and unrelated conversation screenshots are omitted.

issues.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

The ChatGPT Work/desktop application version has not been independently verified from the About dialog. The separately installed CLI reports `codex-cli 0.136.0`; this is provided for context and should not be treated as the affected application's version.

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT Pro.

### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0, running native PowerShell.

Observed on October 28, 2026.

### What issue are you seeing?

In a ChatGPT Work conversation using a local Windows command executor, outgoing TCP connections fail immediately with Windows socket error **10013 / WSAEACCES**.

I added the following configuration, restarted the application, and subsequently granted Full access in the UI:

```toml
[windows]
sandbox = "elevated"

[sandbox_workspace_write]
network_access = true
```

The executor verified that the network setting is present in the user configuration file. Nevertheless, repeated checks in the same conversation still show:

- A direct TCP connection to my SSH server on port 22 fails with native socket error `10013`.
- A direct TCP connection to `1.1.1.1:443` fails with the same error. This test does not depend on DNS.
- `[System.Net.Dns]::GetHostAddresses('github.com')` fails with a host-not-found error.
- `CODEX_SANDBOX_NETWORK_DISABLED=1`.
- `CODEX_NETWORK_PROXY_ACTIVE` is not set.
- `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY`, and `ALL_PROXY` are not set.
- The effective execution context supplied to the agent still describes `workspace-write` with restricted network access.

The user-selected UI state and the policy reaching the executor appear inconsistent. I cannot determine whether the source is session permission propagation, a higher-priority policy, or another Windows sandbox issue.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Start a ChatGPT Work conversation with local Windows command execution.
2. Add `[sandbox_workspace_write] network_access = true` to the user configuration.
3. Restart the application and grant Full access in the UI.
4. Ask the agent to test SSH and general TCP connectivity.
5. Observe that the executor still reports the disabled-network flag and rejects outgoing connections.

A minimal PowerShell probe for the affected execution environment:

```powershell
$probeClient = [System.Net.Sockets.TcpClient]::new()
try {
    $probeTask = $probeClient.ConnectAsync('1.1.1.1', 443)
    if (-not $probeTask.Wait(5000)) {
        throw [System.TimeoutException]::new('TCP connection timed out')
    }
    'CONNECTED'
} catch {
    $probeError = $_.Exception.GetBaseException()
    $probeError.Message
    if ($probeError -is [System.Net.Sockets.SocketException]) {
        'NativeErrorCode: ' + $probeError.NativeErrorCode
    }
} finally {
    $probeClient.Dispose()
}

[Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable('CODEX_SANDBOX_NETWORK_DISABLED')
```

Observed results: native socket error `10013`, followed by the environment flag value `1`.

### What is the expected behavior?

The command executor should honor the effective network permissions selected for the conversation. If a higher-priority policy intentionally prevents access, the UI should identify that policy and its source and explain which supported setting can change it.

Changing configuration and granting access should not leave users repeatedly testing an execution environment whose effective permissions silently remain restricted.

### Additional information

- Related reports: #53278 and #55828. This may share their root cause; I cannot establish that from the available diagnostics. Please consolidate this report if appropriate.
- Tailscale was considered during troubleshooting. Later checks showed no Tailscale interface or routes, with the default IPv4 route going directly through the Wi-Fi gateway, but both TCP tests continued to fail with `10013`. This does not conclusively exclude every local networking cause.
- Connectivity from ordinary, non-sandboxed PowerShell has not been independently verified in this report.
- No SSH authentication was attempted during the TCP probes. Private server addresses, credentials, keys, and raw private logs are omitted.

issues.body:
## Summary
Codex Windows sandbox setup repeatedly fails with `helper_sandbox_lock_failed` / Win32 error 5 on `%USERPROFILE%\.codex\.sandbox-bin` in app version **26.1103.3517.0**. The directory initially granted SYSTEM `(M)` but not `WRITE_DAC`, matching #59038 and the legacy ACL repair in #59745. **Manually adding SYSTEM `(M,WDAC)` succeeds, but restarting the application still does not complete setup.** The exact error after restart has not yet been re-collected.

## Environment
- Windows 11, build 22631 (reported previously by user; not re-verified for this run)
- Codex Windows app MSIX package: `OpenAI.Codex 26.1103.3517.0` (package status: Ok)
- `~/.codex/config.toml`: `[windows] sandbox = "elevated"`
- App shows **"Windows setup didn't finish" / "Setup stopped"**, retry unsuccessful.
- User also reports approval modes cannot be changed in desktop app; causal connection unconfirmed.

## Observed errors before manual ACL repair
```text
setup_error.json:
{
  "code": "helper_sandbox_lock_failed",
  "message": "lock sandbox bin dir \\?\C:\Users\<redacted>\.codex\.sandbox-bin failed: open directory ... NtCreateFile: Access is denied. (os error 5)"
}

[2026-11-07T04:09:35Z] WFP setup failed for CodexSandboxOffline: BuildSecurityDescriptorW failed: 0x00000534
[2026-11-07T04:09:35Z] setup error: helper_sandbox_lock_failed: lock sandbox bin dir ... NtCreateFile: Access is denied. (os error 5)
```
`0x534` is ERROR_NONE_MAPPED, potentially a separate Windows Filtering Platform security-descriptor/SID resolution issue; whether it contributes to failed setup is unknown.

## ACL inspection and attempted workaround
Before:
```text
CodexSandboxUsers:(OI)(CI)(RX)
NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM:(OI)(CI)(M)
BUILTIN\Administrators:(OI)(CI)(M)
<current user>:(OI)(CI)(M,WDAC)
Owner: <current user>
AreAccessRulesProtected: True
```

The user backed up the existing directory ACL, then ran:
```powershell
icacls "$env:USERPROFILE\.codex\.sandbox-bin" /grant 'SYSTEM:(OI)(CI)(WDAC)'
```
Result: command completed successfully. A subsequent `icacls` verified:
```text
NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM:(OI)(CI)(M,WDAC)
```
**After app restart, Windows setup still fails.** We do not yet know whether the app rewrote the ACL again during retry or whether setup advanced to another error.

## Reproduction
1. On Windows app version 26.1103.3517.0, configure elevated Windows sandbox.
2. Retry Windows setup from desktop app.
3. Inspect `%USERPROFILE%\.codex\.sandbox\setup_error.json` and sandbox logs.
4. Observe `helper_sandbox_lock_failed`, error 5, opening `.sandbox-bin`, along with WFP security descriptor failure.
5. Grant SYSTEM `WRITE_DAC` on the sandbox bin directory and verify it is present.
6. Restart Codex: setup still not successful.

## Expected behavior
Setup/re-provisioning should repair legacy ACLs safely and persistently, or report the *actual new blocker* after ACL correction. Please verify whether #59745 fully addresses installed Windows desktop builds, including any ACL reapplication and WFP setup errors.

## Related
- #59038 — SYSTEM denied WRITE_DAC on `.sandbox-bin`
- #57617 — protected ACL and recurring sandbox lock failures
- #50520 — recurring ACL reversion
- #59744 — same lock error in a newer desktop build
- PR #59745 — Repair legacy Windows sandbox bin permissions for SYSTEM (merged 2026-11-05)
- PR #60042 — Centralize Windows sandbox filesystem override resolution (merged 2026-11-07)

_This report intentionally omits the local Windows username and host name._

issues.title: Dots: hallucinated completion claims, cloud/local confusion, missing updates, and an unexplained “Paused” state

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

issues.body:
## Summary

I am reporting several problems I experienced in one ongoing dot conversation, mainly on November 6, 2026. I asked my dot to improve an existing job-research workflow on its own cloud computer, using Superpowers as part of a full implementation plan.

My main concern is hallucination: confident, inaccurate or unsupported claims about the dot's own task completion and prior understanding, followed by corrections only after I challenged them. The examples below concern what it said it had completed or understood; they do not establish a specific model defect or root cause.

The dot gave overly broad completion reports and then acknowledged unfinished implementation, left me repeatedly asking for the next update, and used “local” in a way that made it unclear whether it meant its cloud computer or my PC. When I challenged that, it initially agreed with the premise that it had misunderstood the computer destination, then later said it had found no actual instruction or proposal to use my PC.

Separately, the desktop app displayed the whole dot as “Paused” after I had reported rebooting it. I had deliberately paused the scheduled job search, but I had not intentionally paused the whole dot. A screenshot shows the whole-dot indicator. I cannot establish why it appeared.

These problems made it difficult to trust what was completed, where work happened, and whether work was continuing. I am reporting the symptoms together for context, not claiming they share one cause.

## Environment

- Product: ChatGPT desktop app, using a dot.
- Local platform: Windows desktop, visible in the screenshots. Exact Windows version/build is not verified.
- Work setup: the dot's cloud computer, with a separate local-PC connection visible in the app. The requested implementation was intended for the dot's computer.
- Exact desktop app version/build: not captured in the available evidence.
- Exact active model for the affected responses: not verified. A later tool/model comparison does not establish which model generated the earlier responses.
- Time zone: Philippine Time, PHT (UTC+8). All times below use PHT.
- I reported seeing two desktop updates that day. I do not have evidence identifying their versions or showing that either caused these problems.

## What happened

### 1. Hallucinated or confidently inaccurate completion claims

At 11:13 AM on November 6, the dot presented an eight-phase implementation plan. I approved implementation at 11:18 AM and asked it to pause scheduled searches at 11:45 AM while it finished the improvements.

At 12:00:42 PM, it said:

> “The offline improvements are done and tested, bro, but the full workflow isn’t proven yet because the searches are paused.”

It described the next step as a real search. After I asked whether all phases were done, it corrected itself at 12:15:03 PM:

> “No, bro. I was too broad when I said the offline improvements were done.”

At 12:16:05 PM, its phase breakdown said source-rotation and employer-watchlist improvements were “not implemented yet,” and Superpowers was not verified as installed. These were unfinished implementation items, not merely a live test being deferred because I had paused searches.

There is an important limitation to this complaint: the original 11:13 AM plan itself explicitly said it had found Superpowers reference material, “but not a verified complete installed skill,” and that the plan had not yet been implemented. I am not claiming that original message explicitly said the full plugin was installed. My concern is that the requested full-tool use remained unresolved while later progress and completion messages were too broad and confusing.

### 2. Missing updates and unclear continuation

At 1:13 PM, I asked which phase the dot was on. It replied that it would check. At 1:20 PM, I had to ask again and supplied a screenshot showing that exchange without the promised phase answer.

At 1:21:13 PM, it said:

> “You got my ‘I’ll check’ message but not the phase-by-phase answer. I sent that answer to the wrong reply destination.”

That is the dot's explanation. I do not have independent delivery logs proving whether the cause was reply routing, UI display, or another problem.

There was another gap after a 1:39:27 PM timing-fix update. At 1:53:56 PM, I asked why there were no further updates. At 1:54:02 PM, it replied:

> “I stopped after reporting the timing fix instead of continuing the implementation and keeping you updated.”

The problem was not simply the number of minutes between messages. I could not tell whether the requested work was continuing, complete, or blocked, and had to keep prompting it to clarify.

### 3. Cloud-computer/local-PC confusion and premature agreement

My original request at 11:01 AM said to use Superpowers “on your pc,” meaning the dot's computer. Later updates repeatedly used terms such as “local tests” without clearly identifying the machine.

At 2:09 PM, the dot focused on plugin administrator settings. At 2:10 PM, I clarified that I meant using the GitHub repository and terminal on its own computer. It immediately said it had misunderstood, and repeated that admission before establishing whether it had actually proposed using my PC.

At 2:15 PM, it clarified that “local testing” meant the cloud computer. At 2:16 PM, it reported checking its work records and said the relevant tests ran on the Linux cloud computer. At 2:17:07 PM, it corrected its earlier agreement: it had found no actual instruction or proposal in the checked messages to run this work on my PC. It said the concrete error was focusing on plugin/admin settings instead of the requested GitHub/terminal setup, then making the explanation more confusing.

This report does not allege proven unauthorized execution on my PC. It documents ambiguous wording and an explanation that changed after the dot checked the evidence.

At 2:15:12 PM, it also said the repository had been downloaded but was not installed or activated. At 2:19 PM, it acknowledged that a plan based on saved reference guidance did not establish that the full requested tool had been installed and run. Plugin availability, repository download, installation, activation and actual use need to be reported distinctly.

### 4. Unexplained whole-dot “Paused” indicator after a reported reboot

At 1:23:03 PM, I told the dot I had rebooted it. At 1:25 PM, it reported that the improvement files and saved test evidence remained available, and that the scheduled job search was still intentionally paused. That was its reported check, not proof of complete recovery or a fresh execution test.

A screenshot with the Windows clock showing **1:29 PM, November 6, 2026** shows:

- The dot's right-hand status panel displaying **“Paused.”**
- A separate **“Paused”** indicator at the bottom of the conversation.

I sent it at 1:30:29 PM with the message:

> “LOOK RIGHT NOW YOU JUST GOT PAUSED what happend??? i ddint touch you or anything”

The dot responded afterward. It acknowledged that the whole-dot pause indicator was distinct from the deliberately paused job-search schedule and said it could not identify the cause or an actor.

The screenshot proves the indicator was displayed. It does not establish when the state changed, who or what changed it, whether it was a stale UI state, or how long background work was affected. The reboot happened earlier in the reported sequence, but I do not know that it caused the pause.

## Earlier continuity concerns

On November 4 at 1:57 AM, I had already reported that the dot seemed reset after an earlier pause of almost two hours. On November 5 at 7:44 PM, I described noticing a pause after returning to the app with Alt+Tab. Those are my observations and concerns, not proof that pausing or Alt+Tab caused data loss.

The dot had separately reported missing working-project/history files and degraded searches. Its later review said that file-availability problem appeared before the earlier automation pause. I cannot verify a common cause between those older problems and the November 6 whole-dot indicator.

I was worried about context loss and asked whether a desktop update or model change could explain the behavior. Neither explanation is established. The November 6 conversation alone does not prove that stored context was deleted.

## Observed sequence, not a deterministic reproduction

1. Continue an existing, multi-stage workflow conversation with a dot that has its own cloud computer.
2. Ask it to use an external development tool on that computer, produce a full plan, and then implement the approved plan.
3. Pause only the recurring search while implementation continues.
4. Ask for completion and phase status. Compare the broad “done” reports with later admissions that planned implementation remains unfinished.
5. Ask where “local” work happened. In this case, the dot initially accepted the PC-related concern, then revised that explanation after checking.
6. Separately, after reporting a dot reboot, observe the desktop status. In this case, the whole-dot “Paused” indicator appeared without an intentional whole-dot pause by me.

I do not have a minimal prompt that reliably reproduces all of this or evidence that these steps will reproduce the pause on another account.

## Expected behavior

- Completion reports should match the approved scope and distinguish implemented, tested offline, tested live, blocked and not started.
- Reading reference guidance or downloading a repository should not be presented as equivalent to installing, activating or using the full tool.
- The dot should identify the cloud computer versus the user's PC explicitly and check evidence before agreeing that it used or planned to use the wrong machine.
- Promised updates should appear in the relevant conversation/reply, with a clear explanation when work stops or needs input.
- The UI should clearly distinguish a paused scheduled task from a paused whole dot. Unexpected pause states need a useful explanation or diagnosable event trail.
- Recovery after a reboot should clearly state what was checked and what remains unknown.

## Evidence and request

Two original screenshots were reviewed privately: the 1:20 PM missing-update view and the 1:29 PM whole-dot pause view. They contain unrelated conversation/sidebar details. No screenshots are attached to this report.

Please investigate task-state reporting, continuation/update delivery, machine identification, and whole-dot pause-state transitions around these timestamps. Please also advise which version information or diagnostic export is needed to investigate further. If these are separate issues, please help split or route them rather than assuming one root cause.

Personal details, account identifiers, private document links, job-application information and unrelated sidebar content have been omitted.

### What feature would you like to see?

Allow existing conversations to be linked into a shared, forum-style project discussion that authorized people, supervisors, worker agents, and connected computers can all view and participate in.

Connected computers should be first-class participants through named local agents, with visible machine identity, connection status, assigned work, and execution results.

### Use case and problem

A maintenance task spans a Linux computer and two Windows PCs. Each computer has its own conversation and execution environment. Sidebar grouping helps find the chats, but supervisors still have to retrieve and reconcile separate histories. Completed work can be missed, checks repeated, and the user becomes the messenger between machines.

Cross-chat retrieval is useful, but the requested workflow is a common discussion and task view where all authorized participants can see the same current decisions, ownership, and verification evidence.

### Proposed behavior

- Link or import selected existing conversations while preserving authors, attachments, timestamps, and source links.
- Provide forum-style replies and subthreads for individual issues or machines, alongside one project overview.
- Let authorized humans, supervisors, worker agents, and connected-computer agents post findings, questions, decisions, handoffs, and results.
- Show which computer executed each action and distinguish verified results from plans or unverified claims.
- Give each work item a visible owner and status to prevent duplicate work.
- Provide mentions and user-controlled completion notifications.
- Maintain a shared decision record and current checklist.
- Keep discussion visibility, agent messaging, repository access, device access, and tool approvals independently permissioned.

### Example

When one computer's agent verifies that a connection repair is complete, the other supervisors and workers should see its result and evidence in the same issue thread, without asking the user to repeat the check or relay a screenshot.

### Related request

Related to #48339. This request specifically emphasizes the forum-style shared conversation UI and connected computers participating as named workers, including coordination among several machines used by the same person, as well as broader team collaboration.

issues.body:
## Summary
Direct Ctrl+V image paste in Codex CLI is unreliable for larger screenshots when using macOS Ghostty → SSH → tmux → headless Ubuntu Linux. Small screenshots work, but larger screenshots consistently fail. This significantly degrades remote, cross-platform AI development workflows where visual UI debugging is frequent.

## Environment
- Local terminal: Ghostty 1.3.1 on macOS
- Remote: Ubuntu Linux VM (headless), accessed via SSH with persistent tmux sessions
- Codex CLI: reproduced on 0.164.0 and 0.166.0
- Clipboard integration: cc-clip 0.13.1, Mac clipboard daemon forwarded to Ubuntu over SSH
- Codex's X11 dependency: Xvfb :0, cc-clip x11-bridge, and loopback-only socat bridge from 127.0.0.1:6000 to /tmp/.X11-unix/X0
- XAUTHORITY configured; all related user systemd services running
- Other terminal coding agents in the same environment can accept screenshots normally.

## Reproduction
1. Start Codex CLI in a remote Ubuntu tmux session over SSH from macOS Ghostty.
2. Copy a small image to the macOS clipboard and press Ctrl+V in Codex. It attaches successfully.
3. Copy a larger screenshot (e.g., full dashboard or screen) and press Ctrl+V in Codex.
4. It fails, frequently with `Failed to paste image: no image on clipboard: The clipboard contents were not available in the requested format or the clipboard is empty.`

## Evidence
- Remote clipboard daemon health endpoint reports status ok.
- `cc-clip paste` on Ubuntu successfully downloads the same PNG from the Mac clipboard.
- Native `/usr/bin/xclip -selection clipboard -t image/png -o` successfully retrieved an entire 4480×2862 PNG in a controlled test.
- Codex's X11 bridge logs repeatedly show large-image INCR transfers followed by timeout after 30 seconds, e.g.:
```
x11-bridge: started INCR transfer (924996 bytes)
x11-bridge: INCR transfer timed out after 30s, clearing stalled transfer
x11-bridge: started INCR transfer (737861 bytes)
x11-bridge: INCR transfer timed out after 30s, clearing stalled transfer
```
- Reproduced in both existing and fresh Codex sessions; not solely tmux session state.
- Underlying Codex Linux sandbox and virtual display connectivity tests pass.

## Expected
Remote image paste should work reliably independent of image size, especially for remote Linux development via SSH/tmux. Ideally Codex would provide an officially supported remote clipboard image transport or configurable image-paste backend that avoids fragile X11 INCR transfer paths.

## Actual
Small images work; large images stall or report no image. Repairing persistent X11 service availability does not fix large-image reliability.

## Impact
High for multi-platform, remote workstation, and screenshot-driven frontend engineering workflows. Users can maintain multiple remote agents in tmux but cannot reliably share screenshots with Codex even though the same client and clipboard work with other coding assistants.

## Related discussions
- #25465 (external clipboard reader for headless environments)
- #19143 (image paste through SSH)
- #19698 (Linux/WSL image clipboard failures)
- #6080 (image pasting)
  
I have omitted hostnames, addresses, project names, usernames and other private environment identifiers.

issues.title: view_image fully decodes large images twice with no pixel limit, so a few A0 plans OOM-kill Codex

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: tool-calls
labels.description: Issues related to tool calling

issues.body:
### What version of Codex CLI is running?

0.163.0 (app-server, driven by the Python SDK). The same code is on `main` at ee80baa38e.

### What subscription do you have?

API key (Azure OpenAI Responses endpoint)

### Which model were you using?

gpt-6.1-sol

### What platform is your computer?

Linux x86_64, a microVM with 2 GiB of memory

### What terminal emulator and version are you using (if applicable)?

None (headless app-server)

### What issue are you seeing?

When the model calls `view_image` on a large raster image, Codex decodes the whole image twice before it scales it down to what the model receives. Nothing checks the pixel count before decoding. `MAX_PROMPT_IMAGE_INPUT_BYTES` (1 GiB) limits only the encoded bytes, and a PNG of a few MB can decode to over 400 MB.

A construction drawing at A0, rendered at 300 dpi, is 9933 × 14043 px, about 420 MB decoded as RGB, and one view decodes it twice. A few such views in one turn, plus the rest of the turn, use up a 2 GiB machine. The kernel then kills Codex, and the SDK raises `TransportClosedError` ("Codex process closed stdout").

We measured real 0.163.0 turns against a fake Responses endpoint, under a cgroup memory limit, reading the app-server's VmHWM:

| Turn | Codex peak |
|---|---|
| Six A0 views, default detail, 2 GiB limit | 1167 MiB |
| Same, each image pre-scaled to the size Codex sends | 529 MiB |
| Two A0 views (PNG + JPEG), `detail: "original"` | 1428 MiB |
| Same, pre-scaled | 257 MiB |
| Six A0 views, 1 GiB limit | Codex OOM-killed |

Root cause:

1. `core/src/tools/handlers/view_image.rs` calls `image::load_from_memory(&file_bytes)` only to reject non-images. That is a full decode (about 420 MB for an RGB A0), and the decoded image is thrown away.
2. `utils/image` `load_for_prompt_bytes_uncached` then decodes the whole image again (`DynamicImage::from_decoder`) before resizing it to at most 2048 px / 2,500 patches (6000 px / 10,000 patches for original detail).
3. `estimate_original_image_bytes` in `core/src/context_manager/history.rs` also uses `image::load_from_memory` on whatever data URL it gets, only to read the width and height. #45777 is related.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Make an A0 plan-sized image:
   ```
   python3 -c "from PIL import Image, ImageDraw; im = Image.new('RGB', (9933, 14043), 'white'); d = ImageDraw.Draw(im); [d.line((x, 0, 9933 - x, 14043), fill='black', width=3) for x in range(0, 9933, 40)]; im.save('plan.png')"
   ```
2. Run Codex in a 1 GiB cgroup, e.g. `docker run --memory 1g --memory-swap 1g ...`, and let the model call `view_image` on six copies of `plan.png` in one turn.
3. In our runs Codex was OOM-killed at 1 GiB, and peaked at 1167 MiB at 2 GiB (table above).

### What is the expected behavior?

Codex's memory for one `view_image` call should be bounded by about one decode of the image. Better, an image too large to decode should get a clear answer to the model (crop the part you need, or render with fewer pixels) instead of ending the process.

### Additional information

Possible fix:

- Validate from the header only:
  ```rust
  ImageReader::new(Cursor::new(&file_bytes)).with_guessed_format()?.into_dimensions()
  ```
  This rejects the same non-images without allocating a pixel buffer.
- Read the width and height the same way in `estimate_original_image_bytes`.
- Before the decode in `load_for_prompt_bytes_uncached`, compare `width × height × bytes per pixel` with a budget, or set `image::Limits` on the reader. An oversized image then fails with a message the model can act on, and the process isn't killed.
- Keep the full decode for the resize. We tried a reduced (DCT-scaled) JPEG decode: it blurred thin drawing lines, about 4 dB PSNR worse than Codex's full decode plus triangle resize.

Our workaround is a `PreToolUse` hook on `view_image`:
- It reads only the header, makes the copy Codex would send (same target size, triangle filter, JPEG q85 or PNG, EXIF and RGB ICC profile kept) in a separate sandboxed process, and rewrites `path` to that copy.
- Codex then passes the copy through unchanged.
- The copy matches Codex's own resize within 1/255 for PNG and 42–44 dB for JPEG.

issues.title: Forked threads get 13 extra tools the parent doesn't have, so the fork can't reuse the parent's prompt cache

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: custom-model
labels.description: Issues related to custom model providers (including local models)

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

labels.name: session
labels.description: Issues involving session (thread) management, resuming, forking, naming, archiving

issues.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.1103.31037 (25241)

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT Pro (plan type `prolite`)

### What platform is your computer?

Darwin 27.2.0 arm64 arm

### What issue are you seeing?

Related to #24704, but a different cause: even with a matching cache key, a fork's prompt would not be cacheable, because the fork's **tool list** differs from the parent's.

A forked thread is sent a different tool list than its parent. In every fork I tested, the fork's requests included **13 tool definitions** that the parent's requests never had. The rest of the request was identical to the parent up to the fork point: system instructions, reasoning items, web-search results, messages between agents, and messages.

The extra tools:

- `codex_app`: `complete_conversational_onboarding_task`, `complete_sidebar_onboarding_checklist_task`, `request_onboarding_input`, `request_option_picker`, `setup_codex_step`, `fire_confetti`, `transfer_voice_call`, `consume_usage_reset`, `request_environment_input`, `finalize_environment`
- Pages (`connector_openai_pages`): `create_presentation`, `execute_artifact_code`, `inspect_artifact`

Tool definitions are at the start of the cached prompt, so a fork can't reuse any of the parent's conversation cache. On a long thread, every fork rewrites the whole history to the cache once.

**Measurements.** Parent and fork requests were captured with a local logging proxy; cache numbers come from the provider's usage records. The model provider is a custom Responses-compatible provider serving Claude models. The proxy translates the tool list one-for-one and cannot add tools.

| Test | Parent tools | Fork tools | Fork's first request: input / cached / written |
|---|---|---|---|
| A. Agent-created thread with a web search and a sub-agent; fork on the same model | 285 | 298 | 187,887 / **0** / 180,558 |
| B. Agent-created thread, one turn; fork with no model or settings override | 285 | 298 | 187,300 / 159,135¹ / 20,833 |
| C. Control: fork of a thread that already had 298 tools | 298 | 298 | 212,135 / **206,668 (97%)** / 1,231 |
| D. Real use: fork of a long user-created thread (~770K tokens) | not logged² | 298 | 773,289 / 190,522¹ / **573,580** |

¹ Cached only up to the end of an entry left by an earlier fork with the same 298 tools, never the parent's own history.
² Not logged; an earlier fork of the same thread cached 0 of 763,499 tokens, consistent with a different tool list.

- Excluding the tool list, the fork's request matched the parent's exactly in tests A and B.
- Control C shows forking itself preserves the cache when the tool lists match.
- Normally started threads (by the user or by an agent) had 285 tools; every fork had 298. The model made no difference (same model on both sides).
- Session metadata also differs: the fork has `thread_source: agent_forked_thread` and extra `runtime_workspace_roots` the parent doesn't have.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Start a thread and complete one turn.
2. Fork it, and send one message on the same model with no settings changes.
3. Compare the `tools` array of the parent's last request with the fork's first request: the fork has the 13 tools above; everything else matches.
4. In the fork's rollout, the first `token_count` shows `cached_input_tokens` covering none of the parent's history.

Session IDs are available on request.

### What is the expected behavior?

A fork sends the same tool list as its parent (or goes through the same filtering as a normal thread start), so its first request only adds new content after an already-cached prefix, as in control C.

### Additional information

- **Likely cause:** the extra tools are all situational (onboarding, setup, voice transfer, cloud environment setup, usage reset, Pages document editing). Normal thread start appears to filter them out; the fork path appears to pass the app's full tool list without that filter.
- **Suggested fix:** carry the parent's resolved tool list into the fork, or apply the same filter. A test asserting that a fork's tool list equals its parent's would catch regressions.
- **Impact:** forking is the natural way to branch a long thread, but each fork currently costs a full cache rewrite (test D: 573,580 tokens written for a one-line follow-up). It affects any provider that caches the prompt prefix; on the OpenAI backend it compounds #24704.
- **Workaround:** none in settings. Avoid forking long threads; start a new thread with a summary instead.

issues.title: Windows Desktop saved app approvals are rejected as unrecognized configuration by Codex 0.159.x

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

issues.body:
### Summary

Codex Desktop on Windows saves persistent Computer Use app decisions in a user-config table that both its installed backend and the separate official CLI reject as an unrecognized setting. Removing the table clears the backend warning, but resets the saved approvals. The Desktop save path can write the same setting again, so deletion is a workaround rather than a fix for saving Always allow decisions.

### Observed versions and platform

- Windows x64.
- Codex Desktop 26.928.20755, build 12246; the configured updater reports up_to_date.
- Embedded backend 0.159.0.
- Separately installed official Codex CLI 0.159.2.

### Actual behavior

The configuration notice identifies this key as ignored:

```text
computer_use.windows.always_allowed_app_ids
```

The installed Desktop reader/writer uses a Boolean table such as:

```toml
[computer_use.windows.always_allowed_app_ids]
"chrome.exe" = true
```

This is valid TOML, with no simultaneous array/table definition. Both installed engines reject the field with strict configuration parsing. The documentation's array form also rejected the field in the local compatibility investigation:

```toml
[computer_use.windows]
always_allowed_app_ids = ["chrome.exe"]
```

The same minimal table, tested in a credential-free temporary CODEX_HOME, fails with either backend from both a repository working directory and an empty working directory: four negative cases. The rejection occurs before RPC initialization or any model request, which helps separate the problem from project configuration or account access.

### Minimal reproduction

1. Use an official installed Codex executable and an empty temporary CODEX_HOME, without copying account credentials.
2. Put the single-app Boolean table above in that home's config.toml.
3. Run the executable with:

   ```text
   codex app-server --strict-config --stdio -c features.remote_control=false
   ```

4. Close standard input without sending any RPC requests. Both observed versions exit with code 1 and identify the unknown configuration field.
5. Replace the file with only `approval_policy = "on-request"` and repeat. Both engines exit with code 0 and no unknown-field notice: two positive controls.

After removing the saved-decision table from the actual local user configuration, both engines also passed strict startup from the actual project directory with empty stdin, exit code 0 and no unknown-field notice. All other configuration bytes and values were preserved. No thread was started and no model request was sent.

### Recurrence and verification limits

Read-only inspection of the installed Desktop save/read paths shows that the writer saves this root table and the reader filters its true entries. The migration path imports the older computer-use/config.toml allow-list into the same setting. Moving approvals back to the old file therefore does not establish a durable fix.

The expected recurrence after selecting Always allow again is supported by that save-path inspection. The complete native Windows GUI remove/approve/restart cycle was **not** empirically replayed in this investigation; it should be included in the product team's regression check. Backend parsing after removal was verified, but a refreshed Desktop settings screenshot was not captured.

### Expected behavior

Please make the Desktop reader, writer, backend schema and migration agree on a supported representation. Existing saved approvals should survive migration and reload without an ignored-setting warning. Saving a new Always allow decision should not recreate the warning. The equivalent Windows exes/aumids access-policy fields should not be treated as a substitute for saved app approvals unless the client explicitly supports that equivalence.

Deleting saved decisions, disabling Computer Use or suppressing all configuration warnings does not resolve the saved-approval compatibility defect.

### Related issue and official documentation

- https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/41556 concerns a conflicting array/table definition and startup loop. This report concerns a valid single definition rejected by the backend, and does not claim that startup-loop behavior.
- https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/computer-use documents persistent Windows app decisions and the array representation.
- https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/changelog lists CLI 0.159.2's Windows console-window fix, with no saved-app-decision schema fix identified in that entry.

Only public version information, a generic single-app configuration and sanitized local observations are included. No full user configuration, account identifiers, credentials, private project content, logs or screenshots are attached.

issues.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

Codex CLI / TUI 0.166.0 on native Windows 10, PowerShell 7, Windows Terminal.

### What feature would you like to see?

Please add an opt-in `config.toml` setting that overrides saved session permissions on resume and restores the behavior I previously relied on: reading the current `approval_policy` and `sandbox_mode` from my config each time I resume a session.

The current behavior of restoring saved session permissions could remain the default. Users who prefer the previous behavior could enable the override below.

### Proposed config override

```toml
# Proposed new setting, not currently supported
resume_permissions_from_config = true
```

Suggested behavior:

- `false` or unset: keep the current behavior of restoring saved session permissions.
- `true`: read and apply the current config's `approval_policy` and `sandbox_mode` on every resume. Saved session values must not override those configured values.

This should cover both fresh resumes and reattachment to an already-loaded thread in the local background server. Explicit CLI permission overrides could retain their normal precedence.

I temporarily enabled Full access for setup work, then restored `sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"` in my config. A normal resume still ran with Full access. This made returning to my normal sandbox settings unexpectedly difficult and required an explicit resume command.

The safety concern is that a user can deliberately restrict access in their config and reasonably expect the next resumed session to use that restriction, while the session still has broader access.

At minimum, please prominently warn when resumed permissions are broader than the current config. Requiring confirmation before restoring Full access in that situation would also help.

### Additional information

### Environment

Observed on 5 November 2026 with Codex CLI 0.166.0 on Windows 10, using PowerShell 7 and Windows Terminal.

### Observed sequence

1. I temporarily enabled Full access for setup work in an existing session.
2. I restored and saved my normal config:

```toml
approval_policy = "never"
sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"
```

3. I exited Codex and resumed the same session using normal `codex resume`, without permission flags.
4. `/status` still showed Full access, despite the saved config specifying `workspace-write`.

### Workaround that succeeded

I exited and resumed the same session with explicit settings:

```powershell
codex --no-daemon resume <session-id> --sandbox workspace-write --ask-for-approval never
```

The resumed session then used `workspace-write` with `approval_policy = "never"`. I subsequently exited again and used normal `codex resume`. It remembered workspace-write, so normal resumes now work for this session.

This shows that I had to replace the saved session permissions through a special launch command before normal resume would retain my intended sandbox mode.

### Related change

Potentially related to https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/57227, which was included in 0.166.0 and preserves acknowledged permissions on resume. I have not isolated that PR as the cause with a before / after version comparison. The successful workaround also changed daemon usage, so it does not isolate daemon behavior from permission restoration.

My request is for an opt-in override that restores this workflow: set the desired approval and sandbox policies in the config, then use normal `codex resume` to apply them. The current default could remain unchanged for users who do not enable `resume_permissions_from_config`.

Every time I launch the interactive TUI (`codex`), it hangs indefinitely on the "Waiting for startup" screen. The UI never recovers, Ctrl+C does nothing, and no error is shown to the user. `codex doctor` reports all checks passing (auth, websocket handshake, reachability, sandbox, etc.) at the very same time the TUI is stuck.


### Environment

- ChatGPT/Codex macOS desktop app 26.1027.61615 (build 24141).
- Built-in browser, local development origin `http://localhost:3145`.

### Problem

Browser Use refuses to observe or connect to an open localhost tab after the user explicitly allowed the exact origin. No new approval prompt appears. Restarting the desktop app and manually adding the site permission did not resolve it. An earlier local preview on port 3144 was accessible.

The returned error includes:

> A saved user permission setting blocks this action.
> The origin approval gate did not grant access for http://localhost:3145.
> A saved permission or managed policy denies access.

### Read-only diagnostic findings

1. The development server is listening on 127.0.0.1:3145 and the user can open the app manually.
2. The documented browser tab inventory lists the expected localhost tab.
3. The user config contains:

```toml
[browser_use.origins."http://localhost:3145"]
access = "allow"
```

4. The global browser permission file (`~/.codex/browser/config.toml`) lists this exact origin under `[origins].allowed`.
5. The current conversation's browser session TOML (`~/.codex/browser/sessions/<conversation-id>.toml`) still contains:

```toml
[origins]
denied = ["http://localhost:3145"]
```

This is consistent with a retained conversation-level denial overriding the user's later global allowance. The internal precedence has not been verified by inspecting implementation code.

### Expected behavior / support request

Provide a supported, user-visible way to revoke the persisted denial for this exact origin in the existing conversation and ask for approval again. Please clarify whether the site permission UI should update or expose conversation-level denial state. If this precedence is intentional, the error should name the denying policy source and offer a supported recovery action.

No permission state was edited or deleted during diagnosis. No alternate origin, port, browser, raw CDP or other control channel was used to evade the denial. No private project files, credentials, conversation transcripts, cookies or raw logs are attached.

Related reports: #49453, #53744, #57102. This report adds the confirmed macOS environment and matching global-allow/session-deny state.

issues.title: Expose the final resumable root conversation on native TUI exit

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: TUI
labels.description: Issues related to the terminal user interface: text input, menus and dialogs, and terminal display

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: session
labels.description: Issues involving session (thread) management, resuming, forking, naming, archiving

issues.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

CLI / native TUI on POSIX systems.

### What feature would you like to see?

A terminal session manager can preserve a Codex terminal, but after that terminal exits it cannot reliably resume the exact conversation selected by its user. `resume --last` can select a different conversation. Terminal footers and per-turn hooks do not provide an authoritative final selection, especially after switching without another turn or viewing a subagent.

This is a feature request for an opt-in, metadata-only result from the native TUI. The normal terminal, configuration, authentication, and session storage should remain unchanged.

#### Proposed contract

For POSIX native TUI launches, accept a writable inherited pipe descriptor N >= 3 and opaque invocation ID, for example `--exit-receipt-fd N --exit-receipt-id ID`. Emit at most one bounded JSON line (maximum 4096 bytes) on that private channel at a successful native UI exit:

```json
{"version":1,"event":"native_tui_exit","invocation_id":"caller-generated-value","provider_version":"supported-version","resume_id":"persisted-root-thread-id","reason":"user_exit"}
```

`resume_id` means the final owning root conversation selected by the TUI and available through normal native resume. It must not be inferred from the last request, a title, a displayed subagent, or a fallback primary ID that no longer establishes selection. Use null when a cleanly closed UI has no resumable conversation. Include a distinct `background_exit` reason for intentional daemon backgrounding; a receipt does not assert that tools or model work stopped.

Freeze or settle selection transitions before taking the final snapshot. Emit only after the frontend shutdown and native persistence/resume-readiness contract succeeds. Intentional background exit must not require terminating the backend or its work. Preserve that explicit choice before it is collapsed into a generic user-requested exit reason. Fatal exits, interrupted shutdown, unresolved selection, and persistence failures must not emit a success receipt. The caller also requires actual process exit 0, matching invocation ID, supported schema/provider version, and exactly one complete record.

The native process must keep the descriptor out of tool, hook, plugin, MCP, and subagent subprocesses. Official launcher hops must explicitly forward only the nominated descriptor and close their extra copy. This is a structured control channel, not authentication against arbitrary code running with the same OS privileges. Validate the descriptor before session startup. Use bounded, nonblocking write handling; a closed reader, EPIPE, full pipe, or partial write must leave the receipt unavailable without hanging or changing the normal terminal exit result. The caller must drain while the process runs with bounded storage, and use a bounded post-exit drain deadline so a leaked writer cannot hang cleanup.

### Additional information

#### Source locations inspected

Pinned Codex 0.166.0 commit `6ff1e1ca3b30fc8b914720681fcf5fe62e95f856`:

- `codex-rs/tui/src/app/exit_summary.rs:25`: builds AppExitInfo, currently preferring widget-selected identity, which can be a subagent. Resolve owning ancestry using parent_thread_id, not forked_from_id, and committed selection from app/thread_routing.rs:216. This guarantee is a requested addition, not an existing exit_info property.
- `codex-rs/tui/src/app/startup.rs:1682–1712`: carries exit information through frontend/backend cleanup. Existing shutdown warnings and the nonempty-file resumability hint in app.rs:506 do not establish the requested persistence acknowledgement.
- `codex-rs/cli/src/main.rs:765`: handle_app_exit formats the human terminal summary; this is a possible final emitter once selection/persistence guarantees are explicit.
- `codex-cli/bin/codex.js`: official JS launcher requires explicit extra-descriptor forwarding. Its ordinary exec/spawn paths do not establish that contract; changing only the Rust emitter is insufficient.

#### Acceptance cases

- Start a saved conversation, exit cleanly, and resume the returned exact ID.
- Switch A→B and exit without sending another prompt; return B.
- Fork and exit; return the root actually selected, not merely the last-created root.
- View a subagent; return its owning selected root, never silently substitute the displayed child ID.
- If no provider-confirmed resumable root exists, return null; an empty but persisted resumable root may return its ID.
- Daemon Background versus Exit; distinguish intent without claiming process cancellation.
- Fatal exit, repeated interrupt during shutdown, persistence failure, and launcher forwarding failure; no eligible success receipt.
- Concurrent independent invocations; no crossed records, leaked descriptors, or terminal text in receipts.

Exit-only receipts solve final resume identity. They do not expose live native selection changes in other windows and therefore do not provide cross-window duplicate-conversation exclusion. That would need a separate live selection contract.

#### Related requests

[App-server lifecycle semantics (#20943)](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/20943) concerns turn/run progress, and [hook parity (#21753)](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/21753) tracks the broader hook surface. This request is narrower: final selected-root resume identity from one native frontend invocation, including selection changes that emit no new turn.

issues.title: Native update_goal fails after external completion of the same goal

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.description: Issues related to tool calling

issues.body:
## Summary

A native `update_goal({"status":"complete"})` call can fail after an external app-server client has already completed the same goal. The completion succeeded, but the agent receives `cannot update goal because this thread has no goal` when it repeats completion.

## Observed integration sequence

1. A CLI worker has an active native goal for delivering its result.
2. An integration stores the worker result and completes that goal through `thread/goal/set` with `status: "complete"`.
3. The runtime emits a completed goal event.
4. The worker then invokes the built-in `update_goal({"status":"complete"})` tool.
5. The tool returns `cannot update goal because this thread has no goal`.

This sequence was reported repeatedly in integration runs on 2026-11-02. Result delivery succeeded; the observed impact is an avoidable failed native tool call after completion, rather than lost work.

## Expected behavior

A repeated completion for the same goal should return an explicit already-completed result without another state change. Preserve the error when there is no active or matching completed goal. A stale completion must not complete a different replacement goal; retain enough goal identity at the native completion boundary to distinguish these cases.

The integration already reports that result delivery completed the goal and that no separate goal update is needed. Repeating the integration's report command is harmless, but this does not change the separate native `update_goal` tool behavior.

## Evidence limits and environment

The installed runtime inspected for this follow-up is official `codex-cli 0.166.0` on Linux x86_64. The observed sequence above comes from prior integration evidence; this report does not claim a fresh model-driven reproduction on 0.166.0. No local Codex patch or direct goal-database modification was used. The public core source tree was checked for the owning goal handler; a local wrapper around the integration cannot intercept this built-in tool.

Related issues #24978 and #38854 cover completed-goal clearing/replacement and goal deletion on resume, respectively. This report concerns completion immediately after an external completion, without a resume step.

### What version of the Codex App are you using?

Windows MSIX package `OpenAI.Codex_26.1103.4239.0_x64`. The Desktop logs report `0.167.0-alpha.3.2` for the local app-server and `0.167.0` for the remote Ubuntu app-server.

### What subscription do you have?

Not provided.

### What platform is your computer?

Windows 11 x64, build `10.0.26200.9711`, with Ubuntu 24.04 LTS on WSL2.

### What issue are you seeing?

On the first launch after updating to 26.1103, Desktop automatically switched from legacy WSL mode to the remote WSL flow. The migration logged `stage=completed` and remote Ubuntu connected, but several existing local chats created in legacy WSL mode failed to open. Desktop tried to resume them through the Windows-native local backend, which rejected saved `/mnt/c/...` workspace roots. File links in affected chats also failed to open.

I created a new troubleshooting chat while the local backend was running in Windows mode. It worked at the time. I then restored legacy WSL mode and restarted Desktop. The affected older chats I checked reopened from their original sidebar entries, but the troubleshooting chat now failed with “Unable to load messages.” The Linux backend rejected the Windows workspace root saved by that chat. Its transcript was still on disk. In an isolated app-server test, the same chat ID resumed and all four turns were readable when I supplied the equivalent Linux working directory and `runtimeWorkspaceRoots`.

After switching back, the composer shows a yellow banner saying that legacy WSL mode is active and inviting me to open WSL connections. Clicking it navigates to `/settings/connections/wsl` according to the Desktop log, but the visible settings page selects the SSH tab and lists only SSH hosts. There is no WSL tab or Ubuntu connection to select.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. On Windows, use Desktop in legacy WSL mode with Ubuntu. Create and use a local project chat with a Linux-form workspace root, for example `/mnt/c/Users/<user>/Desktop/<workspace>`.
2. Update to Desktop 26.1103 and relaunch on an installation enrolled in the remote WSL migration. Confirm that the migration completes and the remote Ubuntu app-server connects.
3. Open the existing chat from its original sidebar entry. Observe that it fails to resume with `-32602` because the Windows-native local app-server rejects the saved WSL workspace root.
4. While the local app-server is Windows-native, create and use a new local chat with the same workspace expressed as a Windows path.
5. Restore legacy WSL mode (`runCodexInWindowsSubsystemForLinux = true`) and restart with that mode retained. In my test I also prevented automatic migration from rerunning on that launch.
6. Open both original chats. The pre-migration chat reopens, while the chat created in step 4 fails because its saved workspace root is now invalid on the Linux backend.
7. Click the composer's **Open WSL connections** banner. Observe that Settings shows the SSH list and offers no WSL connection.

### What is the expected behavior?

After migration and after switching back, existing chats should open and continue from their original sidebar entries, with file links resolving in the correct environment. Desktop should route a chat to a compatible backend or translate its saved workspace roots before calling `thread/resume`. If the migration cannot preserve access, Desktop should keep the previous mode and explain why. The banner should open a usable WSL connection screen or explain why WSL connections are unavailable.

Environment:
  - OS: Ubuntu 22.04.1 LTS
  - Codex CLI: 0.166.0
  - Architecture: x86_64
  - Terminal session: tty
 
  Steps to reproduce:
  1. Start Codex CLI in the terminal.
  2. Use the mouse to select text in the Codex output.
  3. Right-click, or press Ctrl+Shift+C.
  4. Try to paste into the Codex input box with Ctrl+Shift+V.
 
  Expected behavior:
  - The terminal copy menu should be available, or the selected text should be pasted into the Codex input box.
 
  Actual behavior:
  - While Codex is running, the terminal right-click menu is unavailable because Codex captures mouse events.
  - Codex displays "Copy sent to terminal", but Ctrl+Shift+V does not paste the selected text.
  - Holding Shift while selecting text bypasses Codex's mouse handling and makes the terminal copy menu work.
 
  This appears to be a terminal mouse handling / clipboard integration compatibility issue.

issues.title: TUI: dark-on-dark prompt input with ServerBox on Android + tmux in light theme

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: TUI
labels.description: Issues related to the terminal user interface: text input, menus and dialogs, and terminal display

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

issues.body:
### What version of Codex CLI is running?

`codex-cli 0.163.0`. This report describes the installed version; reproduction on the latest release has not yet been verified.

### What subscription do you have?

Not provided.

### Which model were you using?

The problem concerns the TUI composer rendering, before a prompt is submitted.

### What platform is your computer?

- Client: Android, using ServerBox over SSH.
- Remote host running Codex: Debian GNU/Linux 13 (trixie), x86_64.
- Multiplexer: tmux 3.5a.

### What terminal emulator and version are you using?

ServerBox on Android; the exact ServerBox and Android versions have not been recorded.

The terminal theme follows the system theme, which was **light** when the problem occurred.

- Outside tmux: `TERM=xterm-256color`.
- Inside tmux: `TERM=tmux-256color`.

Connection path: **ServerBox on Android → SSH → tmux → Codex CLI**.

### Codex doctor report

Not attached. The targeted terminal observations below were collected instead.

### What issue are you seeing?

The Codex question/prompt input field has a dark background, while the typed text also remains dark. The resulting dark-on-dark contrast makes the input very difficult to read.

Using Codex outside tmux through the same client displays the background normally. The problem is visible in the tmux sessions.

Reconnecting ServerBox to a persistent tmux session does not resolve it: the existing Codex process continues running with its previous rendering state.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Connect to a Linux host using ServerBox on Android.
2. Use the system-following terminal theme while the system is in light mode.
3. Start or attach to a tmux session and run Codex CLI.
4. Type into the prompt composer.
5. Observe the dark input background together with dark text.
6. Compare with Codex launched outside tmux, where the background appears normal in this setup.

The affected sessions were long-running. The exact initial trigger, including whether an earlier theme change contributed, has not been isolated.

### What is the expected behavior?

The composer should remain readable with the terminal's light theme, including over SSH and inside tmux. If Codex cannot determine the terminal background, it should use a fallback that preserves foreground/background contrast rather than combining a forced dark background with the terminal's default dark text.

### Additional information

#### Observations from the affected environment

- Captured tmux output contained `ESC[48;5;234m` for the dark background, while the foreground used the terminal default.
- A separate probe inside an attached tmux session sent OSC 10/11 foreground/background queries and received no replies within a two-second timeout.
- This suggests that unavailable terminal color information may be involved. It does **not** establish whether the missing response originates in ServerBox, tmux, or their interaction.

#### Workarounds tested

For an already-running affected pane, overriding palette entry 234 to the terminal default and refreshing the client restored readability without restarting Codex:

```sh
# Run in the affected tmux pane, or supply its pane ID from another shell.
tmux set-option -p -t "$TMUX_PANE" 'pane-colours[234]' default
tmux refresh-client
```

This is a local workaround, not a proposed general fix: it remaps that palette entry throughout the pane and could affect other content using the same color. It can be undone with:

```sh
tmux set-option -pu -t "$TMUX_PANE" 'pane-colours[234]'
```

For a new Codex process inside tmux, `FORCE_COLOR=1 codex` was also tested in a separate window. The explicit dark composer background disappeared, while colored foreground highlighting remained. This workaround changes the color mode and is not equivalent to fixing terminal theme detection.

Neither ServerBox nor tmux source code was modified.

A similar dark-on-dark composer symptom is reported in #41242, but that report concerns Windows Terminal. This report adds the **ServerBox on Android + SSH + tmux** environment; the underlying cause may differ.

issues.body:
### What is the type of issue?
Documentation is missing / confusing.

### What is the issue?
What is the smallest supported way to run `codex exec` as a text-only adviser using existing ChatGPT sign-in, with no model-accessible tools and no tool execution?

The locally reported installation is `codex-cli 0.154.0`, native Windows x64. This is a documentation/configuration investigation; no model-inference verification has been performed.

Required scope: command execution, file editing (including `apply_patch`), image/web/browser/computer tools, collaboration, MCP, apps/plugins, and notification/hook commands. A read-only filesystem sandbox or an instruction asking the model not to use tools does not satisfy this requirement.

Evidence inspected:
- The official configuration reference documents `features.shell_tool` as enabling command execution tools, but does not establish an exhaustive all-tools-off configuration.
- In the official `rust-v0.154.0` config schema, `ToolsToml` contains `experimental_request_user_input`, `update_plan`, and `web_search`; it does not expose `tools.disable_defaults`.
- PR #14525 proposed grouped builtin-tool controls and `tools.disable_defaults`, but is closed and unmerged. We therefore are not treating it as a released solution.
- Related requests: #52780 (app-server text-only worker contract) and #53024 (no-tools startup/event reporting).

Please provide either:
1. An exact supported invocation/configuration for 0.154.0, including interaction with `--ignore-user-config` and coverage of the above capabilities; or
2. The precise supported version/interface that provides this, or explicit confirmation that no such CLI configuration is available.

A credential-free, non-inference verification method for the effective tool set would also help. We are seeking a supported approach within existing ChatGPT usage, rather than switching to separately billed API use.

### Where did you find it?
- https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/config-file/config-reference
- https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/developer-commands?surface=cli
- https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.154.0/codex-rs/core/config.schema.json
- https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/14525

No private paths, project source, credentials, customer data, or session transcripts are included.

labels.name: bug

labels.name: auth

labels.name: dots

issues.body:
### What issue are you seeing?

On 7 November 2026, reading an existing task previously used for desktop work returned `TaskComputerNotAuthorizedError`, with `FORBIDDEN` and `task_computer_not_authorized`. The same task had been readable earlier that day.

The supported environment listing still reported the relevant desktop as connected. A supported project-listing operation for that exact environment succeeded with an empty projects array. A subsequent bounded read of the existing task nevertheless returned:

```text
TaskComputerNotAuthorizedError: This task's environment is not authorized or its access could not be verified. Check your dot's computer access before retrying.
error_code: FORBIDDEN
error_data.type: task_computer_not_authorized
```

Successful metadata access does not establish task-specific authorization. Connected status alone is not a general authorization or health guarantee.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

This is the observed sequence, not a clean-room reproduction:
1. Read an existing desktop-work task successfully.
2. Later, attempt to read that same task and receive the error above.
3. Check the supported environment listing: the desktop is connected.
4. Check the supported project-listing operation for that environment: it succeeds with an empty array.
5. Make one bounded task-read check after those metadata checks: the same authorization error is returned.

The investigation stopped after that rejection. No alternate UI/CLI route was used to access the blocked task, and no credentials, security settings or permissions were changed as part of this investigation.

### What is the expected behavior?

The task should remain readable when its access is authorized, or the error should identify the specific missing prerequisite and a supported way to resolve it.

Please clarify how to verify or repair task-specific computer authorization while preserving the original task and workspace. If this reflects an authorization or routing inconsistency, please provide a supported recovery path.

### Additional information

issues.title: Support restoring goals with zero remaining token budget

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

issues.body:
I’m recovering native goals into another Codex home. An exhausted source goal has zero remaining budget, but `thread/goal/set` rejects zero. Could the App Server expose a way to restore that state without granting fresh allowance?

Using the CLI App Server on Linux with Codex 0.166.0, a controlled source snapshot with a budget of 225 and usage of 225 leaves zero tokens. The receiving goal must preserve that limit. A new goal starts its usage counter at zero, so restoring the original positive budget would grant fresh allowance.

1. Create a disposable thread through the App Server and retain its ID.
2. Send the following request with that ID; the server returns error `-32600`.

```json
{
  "id": 3,
  "method": "thread/goal/set",
  "params": {
    "threadId": "<thread-id>",
    "objective": "Continue a bounded task.",
    "status": "paused",
    "tokenBudget": 0,
    "origin": "automatic"
  }
}
```

The error message is `goal budgets must be positive when provided`. Reading the goal after a server restart returns `null`. Using `budgetLimited` instead of `paused` gives the same error. A remaining finite budget of 20 and an absent budget both restore correctly across restart.

The needed behaviour is to preserve the objective and zero remaining allowance without starting continuation. Neither a positive replacement budget nor an unlimited budget preserves the source limit. Forking an existing native goal preserves its accounting, but that requires the goal to exist in the receiving home already.

The [0.166 validator](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/6ff1e1ca3b30fc8b914720681fcf5fe62e95f856/codex-rs/ext/goal/src/tool.rs#L427-L445) rejects non-positive values. The [public request](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/6ff1e1ca3b30fc8b914720681fcf5fe62e95f856/codex-rs/app-server-protocol/schema/typescript/v2/ThreadGoalSetParams.ts#L7-L11) has no used-token counter. Current main also retains the zero-budget rejection.
