It may be binary or too large.”** The Gateway reported a read failure, not an unsupported format or excessive size. This sends the user toward changing the file instead of checking its availability. ### Steps to reproduce 1. Put a small UTF-8 `Project notes.txt` in a test agent's workspace and open **Files** in iOS. 2. After its directory entry loads, temporarily move the file out of that workspace on the test Gateway. 3. Open the still-listed `Project notes.txt` entry. The Gateway returns `workspace_file_not_found`. 4. Restore the same file, go back to the directory, and open it again as a success control. The native run below emulates this one-time missing-file response through an isolated protocol fixture. No files were removed from a daily Gateway. ### Expected behavior Explain that the file could not be read or is unavailable. Reserve size/format guidance for errors that actually indicate those conditions. The existing Gateway contract already distinguishes missing, oversized, and unsupported files; no new protocol or preview limit is needed. ### Actual behavior The missing-file response becomes the binary/too-large message. There is no Retry action in the preview. Returning to the folder and reopening after the file is available shows the text on unchanged app code. This control is not a fix. ### OpenClaw version iOS Debug **2026.10.10 (1193)** at `b6bea62cd79b458b3c72b7622381180563cb057e`, which includes an unrelated conversation-artifacts proposal. The affected `AgentWorkspaceFilesScreen.swift` is byte-identical to upstream `8a34fd4688c9e43a583e281134149f4e728fce98`. Not an App Store reproduction. ### Operating system iPhone 17 Simulator, iOS 27.0; Xcode 27.2 (27B52), English, Light appearance. ### Install method Locally compiled Debug app; XCTest drives the native Files UI against an isolated loopback protocol fixture. ### Model Not applicable; no inference. ### Provider / routing chain iOS Files → `agents.workspace.get` → controlled response matching the Gateway's missing-file contract. ### Logs ```text 08:56:54.165Z agents.workspace.get "Project notes.txt" → INVALID_REQUEST, "workspace file not found" → details.type: workspace_file_not_found 08:56:58.719Z agents.workspace.get "Project notes.txt" → success, text/plain, utf8, 52 bytes ``` The file bytes in the successful control have SHA-256 `99fa98ba5dcc934ba194674e681e041f3013edda1f0b15159a4e902c83dd631c`. The two directory reads succeeded; there were two initial socket connects and no `chat.send`. Only the first file read was refused. This is native-client evidence with an emulated Gateway response, not a production outage or full-Gateway execution. ### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence Original Light-mode XCTest captures, English, iPhone 17 Simulator. Full frames, no annotations or mockups; Debug, not App Store. The second image is a success control on unchanged code. | Missing-file response | Same file available after returning and reopening | | --- | --- | | | | One valid native observation run passed in **33.591 s** (60.265 s Xcode test operation). Assertions cover the wrong guidance, no Retry/Try Again control, disabled Share during failure, and rendered text with Share enabled after reopening. This test asserts the reported defect and its control; it is not a red/green fix test. ### Impact and severity Incorrect recovery guidance when a listed workspace file becomes unavailable, for example after it is moved by the user or an agent. The preview cannot determine that the file is binary or oversized from this response. This report does not claim data loss or a network failure. Normal-use frequency and App Store impact have not been measured. ### Additional information [`AgentWorkspaceFilePreview.load`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/8a34fd4688c9e43a583e281134149f4e728fce98/apps/ios/Sources/Design/AgentWorkspaceFilesScreen.swift#L320) maps every thrown error to the same format/size hint. The [Gateway read owner](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/8a34fd4688c9e43a583e281134149f4e728fce98/src/gateway/server-methods/agents-workspace.ts#L150) instead reports `workspace_file_not_found`, `workspace_file_too_large`, and `workspace_file_unsupported` separately. A focused repair can give truthful read-failure feedback while retaining appropriate format/size guidance and existing path protections. A local Retry is one possible recovery improvement; automatic reconnect, new formats, a higher size limit, and an editor are outside this report. A regression should distinguish a missing-file response from a genuine unsupported/too-large response, and allow a later successful read without retaining stale preview bytes. I checked open and closed issues/PRs for the preview type, exact message, RPC, and missing-file error; no exact equivalent was found in that search. #100767 introduced Files and contains related directory-load recovery feedback; this report concerns the file preview's error classification. #144884 proposes configurable preview limits and does not change this Swift error handler.

issues.body:
### Summary

Since plugin generation capture landed (#144252, first shipped in 2026.9.6), a Gateway with an external or workspace plugin that has a large package or dependency tree blocks its event loop for minutes. It happens at startup, and again whenever the prepared model runtime republishes. While the loop is blocked the Gateway accepts TCP connections but answers nothing, including `/healthz`, WebSocket RPCs and channel polling.

`capturePluginGenerationArtifact` (`src/plugins/plugin-generation-artifact.ts`) copies the plugin package synchronously on the main thread. When no `entryFile` is set, `copyPackage` copies the whole root. It then walks and copies the dependency tree through `capturePluginDependencies` → `linkDependency` → `copyPackage` → `copy`.

### Evidence

**Isolated repro on origin/main `4d4d99d`**, using a synthetic 878 MB context-engine plugin:
- The Gateway stalls for 219 s before it starts listening, then for another 168 s.
- It logs `prepared model runtime startup degraded after 120000ms (workspace plugins; agent main)`.

**Production Gateway on 2026.9.6.** The plugin root is a Bun global install: a 134 MB package whose sibling `node_modules` hold 1.5 GB across 221 packages.
- **Startup:** the process started at T+0 and logged `http server listening` at T+2m20s. `/healthz` timed out until about T+7m.
- **Stacks:** four inspector samples taken during the hang all show the same stack:
  ```
  realpathSync / path.join
  ← pluginNativeNamespaceMemberPath / resolvePreparedSource
  ← copy (recursive)
  ← materialize ← copyPackage ← linkDependency ← capturePluginDependencies ← captureDependencies
  ← materialize ← copyPackage ← capturePluginGenerationArtifact
  ← bindPluginInstanceModuleLoader ← loadPluginModule ← loadRuntimePluginCandidate
  ```
- **Earlier, during a prepared-runtime republish:**
  - The event loop was blocked for 124 s (`eventLoopDelayMaxMs=124352`).
  - Telegram polling stalled.
  - `config.patch` took 125 s and returned `UNAVAILABLE`, followed by `prepared model runtime reload failed after config commit: prepared model runtime publication (workspace plugins; agent main) timed out; restarting gateway`.
  - The Gateway then restarted, and startup blocked again.
  - Separately, the Control UI's provider sign-in stayed on a blank tab for the whole outage. That is covered by #160954.

A `thinkingDefault` patch alone hot-applies in 50 ms in the isolated repro. The republish in production was probably already pending. Candidate cause: #160120, a refresh loop triggered by an auth profile that fails to resolve. That link is being verified.

### Impact

- Any install with a large external or workspace plugin.
- The Gateway becomes unreachable for minutes on every startup and on every prepared-runtime republish.
- Config hot reloads can escalate into restarts, which block again.
- 2026.7.35 is not affected; 2026.9.6 (npm `latest`/`beta`) is.

### Expected

Capture should not block the Gateway event loop for more than a bounded time. An unchanged plugin should reuse its existing capture instead of being recopied.

prs.title: fix(worker): reject non-UTF-8 Git paths in the workspace manifest
prs.body:
Related: #191574

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: a workspace capture reports success while the worker receives a workspace without a tracked file whose name is not valid UTF-8.

`git ls-files -z` returns names as bytes, and two decodes on the capture path turned them into strings: `bad\xff.txt` becomes `bad\uFFFD.txt`, the `lstat` for that spelling misses, and both owners read the miss as "nothing to do".

- Gateway transfer inventory: `readBoundedGitPathCandidates()` yielded the replacement spelling and `inspectFile()` stat'd it, so the file never entered the rsync `--files-from` list.
- Worker manifest script: `nulPaths()` decoded the whole list, `addEntry()` missed the same way, and the published inventory omitted the file while exiting 0.

On `4045f09b701` a built Gateway and a real node worker show the whole failure: `sessions.dispatch` returns `ok: true` with an `active` placement while the worker's workspace holds 2 of the 3 files.

## User Impact

- An existing tracked file whose bytes cannot be a manifest path stops the capture before any transfer with `worker workspace Git paths must be UTF-8; rename the invalid path before retrying`, the wording and policy [local-workspace-inventory.ts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/deed97ef3866dd49e6b7029e921d6fef8d7438eb/src/gateway/worker-environments/local-workspace-inventory.ts) already uses; renaming the path and retrying dispatches normally.
- A Git name whose file a reclaim already removed stays a deletion, and an ignored file nothing selects captures as before, even when a valid tracked file carries its replacement spelling.
- Valid UTF-8 workspaces are unaffected. When both `bad\uFFFD.txt` and `bad<0xff>.txt` are tracked, capture refuses instead of transferring one and dropping the other.

## Why This Change Was Made

- `readBoundedGitPathCandidates()` yields each name with the bytes Git reported and `inspectFile()` merges `selected` and `ignored` by those bytes. The refusal runs before the decoded-name dedupe because a valid `U+FFFD` file can claim that spelling first and hide the file holding the invalid bytes; a name whose file is gone stays a deletion.
- [workspace-sync-scripts.ts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/deed97ef3866dd49e6b7029e921d6fef8d7438eb/src/gateway/worker-environments/workspace-sync-scripts.ts) mirrors it in the generated script: `nulPaths()` records undecodable names per list, so only a name the capture admits (the index, or `.worktreeinclude`) fails, while a plain ignored name cannot fail the tracked file spelled the same; a staged input selected out of the ignored list still refuses.
- Both generated assets come from `pnpm runtime:scripts:gen`, never hand-edited; the added test lines are recorded in [undecodable-workspace-git-paths.txt](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/deed97ef3866dd49e6b7029e921d6fef8d7438eb/config/test-lines-allocations/undecodable-workspace-git-paths.txt).
- Gap: a complete (`walk`) capture is unreachable through `sessions.dispatch` (session worktree, repository workspace, or a device folder that transfers nothing), so it rides on the committed test.

## Evidence

Each arm builds that commit (`pnpm build`) and runs an isolated Gateway (`node dist/index.js gateway run`) plus a real node worker (`node dist/index.js node run`) paired over the tunnel; a fixture repository commits `README.md`, `tracked.txt` and `bad<0xff>.txt`, and `sessions.dispatch` sends a worktree of `main` to the node.

```
# head deed97ef386 — OpenClaw 2026.10.10 (deed97e)
$ git -C .../worktrees/proof-indexed-head ls-files -z | od -c
0000000   R   E   A   D   M   E   .   m   d  \0   b   a   d 377   .   t
0000020   x   t  \0   t   r   a   c   k   e   d   .   t   x   t  \0
{"ok":false,"error":{"code":"INVALID_REQUEST","message":"worker workspace Git paths must be UTF-8; rename the invalid path before retrying","retryable":false}}
--- exit: 1
remote workspace: <none>
[ws] ⇄ res ✗ sessions.dispatch 252ms errorCode=INVALID_REQUEST errorMessage=worker workspace Git paths must be UTF-8; rename the invalid path before retrying
```

```
# base 4045f09b701 — OpenClaw 2026.10.10 (4045f09)
{"ok":true,"placement":{"state":"active","workerBundleHash":"8f402f5f...","workspaceBaseManifestRef":"sha256:8d0d180f..."}}
--- exit: 0
$ ls -b .../workspaces/d5d094f593e66f7c/0f8c924116116735f1e4f081fe60882b/2
README.md
tracked.txt
```

```
# head deed97ef386, after `git mv bad<0xff>.txt bad.txt`
{"ok":true,"placement":{"state":"active","workerBundleHash":"10dc7c75...","workspaceBaseManifestRef":"sha256:aef6c9ea..."}}
--- exit: 0
$ ls -b .../workspaces/ceec64aa07caeec8/44d00024b9be203c1c176b1e8c04e28d/2
README.md
bad.txt
tracked.txt
```

- [workspace-sync-inventory.test.ts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/deed97ef3866dd49e6b7029e921d6fef8d7438eb/src/gateway/worker-environments/workspace-sync-inventory.test.ts): `refuses a transfer list when an existing Git path is not UTF-8` and `refuses a transfer list when a valid file already claimed the spelled name` are red without the guard (`promise resolved "…/inventory" instead of rejecting`) and green with it.
- [workspace-sync-manifest.test.ts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/deed97ef3866dd49e6b7029e921d6fef8d7438eb/src/gateway/worker-environments/workspace-sync-manifest.test.ts): `admits a tracked file whose spelled name an unselected path shares` is red without the split (`Error: worker workspace Git paths must be UTF-8…`, capture exit 1) and green with it; `rejects undecodable Git paths only when capture admits them` covers the index side.
- Five affected worker-environments suites → 69 tests passed.
- Surface: 465 added, 79 removed lines across 8 files (source +139/−27, tests +176, generated +148/−52, allocation +2).
- `runtime:scripts:check`, `oxfmt --check`, `oxlint` (0 warnings, 0 errors) and `git diff --check` all clean.
- `check:test-lines-ratchet --base 4045f09b701` → `Test lines OK: 6479735; ceiling: 6479735; slack: 0`.
- Gap: the targeted `tsgo` typecheck cannot run on this host (pinned `@tsrs` needs glibc 2.29, host has 2.28); CI runs it for this head.

prs.title: fix(signal): inbound message bursts pile up in memory and are lost on restart
prs.body:
Related: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/127383

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: a burst of inbound Signal messages piles up in Gateway memory, and is lost on restart or crash, because each message waits for its own database write and drain pass before the next one is stored.

This addresses part of the linked issue: the lasting pile-up and the loss. It adds no bound on memory (see the accepted edge cases below), so the bound that issue asks for stays open there.

## User Impact

User impact: a Signal account that receives a large burst (signal-cli pulling its backlog after a reconnect, or a busy group) moves the whole burst into the durable inbound queue within seconds. Nothing is dropped. A restart, shutdown or crash right after the burst loses none of the messages OpenClaw has read, and they are delivered in order, as before. Delivering a backlog of that size is slow, though; see the drain follow-up under Not covered.

This replaces the earlier revision of this PR, which paused the WebSocket while a message was stored. The signal-cli-rest-api container drops messages for a client that does not keep up (see Evidence), so the client must keep reading at full speed and the backlog has to go to the durable queue, not back to the container.

## Why This Change Was Made

On `main`, the Signal receive handler awaits `admit` for one event and then `waitForPumpIdle`, a full drain pass, before the client hands it the next frame. That is about 55 messages per second here. Everything the socket reads in the meantime stays in the client's promise chain, in memory, until its turn.

Now:
- The container client hands each decoded frame to the receive handler in arrival order without waiting for earlier ones. A shared promise still joins them for close and failure.
- The Signal ingress groups the events that arrive while one append runs into the next `admitBatch` transaction (up to 10,000 rows, about 0.4 s). Receive settles at the durable append; claiming and dispatch run on the drain as before. If a batch append fails, its events are appended one by one, so only the event that cannot be stored (or all of them, if the store is down) rejects.
- A graceful stop first appends every event the socket already read, then stops the monitor. If that takes longer than the client's 1.5 s shutdown wait, the client log now says the ingress stop still stores the events, instead of "messages may be lost".

The per-receive `waitForPumpIdle` came from https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/111449, so that messages accepted just before shutdown were not abandoned before their durable claim. `monitor.stop()` already awaits the admission tail and the pump before it returns, so that shutdown guarantee stays. A row appended just before stop is not claimed in that process, but it is durable and is claimed on the next start.

Batching needs one fix in shared admission: pending rows drain by `(receivedAt, eventId)`, and one batch shares one `receivedAt`. In a group lane, event ids come from different senders, so a lane's arrival order need not be its id order. Admission now steps `receivedAt` by 1 ms when a lane's next event would sort ahead of its previous one, and a later admission never ties an earlier one. Every lane drains in arrival order. The SDK docs for `admitBatch` now say so.

Accepted edge cases, also named in the code:
- There is no bound on received events waiting in memory. While SQLite keeps up, the wait is short: the 100,000-frame burst below was durable in 7.6 s. If the state database stalls (full disk, broken database), later events wait in memory without limit, as they do on `main`. A bound would have to drop events or stop reading. Dropping recreates the loss this PR removes, and the container has no flow control: a client that stops reading makes the container drop instead (see Evidence). So the stall is made visible instead of bounded: past 50,000 waiting events (about 200 MiB of decoded messages) the ingress logs one error naming the state database, and logs again if the backlog drops and comes back. Nothing is dropped.
- The stepped `receivedAt` can run ahead of wall time for a very large group burst (1 ms for each out-of-order event, about 14 s for 100,000 frames from 7 senders). The step is kept in memory only. If the Gateway restarts inside that window, a new message in the same group can drain ahead of older backlog rows of that group. This is rare and visible, and nothing is lost. Matrix seeds its own arrival time from the queue at start; shared admission does not, because a read at every start is not worth this case.

## Evidence

Tested at `377edf16faf` (base `upstream/main` `210d3df7f65`). The measurements were taken at `eda993f7f21`. Since then, a variable rename, test assertions and comments, an SDK docs sentence, the shutdown log wording, `waitForIdle` and the test-lines allocation below changed; none of them touches the measured path.

Harness: the plugin's real `streamContainerEvents` client and real `startSignalIngressMonitor`, writing to a real SQLite state database in an isolated state directory. Node 24, Linux x64. A local `ws` server in a worker thread stands in for the container's `/v1/receive` endpoint and sends synthetic receive frames of about 1 KB. The agent dispatch handler holds the first event, so the numbers measure receiving and storing. No Signal account.

100,000 frames, one direct-message lane: base stored 4,939 in 90 s; this PR stored all 100,000 in 7.6 s.

<details><summary>100,000-frame table</summary>

| | base | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| frames read by the client | 100,000 | 100,000 |
| durable in SQLite | 4,939 after 90 s | 100,000 after 7.6 s |
| heap growth | +129.4 MiB, still held at 90 s | peak +344 MiB during the first second, back to −1.3 MiB at 8 s |
| graceful stop | 93,207 receives failed with "Channel ingress monitor is stopped"; drain timed out, "messages may be lost" | nothing waiting |

</details>

The same run with 7 senders in one group lane: all 100,000 durable after 7.7 s, rows in arrival order, heap back to −1.3 MiB. The backlog warning fired once in both runs. The higher transient peak is the decoded burst plus the batch being written; on `main` the same burst stays in memory for as long as it takes to store at about 55 per second (about 30 minutes for 100,000).

Crash (`kill -9` mid-burst, then reopen the state directory and count rows):
- This PR: killed at 1.35 s with 31,046 receives settled. After restart, SQLite has 31,046 rows, contiguous from the first frame. Every appended frame survived.
- Base: at 30.9 s only 3,000 were durable while all 100,000 had been read. After restart, 3,001 rows; the other 96,999 were only in memory.

Delivery order after release, 2,000 frames, 7 senders in one group lane: both sides delivered 2,000 of 2,000 in order per lane (base 24.4 s, this PR 23.9 s), so dispatch speed is unchanged.

Real container: `bbernhard/signal-cli-rest-api:latest` (0.101) in json-rpc mode, with the signal-cli daemon inside it replaced by a synthetic JSON-RPC stand-in that sends receive notifications. The container itself drops messages. Its JSON-RPC reader hands each notification to the WebSocket handler with a non-blocking send, and drops it when the channel cannot take it:
- At 0.101, the image used here and the latest release, the receive channel is unbuffered ([`jsonrpc2.go` line 276](https://github.com/bbernhard/signal-cli-rest-api/blob/0.101/src/client/jsonrpc2.go#L276)), so a notification that arrives while the handler is still writing the previous one is dropped, however fast the client reads.
- At https://github.com/bbernhard/signal-cli-rest-api/commit/787d204e155d0c73840a615a5e90c697bacaa6f1 on `master`, the channel holds 64 entries ([line 378](https://github.com/bbernhard/signal-cli-rest-api/blob/787d204e155d0c73840a615a5e90c697bacaa6f1/src/client/jsonrpc2.go#L378)). The buffer came with https://github.com/bbernhard/signal-cli-rest-api/commit/ad0c2310325154b59b8bb5523e29a132a82326f8 (a manual receive mode) and is in no release yet. Once 64 are waiting behind the handler's write, the next one is dropped the same way.

In both versions, a client that pauses keeps the handler's write blocked, and every notification after that is dropped. That is why this PR keeps reading.

Measured through the container (0.101):
- 100,000 notifications at full speed: the container passed about 13,500 to OpenClaw on both sides. This PR stored all 13,594 it received, with +0.7 MiB heap. Base had stored 2,851 of 13,465 after 30 s, and its stop timed out with "messages may be lost".
- Paced at 20 notifications every 10 ms (20,000): the container still passed only 2,514; this PR stored all of them.
- One notification every 10 ms (2,000): this PR received, stored and delivered all 2,000 in order.

That loss is in the container and needs an upstream fix.

Regression tests (each fails on base and passes with this PR; the other tests in these files pass on both):
- `extensions/signal/src/signal-ingress.test.ts`, "appends a burst of received events in a few transactions, not one each": 50 concurrent receives, at most 2 appends. Base: `expected 50 to be less than or equal to 2`.
- `src/channels/message/ingress-monitor.admission.test.ts`, "keeps each lane in arrival order when event ids do not sort that way". Base drains the lane as `sender-a:0, sender-a:2, sender-b:1`.
- `extensions/signal/src/client-container.websocket.test.ts`, "drains accepted and socket-buffered events before resolving shutdown", now also asserts that frame 2 reaches the receive handler while frame 1 is still held. Base: `expected [ 1 ] to deeply equal [ 1, 2 ]`.

Checks:
- The touched test files pass.
- So do the other durable-ingress suites in `src/channels/message`, and the consumers of shared admission: Signal (`extensions/signal/src`, 37 files), LINE `webhook-spool`, Matrix `monitor/ingress` and Telegram `polling-session`.
- `pnpm check:changed` against the base passes typecheck, the source ratchets (including the SQLite worker and dialect ratchets) and lint on the changed files. It is red only outside this diff: the changelog attribution guard on existing `CHANGELOG/records/2026.11.1.md` lines, the unused-export scan on `extensions/deep-research`, and the format lane on untracked local scratch files.

<details><summary>Test cost</summary>

Test cost (`pnpm test <file> --maxWorkers=1`, local; CI seconds come from this PR's run):

| Test file | local | new test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `extensions/signal/src/signal-ingress.test.ts` | 11.3 s (9 tests) | 574 ms |
| `src/channels/message/ingress-monitor.admission.test.ts` | 4.7 s (18 tests) | 114 ms |

</details>

Test-lines ratchet: `main` had 4 lines of slack and these regressions add 51, so this PR adds `config/test-lines-allocations/signal-receive-batch-order.txt` for exactly those 51 lines and leaves the shared baseline unchanged. `scripts/check-test-lines-ratchet.mts --base 210d3df7f65` passes (slack 4).

Simplify pass: no further changes. Every hunk serves the fix, and each test catches a named failure. Against `main`: production +96/−18 (Signal client +10/−6, Signal ingress +58/−5, shared admission +28/−7), tests +53/−2 (net +51), plus the two-line allocation record and two lines of SDK docs. The earlier socket-pause revision and its loopback test are gone.

Not covered:
- A real Signal account or a real signal-cli daemon; the container run uses a synthetic daemon stand-in.
- A full Gateway with a real agent and model: dispatch is held, because the change is in receiving and storing.
- Delivering a very large backlog, which this PR makes reachable. Because it stores the whole burst, the shared ingress drain can now face 100,000 pending rows, and each drain pass lists every pending row (about 3.3 s at 100,000 rows). With the 100,000-frame burst stored, 65 rows were delivered in 120 s (66 in a second run). On `main` the same burst never gets there: that run stored only 6,328 rows and delivered 4,399 of them, and the rest of the burst was still in memory when the run stopped, so it was lost. "Lost" becomes "stored and delivered slowly". The drain cost is a follow-up in the shared ingress drain, not part of this PR.

prs.title: fix(ui): keep a session row highlighted while its context menu is open
prs.body:
## Problem

Fixes: when you right-click a session in the Control UI sidebar, the row loses its highlight as soon as the pointer moves onto the menu, so nothing shows which session the menu acts on.

## User Impact

User impact: the session row keeps its hover highlight while its context menu is open, so it's clear which session Pin, Rename, Archive and the other actions apply to.

## Why This Change Was Made

Session rows and catalog rows already track whether their menu is open (for `aria-expanded`). They now also set a `sidebar-recent-session--menu-open` class. In the stylesheet, that class gets the same fill as `:hover` in each rule where a row has a hover style: normal rows, pinned rows, active rows and colored active rows. Each new selector has the same specificity as its `:hover` counterpart, so selected and active fills still take precedence in the same order. Hover-only action buttons and badge swaps are unchanged; only the row background is kept.

## Evidence

- New sidebar test `keeps the context-menu row highlighted until its menu closes`: it fails on base (`expected false to be true`) and passes with the fix. It opens the menu with `contextmenu`, checks the row is marked, closes the menu with Escape and checks the mark is gone.
- `pnpm lint:ui:styles` and `oxfmt --check` pass on the touched files.
- Mock Control UI (`pnpm dev:ui:mock`, synthetic data) driven with Playwright: I right-clicked "Mobile layout smoke test" and moved the pointer onto "Rename…".

prs.title: improve(plugins): load managed snapshots from shared trees
prs.body:
Related: #187350

## What Problem This Solves

Managed plugins currently repeat full source validation and copying during cold startup. This draft implements the approved shared real tree plus background scrub design; it is not ready to land.

## User Impact

The first pushed commit only prepares owner operations and exact byte transport. It does not enable a snapshot reader or re-enable eager publication. Publisher suspension is already merged in #194456 (`2699510898c6`).

The intended reader keeps real plugin files, verifies each loaded module against an authenticated manifest, and moves unused-file validation into a bounded background scrub. Tampering retires the snapshot with a path-bearing warning, keeps the process running, and triggers fresh capture on the next start.

**BREAKING (pending reader activation):** Managed snapshot generations accept only modules in the install-time dependency closure, including dynamic require and re-anchored createRequire. `ERR_PLUGIN_SNAPSHOT_DEPENDENCY` names the module and asks users to declare it and reinstall/update, or use a local development source. Local/dev sources remain unchanged. Existing installs qualify for lazy publication only when persisted content and closure digests match; the first publication run finishes with its already prepared generation.

## Why This Change Was Made

A sealed manifest binds per-file digests and resolution metadata with less startup I/O than a full-byte pack. Startup will authenticate that unit through a pinned guarded open and check root/owner identity without scanning or copying every child. Module load must evaluate verified bytes. Scrub must revalidate bytes, type, owner, mode, link count, membership and exact identity through the existing preparation worker pool. Independent instances retain separate module evaluation and native admission.

The currently shipped cold path scans/hashes the closure, repeats identity checks after authority awaits, then copies/hashes a runtime capture. The proposed path moves detection of unused-file edits and raw asset reads to the scrub; it must not move used-module or resolution integrity checks to that delayed phase. Full native/child handling and the performance gate are still in progress.

## Evidence

The pushed foundation passed 44 focused tests, including the preserved owner/lazy-publication cases, optional publication ENOSPC behavior, quiet owner retirement, and exact Buffer transfer. The new byte-transfer regression failed first. Scoped typecheck, lint, formatting and whitespace pass. Independent P0–P2 review is clean for the six-file pushed foundation; it does not certify the unfinished reader.

Pending before landing: full acceptance matrix, alternating five-per-arm second-start benchmark with A/A controls and two file counts, separate first-publication/scrub cost, native Windows proof, complete independent review and exact-head CI. Publication stays suspended unless all gates pass. No release or fs-safe pin change is included.

prs.title: perf(sessions): persist active transcript facts for hydration
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

**Approved by Peter (2026-11-06) together with a separately reviewed, paced after-ready backfill follow-up.**

Cold transcript hydration reads small byte-count and dependency-navigation values stored after the payload in `transcript_events`. SQLite traverses payload overflow chains to reach those columns. Actor hydration also totals the entire active path, so a 512-event request can incur this cost across tens of thousands of events.

## User Impact

Agent schema 41 adds an initially empty `session_transcript_active_event_facts` companion keyed by `(session_id, seq)`. A fact stores exactly `coalesce(event_utf8_bytes, octet_length(event_json)) + 1` and the existing guarded dependency projection. `{}` means a known non-candidate; a missing row means unknown. CASE-gated readers use facts when present and retain the exact previous expressions otherwise. There is no reader backfill.

On the synthetic 34,153-event path, full coverage reduces actor hydration CPU by 79.0% and VFS spans by 96.6%. Cron-context CPU and sampled allocation are approximately neutral. Existing rows do not receive this benefit immediately: 512 ordinary, well-formed appends cover a recent 512-row window, but historical dependency candidates and full-path totals remain uncovered until a normal rewrite/rebuild. Cold transitions clear facts; restored rows start unknown.

Older readers are not allowed through an additive-table exception: their writers cannot maintain these facts. Older schema-40 admission refuses schema 41. Rollback requires restoring the verified scoped migration backup and then using the matching older build.

## Why This Change Was Made

The empty table avoids `ADD COLUMN` validation scans on existing STRICT tables. Payloads remain authoritative; the companion is a derived projection owned by the active-row lifecycle. SQLite uses `STRICT, WITHOUT ROWID`; PostgreSQL receives the same primary/foreign-key contract through the existing schema generator and migration owner.

| Mutation owner | Facts lifecycle in the same transaction |
| --- | --- |
| Normal append and full replacement | Reuse prepared payload/byte facts; ordinary rows use a compact insert. |
| Rebuild/import/branch selection | Carry compact facts through the existing source read, prepared chunks, and catch-up. |
| PostgreSQL append | Insert through a writable CTE dependent on the active-row `RETURNING` relation. |
| Payload rewrite and direct payload updater | Clear changed facts, including index-preserving rewrites. |
| Eligibility changes | Replace the active projection and its facts through the existing rebuild owner. |
| Cold transition/restoration | Clear facts before representation changes; restored rows remain unknown. |
| Branch retirement, reset, compaction, suffix replacement, deletion | Cascade from retired active rows; new uncovered suffix rows retain fallback. |
| Cross-engine port | Omit derived facts and use destination-native fallback; do not copy encoding-dependent projections. |

Malformed/deep legacy input retains its previous acceptance and reader-error behavior. A review caught eager projection of scalar placement data failing at append time; the writer now leaves those facts unknown, with an append/rebuild regression. Connection-owned prepared templates retain only single-row/full-chunk shapes and bind fresh session IDs and values.

Runtime growth is necessary for the approved schema and transactional lifecycle across both engines. The shared metadata reader replaces the old payload-backed accounting queries, and the guarded dependency expression has one owner. Runtime source is +797/−152 (**+645 net**), generated catalogs +108, scripts (proof, inventory, and wrapper closure) +1,554, and tests +890. The requested non-test/non-doc diff is **+2,310 net** including tooling. This is an additive schema/lifecycle change, not a net-deletion optimization; the initially empty upgrade and exact legacy fallback require the additional writer, invalidation, migration, and engine-port contracts.

## Evidence

Original measurement baseline: `ac008ae0b850ff5082a247924e5b9e636edbb1ce`, agent schema 40; original published candidate: `b411052a21bc9c417b996d80a9e71889e8a815b6`. The PR was rebased onto main `d5d54833f9e4c2a38dec517804a057bc71af5d3e`; reviewed head: `441bd5686cb75b07aa015832679ddfb41c15d12e`. Fresh proof used main `1f7035c15f3d6f89b7336c0d273ddcb18b8ff060`; the final rebase is patch-identical across all five PR commits, with no intervening session/state/database-engine changes or migration-path changes. Original owner/70 GB measurements below are retained evidence, not re-measurements on the rebased head. Synthetic data only: 6.3M active rows across 25,130 sessions, including 20k–50k-event paths, on a physically allocated 70.010 GB fragmented SQLite file (about 54.32 GB non-free pages). No Team database was opened/copied and no load was sent to Team. Large fixtures were deleted after proof; reports, profiles, and small scoped backups were retained.

The reproducible fixture, VFS extension, real-owner runner, and commands are in `scripts/perf/transcript-active-facts.{py,ts,md}` and `transcript-active-facts-vfs.c`. Both arms enable the native statement cache used by the production database owner. Earlier uncached/fixture-setup runs remain diagnostic evidence and are not pooled with final results.

**Rebased upgrade and integration proof (2026-11-06):** main remains agent schema 40 and the candidate is 41. A fresh synthetic 1M-row, 1.335 GB database upgraded through the real owner in **36.366 ms**, with **86,116 logical read bytes / 22 VFS spans** and **28,872 WAL bytes/growth**; the companion remained empty. Scoped backup took **100.859 ms**, retaining a **12,288-byte** snapshot. This rerun reports migration WAL writes before outer connection-close checkpoint writes, so it is not a write-volume reduction claim against the earlier table. The exact 40→41 DDL, preflight/finalizer, integrity scope, and backup owners are unchanged; the 70 GB fixture was therefore not regenerated. Fresh main-40 admission refused schema 41. Scoped restore recovered both markers to 40, removed facts, and preserved checked payloads in **9,164.782 ms**. Restore wall time includes maintenance admission on a host at roughly 81 load; without matched controls this is neither attributed to a regression nor presented as a speedup. The 1.33 GB fixture was deleted.

The rebase preserves #194359's exact published v16 memory FTS/shadow admission and memory-before-transcript migration order, plus 7bc0ae72/dc16abf7's lazy FTS streaming, byte-bounded sync batches, streaming manual trimming, and digest checks. Writer-history audit across sessions/state/database-engine found no new writer owner: existing active-row chunks still carry facts; manual trim still replaces rows transactionally; cross-engine port rebuilds FTS while leaving facts unknown. Extended the existing sync-batch and manual-trim tests with exact facts and rollback assertions. A small cleanup moves pure facts derivation into the existing projection-append preparation owner without adding SQL runtime imports. The fresh regression against current main `1f7035c` fails with one native dependency projection; the final candidate passes with zero, preserving three facts, identical events, and 441 serialized bytes.

**Upgrade through the real migration and scoped-backup owners:**

| Active rows / file | Backup wall | Migration wall | Main bytes read | Total bytes written | WAL growth | Backup size |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1M / 1.336 GB | 60.07 ms | 30.53 ms | 94,308 | 82,192 | 41,232 | 12,288 B |
| 10M / 13.479 GB | 75.38 ms | 35.92 ms | 86,116 | 57,544 | 28,872 | 12,288 B |
| 6.3M / 70.010 GB | 126.52 ms | 28.18 ms | 98,404 | 73,976 | 37,112 | 12,288 B |

The original campaign 1M result is the named canonical rerun; the earlier 1M run was 33.68 ms and is retained. All scales show bounded page work. Existing-data work consists of the single `schema_meta` record, version markers, and schema-catalog validation. The backup records `schema_meta`, the prior user version, and the companion's absence. There is no ALTER, existing-row index build, transcript scan, or transcript copy. Exact 40→41 quick finalization checks the new empty table/FK; earlier crossings and explicit FULL verification retain global foreign-key validation. Separate whole-update backups/maintenance are outside these version-phase timings. PostgreSQL's existing backup scope is unchanged.

**Real hydration owners, five untraced samples per arm/state:** actor hydration runs inside `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` with its 513-row navigation window and full active-path total; cron-context is the actual bounded-context core with a 512-event limit, not the entire cron job or RPC.

| Facts / owner | CPU base → candidate | Wall base → candidate | VFS spans base → candidate | Pager visits base → candidate |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Empty / actor | 596.736 → 183.936 ms | 2264.438 → 248.128 ms | 84,188 → 84,189 | 337,803 → 406,108 |
| Empty / cron-context | 75.659 → 68.112 ms | 76.333 → 83.232 ms | 6,348 → 6,350 | 91,155 → 93,968 |
| Latest 512 / actor | 133.069 → 139.198 ms | 130.631 → 137.266 ms | 84,188 → 82,978 | 337,803 → 435,185 |
| Latest 512 / cron-context | 58.324 → 56.029 ms | 53.929 → 51.247 ms | 6,348 → 5,134 | 91,155 → 89,561 |
| Full / actor | 130.740 → 27.419 ms | 129.970 → 25.664 ms | 84,188 → 2,826 | 337,803 → 142,672 |
| Full / cron-context | 59.406 → 59.844 ms | 53.955 → 50.001 ms | 6,348 → 4,465 | 91,155 → 86,682 |

SQLite page caches were cold (mmap off, 2 MiB cache), while OS cache was uncontrolled. The empty/base mean includes a large first cold-OS-cache outlier; all samples are retained, and no empty-coverage speedup is claimed. VFS spans count requested 4 KiB intersections, not physical disk I/O. Mean host load was 34.2/32.2/31.2 for empty/partial/full. Five samples do not establish p95/p99 or an adverse tail result.

For full coverage, metadata spans per requested row fall 2.432→0.057, actor spans normalized to 512 rows fall 164.430→5.520, and cron-context spans fall 12.398→8.721. Dependency scanning remains necessary: spans per selected candidate fall 16.142→11.819 across 155 candidates. General actor navigation still reads its latest 513 payload rows.

**Separate allocation and append measurements:**

| Owner | Iterations per side | CPU base → candidate | Sampled JS allocation base → candidate |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Actor hydration, full facts | 200 allocation calls; 5 untraced calls | 130.740 → 27.419 ms/call | 1,600,619 → 1,599,478 B/call (neutral) |
| Cron-context, full facts | 200 allocation calls; 5 untraced calls | 59.406 → 59.844 ms/call | 20,644,870 → 20,655,593 B/call (neutral) |
| Append, mixed payload sizes | 25,000 timing; 10,000 allocation | 2.824699 → 2.890754 ms/op (+0.066055 ms, +2.34%) | 1,380,655 → 1,388,032 B/op (+0.53%) |

Append timing uses five AB/BA pairs and four fresh identical-code A/A pairs, 5,000 operations per arm. A/A signed spread was −5.51% CPU and −10.90% wall, larger than the candidate's +2.34% CPU/+3.52% wall. The small measured cost is within these controls, rather than a proven regression. Retained file growth adds 29.49 B/append; cumulative native writes rise 396,081→403,254 B/op (+1.81%). Allocation uses separate counterbalanced sampling passes with collected allocations included; these are not GC or retained-heap measurements.

**Correctness, plans, and recovery:** full/partial/absent facts return identical actor/context outputs, including reset, compaction, branch changes, pending automation, ineligible assistants, malformed/legacy rows, rewrites, cold storage, and rollback. Both engines use the companion primary key. PostgreSQL `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` shows all four payload fallback subplans never executed under full coverage; partial/no coverage exercises the old expressions. The work-count regression runs the frozen main reader against the same real-writer fixture: main performs one native dependency projection and fails the zero-projection assertion; candidate performs zero and passes, with identical events and 441 serialized bytes.

The actual pinned schema-40 admission implementation rejects schema 41 before data reads. In the original campaign, the real scoped restore returned both markers to 40, removed the companion, and preserved selected payload bytes in 103.35 ms; the fresh rebased restore and its host-load caveat are reported above. This proves the old admission path, not startup of a packaged older Gateway binary. With owners stopped, use `openclaw database restore-migration-backup` with the verified pre-upgrade scoped snapshot before starting the matching older build; manually lowering version markers is not a rollback.

**Adoption/backfill decision:** a recent window takes approximately `512 / active-appends-per-second` seconds to cover; historical totals and dependencies do not age out merely because that window is covered. A proposal-only synthetic probe populated 34,153 facts in 67 batches of at most 512: 25.0 s wall, 4.0 s CPU, 345.5 MB logical reads, 3.0 MB cumulative writes, with a 2.42 s maximum batch. Straight-line 6.3M extrapolation is about 63.7 GB logical reads, 548 MB writes, 12.3 minutes CPU and 77 minutes wall before pacing—not a production forecast. Peter approved a paced after-ready backfill as a separately reviewed follow-up. Another lane will implement it after this PR merges; this PR implements none.

Rebased local proof: the initial six session files passed 79 tests; after the pure-helper move, the final cold-storage/rebuild/eligibility run passed 48 tests. SQLite migration/index/admission/FTS proof passed 54 tests. Real PostgreSQL migration/portability passed 11 tests with one intentional skip; Doctor and append passed two selected cases, and append passed again on the final owner. Generator/catalog/descriptor/JSON checks passed 211 tests. PostgreSQL artifacts were regenerated and verified byte-identical. Scoped lint/format, root test types, session/state/infra test types, wrapper closure, worker registry, and the exact 890-line test allocation passed. The allocation covers the existing distinct migration/lifecycle/cross-engine contracts plus 40 lines checking facts through the newly bounded sync-rebuild and manual-trim paths. Current-head CI will be recorded after publication.

The first CI run exposed three lifecycle cases in addition to two static guards; all have focused red/green proof and review. Canonical-index repair now handles an FK-backed unique index only after physical verification, with complete integrity revalidation inside the repair transaction; orphans, duplicates, unknown mismatches and physical corruption remain refusals (21 owner tests plus the real reopen regression). Historical PostgreSQL Doctor rebuilds consume admitted predecessor schema facts, while a missing current-schema table remains an error. Schema38/39 upgrades retain their metadata-only precheck and global post-migration FK validation (12 migration tests). SQL annotation placement and the exact worker-only invalidation classification satisfy their guards without raising a baseline. The exceptional damaged-index repair may repeat an integrity scan; the normal upgrade and hydration measurement paths are unchanged.

The third CI run caught three migration test hooks still matching the old version-publication SQL punctuation after adoption of the shared writer. Updated those hooks (including the creator-migration sibling) to match the canonical statement. Both focused files pass all seven tests, preserving independent-reader atomicity, injected-failure rollback, and real maintenance-lease loss. This is a test-only repair with zero net line growth; fresh independent review is clean.

The later dialect guard also caught raw JSON and schema-version sites. These now use the existing engine JSON path/type helpers and canonical version writer. The SQLite predicate and bindings are byte-identical to the measured version; the guard passes with design constructs unchanged and engine-maintenance sites reduced by one. Four focused files pass 25 tests, and a real PostgreSQL probe verifies 12 native JSON type cases. No dialect exemption or baseline was added.

Review: **Codex autoreview completed all 16 passes with no accepted/actionable P0–P2 findings**, including the rebased working tree and the final preparation-owner cleanup. The helper verified the captured source before publishing its scoped-clean result.

Limits: no whole-Gateway main-thread CPU, allocation rate, GC seconds/min, event-loop p99, sessions.list p99, RSS, or heap result is claimed. These are synthetic owner measurements; OS-cold physical I/O and full older-binary startup were not measured.

prs.title: fix(gateway): recover automatically when the main thread wedges
prs.body:
Related: #190964

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: a Gateway with a permanently blocked main thread stays alive but unresponsive until an operator kills it.

## User Impact

A supervised Gateway now records `main-thread stall recovery:` and kills itself after five continuous minutes without a heartbeat, allowing its existing supervisor to restart it and existing crash recovery to resume eligible runs. Inspector/debugger pauses and conflicting startup profiling are exempt. Laptop sleep resets the observation window. There is no new configuration or schema change.

Foreground and `gateway:watch` processes require an external supervisor to respawn. SIGKILL cannot perform graceful shutdown; the existing persisted crash-recovery eligibility and authority checks remain in force.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing worker already owns the heartbeat and in-progress stall diagnostics. Give that owner the terminal decision, rather than adding another watchdog. Five minutes leaves generous headroom over observed ordinary stalls lasting tens of seconds while bounding otherwise hour-scale outages. SIGTERM requires the blocked JavaScript handler; SIGABRT can create a process-sized core dump.

The observer now runs independently of optional V8 profiling, including on the macOS app's Bun runtime. It reuses the existing bounded stack capture when available, synchronously writes the terminal fact directly to service stderr, and never waits indefinitely for inspector capture. Node inspector revalidation is capped at one second. Systemd, launchd and app child restart policies are unchanged.

## Evidence

- Three fake-clock owner cases pass on Node and pinned Bun: before/at deadline, fresh heartbeat, inspector suppression/detachment, suspended observer and pending inspector request. Both original required regression cases fail on the pre-fix observer because no terminal fact or kill occurs. The new 89-line test allocation is for these independent process-lifecycle invariants.
- Existing Node logging suites: 22 passed, one Linux-only test skipped on macOS. Existing Gateway event-loop health suite: 19 passed. Final observer cases: Node 3/3, Bun 3/3, under one second test time each; wrapper cold-build costs are separate. Hosted CI seconds are pending.
- Real five-minute Node spin: terminal diagnostic at **300,181 ms**, then SIGKILL; five bounded in-progress profile reports precede it. Accelerated interleaved controls: **0/6** baseline processes self-terminate, **5/5** candidates self-terminate. Real native blocking and Bun probes also self-terminate; inspector-enabled Node stays alive beyond the deadline.
- Healthy owner overhead, one million callback/heartbeat iterations with A/A controls: median thread CPU **65.19 → 74.44 ms** (about **9.25 ns/tick**); sampled allocation **48.02 → 47.77 B/tick**, overlapping control ranges. This is no throughput claim. The synthetic fixture retains 65,000 paths; it does not reproduce a large on-disk database, physical workspace or btrfs. No production data was used.
- Codex autoreview of the full local candidate against `1f7035c15f3d6f89b7336c0d273ddcb18b8ff060`: **scoped-clean, P0–P2**, no actionable findings. Simplification retains one heartbeat owner and existing diagnostics/supervisors/recovery. Production delta **+73 lines (+88/-15)** is the new terminal action plus Bun/debugger/suspension safety; no scan, cache, manager or compatibility layer was added.
- Full `pnpm build` passed. The production CLI reached `/readyz`, self-terminated after the accelerated heartbeat deadline with `elapsedMs=300215`, and a fresh CLI on the same synthetic state reached readiness. The harness then stopped that fixture. Initial cold-source and shared-lock setup failures are excluded from this passing proof. Linux systemd and macOS launchd/app respawn policies are source-audited; no live services were restarted. No Control UI imports these logging modules.
- `pnpm check:changed` caught a timeout callback type overload and a test parameter reassignment; both were corrected. Core/state-logging typechecks, targeted lint and final owner regressions pass. The full changed-check command is being rerun against the committed revision before marking ready.

prs.title: fix(control-ui): prevent Subagents collapse during chat reload
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes a signed-in reload of a chat deep link briefly collapsing cached Subagents before live activity appears, moving Outputs and Automations twice. With four or more ordinary children, the three-row receipt also grew into an unbounded live list.

## User Impact

Subagents keeps its cached geometry while Activity loads and while a covering child read is pending. The default ordinary-child preview stays at three rows; Show more exposes every live child after a complete answer. Cached display facts confer no actions or query hydration. No config, protocol, cache shape, schema version, or store changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

Synthetic attribution reproduces 142 → 81 → 142 px. During the 81 px frame, the live custom element is connected with no row DOM even though its props already contain the correct cached row. Its separate Solid root commits roughly 95–106 ms later. The child query starts and answers after the collapse and regrowth. Rendering Activity in the parent Solid tree removes that intermediate empty host and its registration/types. A pending covering read cannot replace the receipt.

The smaller parity fix reuses the receipt's existing three-row bound and the existing expansion signal/control rather than storing or rendering an unbounded default list. The application changes are net **−4 production LOC**. The requested broader diff filter includes QA tooling and a TSX test: **+302/−80 (net +222)**; the growth supplies native three/four-child seeding, real receipt qualification and row-count evidence, without adding product state. The proof-tool growth implements the campaign contract that every measured reload starts from a real ordinary-child receipt and checks physical row-count parity, including the previously missing native four-child fixture.

## Evidence

**Ready for review; the campaign lead owns landing.** Candidate AB performance and layout gates pass. Overall qualification is still running: identical-build native A/A has two strict first-painted-rows control flags, the earlier exact-head qualification has three test-job failures under classification, and the full Node UI suite is running.

The campaign measured 14 visible states during a signed-in dashboard deep-link reload. This change addresses the Subagents adoption interval using synthetic data. Quiet AWS c7a.4xlarge comparison: one fixed instance, 11 interleaved AB pairs and 11 A/A pairs per route group; 352 warm captures across 16 groups, none discarded. Captured asset names and native index SHA-256 values match the expected frozen build in 352/352 captures. Complete geometry/RPC reports were saved independently; the bulk PNG archive exceeded the downloader’s 1 GiB limit and was not retained locally. The wrapper therefore ended with artifact/cleanup exit 7; the complete report exports remain available, and the lease was subsequently verified released through its owner. Baseline `3caa42353988bd9f30b1f5784a940dc640fffd19`; candidate `659a59b3e5d1da7e97f86bc0f4cd584927250054`.

| Active chat profile | Main stable | Candidate stable | Measured geometry |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Team-scale ordinary child | 10/11 | 11/11 | Main 142 → 81 → 142 px, 61 px range / 122 px cumulative; candidate 142 px throughout, one actual row |
| Native four children | 1/11 | 11/11 | Main 234 → 295 px in 10 captures, 3 → 4 rows; candidate 270 px throughout, three-row preview plus More |
| Native original three-child fixture | 11/11 | 11/11 | Both 234 px throughout with three actual rows |

Every candidate active capture also has zero Outputs/Automations top-position range and zero cumulative movement from first populated Details through final. Team A/A reproduces the transient in 4/11 and 3/11 identical-main captures. Native four-child A/A has growth in 10/11 captures in both arms. The native original fixture remains stable 11/11 in both A/A arms.

All eight AB route groups pass the stated hard secondaries. First-painted rows paired medians range from −16.13 to +7.87 ms, all below the +16 ms failure limit. Team active final rows improve by paired median −29 ms, better in 9/11 pairs. Native four-child CLS improves by paired median −0.002251, better in 10/11. Native four-child LoAF has arm medians 350 → 352.6 ms and paired +18.6 ms, with 5 better / 6 worse and overlapping IQRs [333.75, 364.05] / [335.05, 359.4]; this is noise under the standing regression rule.

The RPC census has identical method counts in 86/88 AB pairs and every A/A pair. The first native active-chat pair for each three/four-child profile has one extra candidate `session.suggestions.list` request (185 request bytes / 115 response bytes); the remaining pairs and all Team routes match. This is recorded separately from the unchanged CI benchmark request counts.

The native three-child A/A controls exceed the strict first-painted-rows paired-median limit: +19.84 ms for chat and +31.92 ms for dashboard, each 4 better / 7 worse with overlapping IQRs. Both use the identical baseline build. These retained controls are a measurement-validity gap, not evidence of candidate runtime cost. Other A/A groups pass the hard secondaries. Full median/IQR and per-pair tables follow below.

| AB route | Selected snapshot bytes, both arms | Sidebar snapshot bytes, both arms |
|---|---:|---:|
| Native active three-child chat | 115335 | 174711 |
| Native active dashboard | 116109 | 174625 |
| Native active four-child chat | 115394 | 175458 |
| Native archived chat | 113982 | 174580 |
| Native archived dashboard | 115742 | 174580 |
| Team active chat | 58361 | 114644 |
| Team archived chat | 57121 | 114343 |
| Team dashboard | 56094 | 114644 |

The Team-shaped 240-message reload regression is red on main for the exact 61 px section-height delta and green in all three candidate cases: one-child transient, four-child parity/expansion, and module failure. A pending-child regression is red on main when a partial live row displaces cached display, and green with the readiness guard. All changed consumer tests pass; single-file test costs are below. Historical minimal attribution reproduced the transient in 2/10 clean-main captures on lease `cbx_9ada7d54d04e` (released), with the live host empty for 95–106 ms while cached presentation remained populated.

Detached local review is clean through P2. Final comparison and full UI suite: lease `cbx_a9378b73928f`, run `run_b08a26136c9be2f865b020dcc523c2de`. Focused owner/consumer tests passed there before measurement. The full UI attempt was terminated by the launcher’s five-minute no-output watchdog (exit 143) because its JSON-only reporter suppressed progress; it produced no JSON verdict. A retry using Node and the existing CI pattern (`--reporter=default --reporter=json --outputFile.json=...`) is running on lease `cbx_58fb3b717ecb`, run `run_11770adbf7da9338047db84a5055604e`; the measurement lease is released. Changed checks completed: types, format, lint and all other guards passed; the sole failure flags untouched historical changelog credits. The exact attribution guard fails on pinned main and head with byte-for-byte identical output (1241 B), so this failure is inherited. The Node run has reported a retained-mobile-page failure in `session-progress-submit.e2e.test.ts`; its exact case will be compared with pinned main after the full run. No full-suite pass is claimed.

[Exact-head CI](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/42327278191) completed with three failed test jobs, 55 successful jobs, 23 skipped jobs, and the failed aggregate. Its performance job passed: normalized chat boot 1289528 → 1289529 B (+1), startup 89812 → 89812 B, request counts unchanged. The printed absolute chat cap has inherited debt in both arms; the CI-owned comparison accepts this head. No cap changed. An earlier dispatch failed only because its validation tier rejected a frozen alternate target, before app checks ran.

CI failures under classification: one-pixel RTL composer assertion under Bun (the same job passes all 13 cases under Node), Knowledge saved-indicator timeout, and WebKit older-history movement assertion. Local single-file head replays pass: composer 13/13 (8.55 s), Knowledge 1/1 (16.59 s), selected WebKit case 1/1 (21.33 s). A later main CI run also passes the composer and Knowledge cases. Matching pinned-main failure evidence is not yet available; the failures are not claimed inherited or fixed. No unrelated CI jobs have been rerun.

Release-note context: chat reloads preserve Subagents and following Details geometry during live activity adoption; ordinary-child previews stay consistent between cached and live content.

### Inspected synthetic Details strips

These are 2200 × 1180 synthetic regression captures. Before is the red-on-main four-child case; after is the passing candidate. Cached → live Subagents is 264 → 325 px before, 300 → 300 px after. The candidate includes the disabled cached Show more control, which becomes usable after the complete live answer.

prs.title: improve(sessions): cover the legacy transcript repair and compaction contracts
prs.body:
Related: #189396

## What Problem This Solves

Two modules on the session-recovery path had no test coverage at all:

- `src/config/sessions/legacy-compaction-history.ts` — read by `disk-budget.ts` to keep stored compaction snapshots from looking unreferenced during cleanup.
- `src/config/sessions/legacy-transcript-repair.ts` — the shared input to Doctor's transcript repair (`src/commands/doctor-session-transcripts.ts`) and the sqlite import spool (`session-accessor.sqlite-import-stage.ts`).

No production code changes. This is coverage for behavior that already exists.

## Why This Change Was Made

`legacy-compaction-history.ts` carries a contract in a comment that nothing enforced:

> Malformed references must fail closed, not make protected history reclaimable.

That contract splits deliberately: `readLegacyCompactionSnapshotPaths` throws on malformed input so protected checkpoint files can never be treated as unreferenced, while `readLegacyCompactionMetrics` degrades to an empty list because metrics only enrich history. Both halves were untested, so a future change could quietly make the path reader return `[]` and let cleanup reclaim files it is supposed to protect.

`legacy-transcript-repair.ts` is pure, dependency-light, and sits upstream of both recovery entry points, but had no tests either.

## What The Tests Cover

`legacy-compaction-history.test.ts` (11 cases):

- Empty/absent checkpoints read as no history.
- Metrics keep only checkpoints that name a post-compaction entry; non-finite token measurements are dropped rather than thrown.
- Snapshot paths are collected from both compaction sides and trimmed; blank paths are skipped.
- Five malformed shapes (non-array checkpoints, non-record checkpoint, missing pre-compaction side, missing post-compaction side, non-string snapshot path) all **throw** from the path reader while the metrics reader still returns `[]` — pinning the asymmetry that keeps protected history unreclaimable.

`legacy-transcript-repair.test.ts` (8 cases):

- `selectActivePath` walks parents back from the last entry when no leaf is recorded, ignores `session` header rows, and returns no path when there is nothing to walk.
- `transcriptRepairUserKey` keys only user messages with an id, reads both plain string and part-based content, and drops text with no runtime context when stripping.
- The strip/raw asymmetry is pinned: stripping removes the runtime-context markers so a rewritten copy still matches its original.
- `hasBrokenPromptRewriteBranch` flags a rewritten branch the active path no longer reaches, and stays false when every entry is on the active path.

## Real Behavior Proof

Unit coverage of the helpers does not show the contracts holding at the entry points that own them, so the same behavior is now driven through both shipped consumers, against real files on disk.

**Doctor — rewritten transcript branch** (`src/commands/doctor-session-transcripts.test.ts`)

`detectSessionTranscriptHealthIssues()` is called against a real `<dir>/agents/main/sessions/session.jsonl` tree. The transcript holds an active user turn plus its discarded copy, which still carries the internal runtime-context markers the active copy was rewritten to drop:

```
 ✓ src/commands/doctor-session-transcripts.test.ts > reports a rewritten branch that the active path no longer reaches
 ✓ src/commands/doctor-session-transcripts.test.ts > stays quiet when no user turn was rewritten
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  8 passed (8)
```

Doctor reports one issue with `broken: true`, `originalEntries: 4`, `activeEntries: 3` — the orphaned copy is classified as a rewritten branch, and the same transcript without the copy produces no issue.

**Cleanup — malformed legacy references** (`src/config/sessions/disk-budget.test.ts`)

`pruneUnreferencedSessionArtifacts()` runs over a real sessions directory containing a checkpoint file, with a session entry whose `compactionCheckpoints` is the string `"corrupt"`:

```
 ✓ src/config/sessions/disk-budget.test.ts > pruneUnreferencedSessionArtifacts > fails closed instead of reclaiming history when legacy references are malformed
 ✓ src/config/sessions/disk-budget.test.ts > pruneUnreferencedSessionArtifacts > keeps a checkpoint that a valid legacy reference still protects
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  23 passed (23)
```

The malformed sweep **rejects** with `Invalid legacy compaction history references` and the checkpoint file is still on disk afterward — cleanup aborts rather than proceeding against a reference set that silently lost its protected entries. The paired case keeps a checkpoint that a well-formed reference still points at, with `removedFiles: 0`.

## Evidence

```
Test Files  1 passed (1)   Tests  11 passed (11)   # src/config/sessions/legacy-compaction-history.test.ts
Test Files  1 passed (1)   Tests   8 passed  (8)   # src/config/sessions/legacy-transcript-repair.test.ts
Test Files  1 passed (1)   Tests   8 passed  (8)   # src/commands/doctor-session-transcripts.test.ts
Test Files  1 passed (1)   Tests  23 passed (23)   # src/config/sessions/disk-budget.test.ts
```

All run through `node scripts/test-projects.mts <file>` (the `runtime-config` and `commands` Vitest projects).

Also checked on this branch, based on `main` (`8f1ef6c9`):

- `run-oxlint.mjs` on the touched files: 0 warnings, 0 errors.
- `run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.core.json`: clean.
- `run-format.mts --check`: no formatting drift.

## Test Line Allocation

`config/test-lines-allocations/legacy-session-recovery-contracts.txt` records the retained net test-line growth (278 lines) per the root `AGENTS.md` cost-budget guidance and `docs/help/testing/writing-tests.md`. The shared scalar is unchanged.

## Scope Note

Three cases were deliberately left out of `selectActivePath`: cycles, a last entry with no id, and a missing parent. In all three the observed behavior is shaped by `transcript-tree.ts` reparsing parentless canonical entries and reattaching parents, not by the fallback walk in this module. Asserting them there would encode the tree's repair semantics rather than this module's, so they belong with `transcript-tree.ts` coverage instead.

prs.title: feat: add HeyGen Voice speech provider
prs.body:
Closes #194470

## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw users cannot speak with HeyGen voices, including the instant and professional voice clones in their own HeyGen workspace.

## User Impact

User impact: after installing the plugin and setting `HEYGEN_API_KEY`, users can set `tts.provider: "heygen"` and get MP3 audio, streamed playback, Opus voice notes, 24 kHz PCM telephony output, and voice listing. Nothing changes for users who do not install it.

Required action: a maintainer must publish `@openclaw/heygen-speech` to npm and ClawHub. The install path does not work until then.

## Why This Change Was Made

This adds an external plugin in `extensions/heygen-speech`, in the same shape as the other hosted speech providers, with no core code change. All synthesis uses HTTP streaming to `POST /v3/models/audio/tts/stream`.

The guarded fetch timeout covers the whole response body, and playback can read a long reply for minutes, so the provider restarts that timeout on each audio chunk. The plugin does not create voices. Its README shows the instant-clone API call.

The config baseline plugin count rises by 21, from 5018 to 5039, for the new plugin entry. The other files outside the extension are repo-required registration, generated inventory, and docs.

## Evidence

Checks at this head on a Linux devbox with Node 24:

- `extensions/heygen-speech`: 27 unit tests passed.
- `src/plugins/contracts`: 1085 tests passed.
- oxlint, `tsgo:extensions`, `tsgo:extensions:test`, the test-line and assertion ratchets, config docs, plugin inventory, docs MDX and links, and dead-export checks passed.

Live runs through the OpenClaw runtime against the production HeyGen API passed 31 of 32 cases at this head:

- All three models streamed over HTTP and returned as 24 kHz PCM telephony audio. MP3 output was decoded with ffmpeg.
- A buffered audio file, an Opus voice note, `language`, and voice listing.
- An instant clone: create, stream, telephony, and delete. A professional clone: stream and telephony.
- `voiceId`, `speakerVoice`, and invalid `model` directives, persona `modelId`, Talk with the key only in the TTS config, and `infer tts convert --voice --model`.
- Refusals for a bad key, a bad voice, a regional language code, a rejected tag, and a professional clone on Turbo. HeyGen's `code` and `request_id` stayed in the errors, and the next turn worked.
- Fallback to the next provider, three turns in a row, release mid-stream, and a dropped connection mid-stream.

The failed case used a 5 s `timeoutMs` on a 16 s professional clone take. The timeout also covers time to first audio, which varies on this path. In 3 retries, 1 passed and ran 7.4 s while audio arrived, and 2 timed out before first audio. With the chunk refresh removed at an earlier commit, the same case failed mid-stream at the timeout.

At earlier commits, two live 429 responses kept `code` and `request_id`. One arrived after a 30 s wait.

Not tested:

- Real Discord voice playback, a real phone call, and Telegram delivery. These runs covered output formats only.
- Talk through a connected client. The runs called the gateway config and synthesis functions directly.
- Long replies at the default timeout. Live text stayed short.
- `openclaw plugins install`, because the package is not published.
- macOS, Windows, and the Bun runtime.

CI: fork run https://github.com/spro-heygen/openclaw/actions/runs/42340064685 was dispatched at this head and had not finished when this was written. At the previous head, GitHub did not start `ios-screenshots` on the fork because of the account's billing or spending limit. `checks-ui (3/3)` failed one Bun-shard browser test on the fork's GitHub-hosted runner, a test this PR does not touch. Its root cause is not confirmed.

Local review: local autoreview and ClawSweeper were not run. Instead, an adversarial agent review and two over-engineering agent reviews ran, and the verified findings are fixed.

prs.title: fix(gateway): reconnect nodes stuck on obsolete connections
prs.body:
Related: #148693

## What Problem This Solves

Nodes can remain apparently connected while requests from an obsolete, replaced socket repeatedly fail with `PAIRING_CHANGED`. Closing that rejected socket lets Android automatically recover instead of staying stuck.

## User Impact

Android withdraws readiness, invalidates its old request lease, reauthenticates automatically and resumes useful node work. The rejected request is not replayed. The already-authorized replacement remains usable throughout the obsolete socket's rejection and closure. Pairing requirements and RPC/outbox retry semantics are unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

Send the rejection before closing only a socket that no longer owns the registered node. A transient pairing lookup failure or same-connection promotion does not disconnect the current owner. Android already implements the reconnect lifecycle; this PR adds consumer regression and native execution proof instead of introducing another recovery mechanism.

Related approach: #148770 by @holny; that branch is untouched. Production grows by 11 lines; 150 JS/TS test/support lines protect response/close ordering, ownership and useful replacement work, with a dedicated justified test-budget allocation. The 290 Kotlin test lines cover the existing client's lifecycle and opt-in emulator proof.

## Evidence

**Final candidate: `2afbb2ec0f0bbda0c317e6d6a940d2883fe270e5`.** [Immutable native Android execution evidence](https://github.com/jason-allen-oneal/openclaw/blob/1951fa7226ac6c6dcc9a956353fbaa10c7fd1173/README.md):

- The candidate APK's production `GatewaySession`, identity/auth stores and OkHttp ran on a dedicated API35 emulator against the built candidate Gateway. `PAIRING_CHANGED` arrived before close **4001**; the callback observed readiness and old-lease validity become false; automatic signed reconnection succeeded without manual intervention.
- The rejected **1024** stats update had no effect: the operator still read **4096**. The reconnected Android client then published **6144**, read back through `node.list`. Wire capture contains one rejected request and one fresh request through the assertion boundary—no replay.
- **Six focused JVM tests and one native instrumentation test passed.** Candidate Gateway and APK builds passed; installed APK hashes match built artifacts. Kotlin lint and the test-line ratchet passed. The bundle retains exact commands, logs, source/artifact identities, earlier formatting failures and cleanup receipts.
- Fresh independent native P0–P2 review of this head, production lifecycle and recovered execution artifacts found no actionable issues. The earlier null-lease fixture finding is fixed. Local autoreview CLI authentication was unavailable; no clean helper review is claimed.

[Earlier Gateway regression evidence](https://github.com/jason-allen-oneal/openclaw/blob/6262df988aa3ed228389a01c2e1942855ff686f8/README.md) retains the failing baseline, 87 passing targeted tests, targeted type/lint/format checks and killed guard mutant. That capture is explicitly bound to `13b077c8432`; subsequent production bytes are unchanged. Both runtime builds retain unrelated report-only UI size warnings.

The native capture proves Android **session recovery**, not full UI rendering, a physical phone or the historical incident's unknown initiating network race. The deterministic trigger is same-identity replacement. The broader issue remains linked rather than automatically closed. Final-head CI/review and another maintainer's security-sensitive approval remain independent gates; no deployment or merge is requested here.

prs.title: fix(browser): profile creation picks a CDP port another Gateway is already using
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #194236. `openclaw browser create-profile` can persist an automatic CDP port already held by an unrelated process because allocation previously excluded only ports listed in this Gateway's config. The new profile then fails to launch with PortInUseError.

Original fix and commits by @Abinithishkumarprabakaran are retained. Credit also to @wr-web (#194250) and @kaguranananana (#194270) for independent duplicate fixes; this PR carries the repair for the canonical issue.

## Changes

Keep allocation at its existing owner: probe each otherwise-eligible automatic candidate with the existing `ensurePortAvailable`, skip only PortInUseError, and await allocation from profile persistence. Preserve explicit configured ports, explicit URLs, existing-session reuse, the range and the existing launch-time guard. The probe does not reserve a port.

Consolidate the real occupied-listener regression into the existing config-rebase case using the existing loopback server helper. Consolidate absent/invalid configured-port cases without dropping assertions. **Tests net0 lines, no allocation**; source +21/-4, docs +2. No new schema, setting or SDK export.

## Evidence

[Exact-head Linux Gateway/CLI launch and CDP receipts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/194295#issuecomment-6702570503).

Built main `1f7035c15f3d6f89b7336c0d273ddcb18b8ff060` twice and candidate `79dfbaf11af4f0c7b3cf4c5b233d633bb183b5b2` twice through the shipped Linux Gateway and browser CLI with real Chromium.

| | Main | Candidate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First run | Saves occupied `26512`; launch exits 1 with PortInUseError | Skips occupied `26612`; saves `26613`; Chromium launches |
| Second run | Saves occupied `26562`; launch exits 1 with PortInUseError | Skips occupied `26662`; saves `26663`; Chromium launches |

Actual CDP `/json/version` confirms Chrome/156.0.8078.79 on the candidate's selected ports. The unrelated listeners remain active. Explicit configured-port controls launch real Chromium at their requested ports on both refs; explicit URL creation saves the exact requested endpoint on all four runs. No fake CDP server, platform override or live browser/account state is used.

- All **17** focused profile/allocator tests pass; consolidated busy-port regression fails on frozen main.
- Formatting and project-routed focused typed lint pass; both exact builds pass.
- Unit coverage retains range limits, invalid/absent profile ports, explicit URLs, existing-session behavior and lifecycle guards.

## Merge Danger

Two-way door for code behavior: reverting restores the prior future-allocation algorithm. Already-created profiles retain their valid saved ports and remain compatible; no state/schema migration is needed. Blast radius is automatic local managed-browser profile creation. Explicit endpoints and launch ownership/availability guards are unchanged.
