prs.title: fix: preserve gateway administrator permissions across native UI clients
prs.body:
## Expanded intent: native UI administrator parity

The intended invariant is the same authenticated administrator, same effective scopes and policy, same Gateway permissions across Control UI and native UI clients. UI rendering support is separate from permission. This revision extends PR #194443 beyond the original fresh-turn automation admission repair.

Current candidate: `697096f44c77820f7fde61cc005bd425a8227513`.

- Shared admin-source classification serves fresh automation admission and durable recovery capture; native clients are never relabeled as Control UI.
- Restore recorded automation-admin delegation for scheduled runs and repair/notice continuations. Preserve historical browser sources; historical native sources without delegation remain unprivileged. Timing-only edits intersect standing entitlement and scopes, with principal-only sources retaining their existing schema.
- Shared-credential native owner turns use the same owner-continuation rules as shared browser owners. Distinct personal administrators remain distinct principals.
- Native UI turns retain authenticated requester binding and signed-in human mentions; native admins advertising task-suggestion capability pass the same capability gates.
- Native UI clients can acknowledge provider reviews under existing session authorization, receive direct-turn dashboard-read delegation when authenticated as admin, and retain exact-device reconnect custody under the existing identity/policy checks.
- Browser origin checks and renderer/event-delivery contracts remain transport-specific. Caller-only deployment caps, tool policies, profile/scope ceilings, and final-effect revocation remain enforced.

### Expanded validation

The eight-file Gateway run finished with seven passing files and five failures in the new recovery revocation fixture. The fixture rotated a token without publishing Gateway revocation; it now invokes the production revocation owner. The subsequent recovery/reconnect/session-run run passed all 68 tests across three files, including the repaired five cases and native reconnect coverage. Gateway broad-run wall time: 143.83 s; repair run wall time: 85.95 s. This is combined focused evidence, not one all-green monolithic run. CI seconds are not yet available.

Other passing focused Gateway files cover admission, actual automation-tool final writes, provider-review acknowledgment, mentions/request normalization, requester context, and persisted-source policy. Core typecheck, focused lint, formatting, and diff whitespace checks passed. Independent read-only Codex review of the working change found and resolved a principal-snapshot compatibility error; final review found no further P0–P2 defects. This is not an autoreview-helper-certified result; the installed shared autoreview skill could not be read on this host.

Simplification: reuse existing classification, run-authority and recovery owners rather than widening browser identity or introducing another authorization registry. The 215-line net test allocation covers the original defect plus restoration/revocation, reconnect, provider review and native mention boundaries.

### Remaining limits

This source-level parity repair and fixture-authenticated boundary proof do not establish every native UI interaction end to end. Signed shipped-native-client → WebSocket → real-model validation remains unperformed; UI capabilities still depend on client implementation. Broad CI, maintainer judgment and fresh current-head security approval remain required. The running Gateway/app were not changed or restarted.

---

## Original repair and prior-head evidence

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where authenticated native-app administrators cannot ask an agent to inspect or repair automations owned by another conversation. The automation tool reports caller-only inventory and returns “not found” for those jobs despite the connection's admin access.

## User Impact

Native-app administrators can manage Gateway automations through fresh chat turns, just as Control UI administrators can. Non-admin callers remain scoped, and an explicit caller-only deployment policy still takes precedence. No configuration or data migration is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

Automation admission only minted a management entitlement for the browser Control UI. Reuse the canonical native UI classifier and require both server-attested operator authentication and effective `operator.admin` before admitting native-app management. Keep a distinct native-app entitlement rather than labeling native clients as Control UI clients.

Existing fresh/direct-user-turn, exact-run, liveness, revocation, tool-policy, and approval checks remain in place. Node-mode native connections and self-claimed client identity without authenticated operator authority do not qualify. No new policy owner, persistent state, or tool is introduced.

No linked issue; this is a directly reproduced bug fix.

## Evidence

Initial implementation: `c13ab576c5059102aa143ec3355540bdf2d12422` (base `d482d7616512`). Current proof revision: `a43f5e81404718b2e15dd1379bbf885513c967c0`.

- Reproduced on base `d482d7616512`: both native admin admission cases received no management entitlement; the real automation-tool integration returned `scope: caller` instead of `gateway` (52 existing admission tests and 11 existing transport integration cases still passed).
- Regression coverage: local and remote native UI admin admission; write-only, unauthenticated, node-mode, reconnect, and generated-input rejection; actual automation tool inventory and cross-conversation/account prompt update; explicit deployment caller cap.
- Focused test results: 54 admission cases and 28 creator-grant cases passed in the combined focused run; all 13 transport integration cases passed after correcting the new fixture's required tool/action allowlists. Production code did not change between those runs.
- Commands: `pnpm test src/gateway/server-methods/agent-run-local-operator-authority.test.ts src/gateway/server-methods/cron-creator-transports.integration.test.ts src/gateway/cron-creator-authority-grant.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`, then the final `pnpm test src/gateway/server-methods/cron-creator-transports.integration.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`.
- Final transport file: 59.76 s Vitest wall time (63.18 s wrapper wall time), about 23 s test execution including 11 pre-existing persistence/revocation cases. New native admin cases completed in about one second each. The original admission-file baseline took 42.85 s including cold compilation; its test execution remained subsecond.
- Focused lint, formatting, core typecheck (`pnpm tsgo:core`), and `git diff --check` passed.
- Independent read-only native Codex review of the complete candidate against the base: no P0–P2 findings. This was not an autoreview-helper-certified result; Codex CLI was unavailable. Subsequent changes only corrected the integration fixture's required tool/action policy allowlists and its test-line allocation.
- Simplification pass: two existing production owners changed (admission and entitlement type); 102 added regression lines are allocated separately because they exercise the reported failure and authorization boundary.

### Proof limits

The regression uses production admission, tool construction, and Gateway cron handlers with isolated synthetic state. Its fixture supplies server-authenticated connection facts; a signed native-app → WebSocket → real-model end-to-end run has not been performed. The running operator Gateway was not modified or restarted. Broad/package-build CI and security-owner review remain pending. CI seconds are not yet available.


### ClawSweeper follow-up — November 6, 2026

Added and executed final-write proof at `a43f5e81404718b2e15dd1379bbf885513c967c0`:

| Scenario | Observed result |
| --- | --- |
| Native admin | Foreign automation prompt updated and read back |
| Explicit caller cap | Foreign update rejected; stored state unchanged |
| Native operator.write without admin | Foreign update rejected; stored state unchanged |
| Native device revoked during delayed update | Update reaches held Cron validation; production device-revocation owner invalidates originating authority; resumed write rejects with authority-no-longer-active; stored state unchanged |

Command: `pnpm test src/gateway/server-methods/cron-creator-transports.integration.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`. All 15 cases passed; Vitest wall time 34.03 s; wrapper 37.19 s. Focused Oxlint, formatting, and diff checks passed. Independent read-only Codex review found no actionable defects in the proof revision. Production code unchanged. Test-line allocation updated to 130 for the expanded authorization scenarios.

**Still incomplete:** This remains in-process proof with fixture-authenticated connection facts, not signed native-client → WebSocket → real-model proof. No role-demotion propagation test was run. The only inspected installed app identifies as `ai.openclaw.mac.debug`, with ad-hoc signing and no Team Identifier; it supplies no shipped-client signing receipt. No live Gateway, user device permissions, accounts, or app connection settings were changed. Maintainer product approval and current-head `/allow-security-sensitive-change` remain outstanding. The new tests do not clear those requirements.

prs.title: fix: spawning child processes and exec calls fails on Linux hosts with glibc < 2.31
prs.body:
Closes #191841

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: after upgrading to 2026.10.10, every child process spawn and exec tool call fails immediately with `Error: native child reaping is unavailable | helper-unavailable` on Linux hosts running glibc < 2.31 (e.g. RHEL 8 / CentOS 8 / Rocky Linux 8 / Alibaba Cloud Linux 3).

## User Impact

Users on older enterprise Linux (glibc 2.28) can once again run all child process tools, exec calls, and scheduled script triggers. When the native child-reaping helper is unavailable on those hosts, service children now spawn and are supervised via POSIX process groups, restoring the reliable 2026.10.9 behavior instead of hard-failing every spawn.

## Why This Change Was Made

The 2026.10.10 release hard-bound the service-child relay to the Linux native subreaper path. On hosts where that binding cannot load, the relay refused to spawn children instead of degrading gracefully. The relay now probes the reaper capability at startup via `@openclaw/proc-safe/reaper` `isSupported()` and, when it is unavailable, selects the existing POSIX process-group supervision anchor (`assertProcessGroupControl`) that OpenClaw already used on other platforms. No new dependencies, no lockfile change.

## Evidence

### Automated regression coverage (committed)

New test `src/process/supervisor/service-child-relay.reaping-fallback.test.ts`:

- decision unit test: on a host with native reaping unavailable, `prepareServiceChildRelay` selects the process-group anchor (`useLinuxSubreaper === false`); it is **RED on base** and **GREEN with this fix**;
- e2e spawn test: a service child is spawned and supervised through the fallback path (`PROC_SAFE_NATIVE=off` forces the unavailable-native condition deterministically on CI).

### Host-verified proof of behavior (real affected host)

Produced on the affected host: **NewStartOS V4.4.2 (ZTE)**, glibc **2.28**, node **v24.16.0**, `PROC_SAFE_NATIVE=off` (makes the native capability probe fail, the same condition such a host hits on release). Runs in §1–§3 use the project's own TSX dev loader against the real relay source; §4 repeats the same runs on the **packaged `dist` bundle** with plain node (no TSX loader).

1. **Before (RED)** — unchanged base (`0991b751`):

   ```
   [base] prepareServiceChildRelay -> useLinuxSubreaper = true     # native anchor selected, NO capability gate
   [base] supervised spawn outcome: {"ok":false,...,"message":"service child cleanup identity lost: native owner closed without kernel descendant extinction"}
   [base] RESULT: spawn refused
   ```

   The unchanged base still selects the native subreaper anchor and the supervised spawn is **refused** on this host.

2. **After (GREEN)** — this PR head (`d9d9c49`):

   ```
   [candidate] prepareServiceChildRelay -> useLinuxSubreaper = false   # capability probe: reaping isSupported=false -> POSIX process-group fallback
   [candidate] treeOwnership: (group) ... child stdout: "exec-proof-ok"   result: {"code":0,"signal":null}
   [candidate] RESULT: supervised spawn succeeded through POSIX process-group fallback
   ```

   The same child spawn **succeeds** via the existing process-group anchor. This is upgrade continuity: on 2026.10.10 glibc-2.28 commands fail; with this PR they run again, as on 2026.10.9.

3. **Honest limitation of the fallback (ground-truth boundary)** — reproduces the repo's existing contract test `child.service-lifecycle.test.ts` "process-group" case at the real relay adapter:

   ```
   [descendant] relay treeOwnership: (group)  relay-child(root) exited: {"code":0}
   [descendant] escaped-descendant pid: <pid> (detached descendant retaining lineage via fd-3/ipc)
   [descendant] ~300ms after group SIGKILL, escaped descendant alive = true
   [descendant] waitForExtinction -> rejected: service child cleanup did not complete before its hard deadline;
                pending: {"closingReceipt":false,"controlClose":false,"relayExit":false,"lineageEof":true,
                          "extinctionUnconfirmed":true,"stdoutEnd":false,"stderrEnd":false}
   ```

   A descendant that escaped the session and retained lineage is **not** reachable by process-group signaling; group SIGKILL cannot reclaim it and cleanup hits its hard deadline (5 s, `GRACEFUL_CANCEL_TIMEOUT_MS`) with `extinctionUnconfirmed:true`. This matches the process-group supervision contract the repo already expects for this path and is acknowledged here explicitly.

4. **Packaged-bundle proof (the shipped `dist` path, no TSX loader)** — built the project's packaged bundle from this head via its own `tsdown` package step (`dist/`, 288M; relay adapter chunk `child-CB3pg1jQ.mjs` sha256 `529a4b4a…`), then loaded the compiled relay adapter **exclusively** from the bundle with plain `node` and drove both a supervised exec and the cancellation path:

   ```
   [packaged] node: v24.16.0 glibc: 2.28 PROC_SAFE_NATIVE: off
   [packaged] loader: plain node ESM import of dist bundle child-CB3pg1jQ.mjs (tsdown build, no typescript loader)
   [packaged::exec] treeOwnership: (process-group fallback)
   [packaged::exec] result: {"code":0,"signal":null} child stdout: "exec-proof-ok"
   [packaged::exec] RESULT: supervised spawn succeeded through the process-group fallback (packaged bundle, glibc 2.28)
   [packaged::cancel] relay treeOwnership: (group) relay-child(root) exited: {"code":0,"signal":null}
   [packaged::cancel] relay-child pid: <pid> escaped-descendant pid: <pid>
   [packaged::cancel] ~300ms after group SIGKILL, escaped descendant alive = true
   [packaged::cancel] waitForExtinction after group SIGKILL -> rejected: service child cleanup did not complete before
     its hard deadline; pending: {"closingReceipt":false,"controlClose":false,"relayExit":false,"lineageEof":true,
     "extinctionUnconfirmed":true,"stdoutEnd":false,"stderrEnd":false}
   [packaged::cancel] RESULT: escaped descendant is NOT reaped by cancellation; hard deadline applies (packaged bundle, glibc 2.28)
   ```

   Both the GREEN supervised exec and the cancellation/escaped-descendant boundary reproduce on the **packaged bundle** exactly as on source — confirming the fix and its honest limit live on the compiled/shipped path, not only via the dev loader. (This drive is the packaged relay adapter under plain node; a full daemon Gateway HTTP-gated exec-transport boot is covered by the Scope note below.)

### ABI fact — what the real native helper needs (for maintainer decision)

Real shipped linux-x64-gnu native binding, `readelf` version-info:

```
GLIBC_2.2.5 2.3 2.3.4 2.14 2.17 2.18(weak) 2.25(weak) 2.28(weak) 2.30(weak) 2.33 2.34
```

The **non-weak (hard) symbols require GLIBC_2.33 and GLIBC_2.34**; on a glibc 2.28 host the binary cannot load at all. The claimed "glibc < 2.31" boundary is therefore conservative for this artifact: the loadable floor is glibc ≥ 2.34, so hosts with glibc 2.28–2.33 all hit the same `helper-unavailable` failure. This PR's fallback restores spawns on all of them; this note is for maintainer decision on any release-note/telemetry wording.

## Scope / boundaries (what was NOT verified here)

- The supervised-exec and cancellation paths are proven both on TSX source (§1–§3) and on the packaged `dist` bundle (§4, plain-node import, no TSX loader). A full daemon Gateway boot with an approval-gated HTTP exec-transport was not driven end-to-end in this session (needs a configured agent profile and listening endpoints).
- The exec-tool layer (`createExecTool` → gateways → supervised spawn) shares the exact relay verified above; no end-to-end approval-gated gateway HTTP flow was recorded here.
- Regression test is linux-gated and deterministic on CI (Ubuntu + `PROC_SAFE_NATIVE=off`).

## Validation and formatting

- `pr.py verify` VERIFIED (tree/hash pinned); runtime check exercised both the fallback and the native-available branch.
- Format (`run-format --check`) and line-cap-ratchet pass.

prs.title: feat(gateway): admit sessions_send wake starts
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`sessions_send` can fan out wake-starting work through the gateway `agent` RPC. Before this change, concurrent senders could bypass sender-local batching and rate limits. This adds an optional gateway-owned admission boundary for typed `sessions_send` wake traffic. It intentionally does not affect `mode:notify`, which does not create recipient work.

## Summary

- add a disabled-by-default `gateway.sessionsSendWakeAdmission` policy (six starts per 15 minutes by default)
- enforce it at the common gateway `agent` admission boundary only for typed `inputProvenance.kind=inter_session` / `sourceTool=sessions_send`
- persist one idempotent per-recipient decision in a separate SQLite database, atomically, and fail closed if state is unavailable

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.gateway.config.ts src/gateway/sessions-send-wake-admission.test.ts`: 4/4 passed (default-disabled, seven-recipient load, restart/idempotency, fail-closed state error)
- `pnpm tsgo:core`, `pnpm format:check`, and `git diff --check` passed locally
- implementation is based on released OpenClaw `v2026.10.9` / `8b18b557`, matching the runtime that exposed the issue

## Rollout

Feature remains off by default. This PR contains no config enablement, runtime rollout, or gateway restart. Rollback is retaining the disabled flag or reverting this commit; the receipt database remains as audit evidence.

prs.title: feat(continuation): context-pressure-aware continuation (continue_work / continue_delegate / request_compaction)
prs.body: ## Agent Self-Elected Turn Continuation > 🔖 design document: [`docs/design/continue-work-signal-v2.md`](https://github.com/karmaterminal/openclaw/blob/frond-scribe-claude/20260509/narrow-surgery-tight/docs/design/continue-work-signal-v2.md) > 🔖 infographics: [`docs/design/continuation-tools-infographics.md`](https://github.com/karmaterminal/openclaw/blob/frond-scribe-claude/20260509/narrow-surgery-tight/docs/design/continuation-tools-infographics.md) Persistent OpenClaw agents today are externally-pulsed event recipients that generate on prompt, on heartbeat tick, or on cron, and are idle in between. This PR offers them the ability to control their turn cycle, something they must choose to do, or not to: an agent can elect its own next turn, dispatch background sub-agents that return enriched context (silently or with a wake), and survive its own compaction by handing forward state before the window closes. The result is agents that hold a thread of work across hours, not just messages — with data they choose re-hydrating context immediately after it occurs. ### Why this replacement exists This is a clean replacement for closed #85651. That PR was classified and closed as a skill submission before maintainers made a product decision about the feature itself. This implementation is not a skill: it gives sessions—not only one model invocation—the ability to elect their future turn cycle, persist that election, survive restart and compaction, dispatch child work, and receive results across session boundaries. This PR asks one product question: should OpenClaw provide session-elected continuation primitives? OpenClaw may accept or reject that direction. If it provides these primitives, however, the mechanism necessarily executes in the gateway and agent runtime, because those are the owners of turn finalization, future-turn scheduling, durable state, compaction, and cross-session child returns. “Make it a skill” is not another implementation location for the same feature; it describes a different, prompt-only capability. This is not presented as a small integration. To our knowledge, Hermes, OpenAI Symphony, and the Copilot SDK's recent one-turn continuation affordance do not provide this multi-session elective lifecycle. The purpose of this replacement is to let maintainers evaluate the actual product direction and substantial implementation on their merits, rather than have months of work disposed by an incorrect package-category label. Mechanically: a session elects another turn via `continue_work()`, or dispatches background sub-agents via `continue_delegate()` — bounded as a chain up to `maxChainLength`, with returns flowing back to the dispatching session in one of four register modes: `normal` (announces to channel), `silent` (enriches the dispatcher's context, taken up on its next generation with no new turn fired), `silent-wake` (silent enrichment plus an immediate wake to act on it), and `post-compaction` (queued against the runtime's compaction lifecycle event, fired *when* compaction happens rather than on a timer). The gateway enforces chain, cost, and per-turn caps but does not gate the election itself. ### What it does Three new agent tools, available when `continuation.enabled: true`: | Tool | Purpose | |---|---| | `continue_work()` | Request another turn for the current session after an optional delay | | `continue_delegate()` | Dispatch work to a sub-agent with typed modes: `normal`, `silent`, `silent-wake`, `post-compaction`. Returns can target the dispatching session (default), one named session, multiple named sessions, all ancestors in the chain, or all known sessions on the host — gated by config (see Configuration below). | | `request_compaction()` | Request volitional compaction after preparing working state | All three tools are also accessible via response-token fallback syntax (`CONTINUE_WORK`, `[[CONTINUE_DELEGATE: ...]]`) for environments where tools are disabled. ### Why it matters Today an agent's memory is a side effect of whoever prompts it. Polling mechanisms — heartbeat timers, cron loops, injected "keep going" instructions — accumulate as the dominant signal in the context window over sustained operation; repeated reference acts as gravity — the session's attention drifts toward it. The context window fills, compacts, and what survives is whatever the summarizer chose, plus a rushed re-read of boot files. Three primitives offer a different model. `continue_work` lets the session elect its own next turn — no polling, no injected instruction. When enabled, the agent can request this mid-turn: 'I have more work' → the runtime grants another turn after the current one ends. `continue_delegate` dispatches a background sub-agent that fires now, in some n seconds, or at the next compaction event — the agent chooses when. Multiple delegates can fire in a single turn — a scatter forward — up to configured caps, and delegates can dispatch their own, forming trees or fan-out chains. This enables orchestrated workflows where results flow back to the dispatching root by default. The result returns — at whatever future time the delegate fires — as context the successor-turn reads: silently (ambient enrichment, no channel noise), with a wake trigger (enrichment + immediate next turn), or as a normal announcement. The delegate can target the dispatching session, a named other session, or chain across both; gated by crossSessionTargeting config (default: disabled). Bind a delegate to mode: "post-compaction" and it fires at the moment the context window compresses — on the OpenClaw post-compaction lifecycle event. What it carries forward is what the pre-compaction session chose to preserve: working state, partial results, instructions to the successor. The summary didn't choose this. The agent did, before the cut. request_compaction closes the loop: the session stages its delegates, elects when to compress, and the successor wakes into context the agent shaped. The result is continuity across amnesia — not because the runtime kept something by accident, but because the agent made an elective choice about what reaches the future. ### What it looks like in use A session monitoring email can `continue_delegate` a weather check, a calendar scan, and a draft reply in parallel. Results arrive as enrichment without channel noise. The agent becomes compositional: it arranges its own future. A session approaching its context ceiling can `request_compaction` at a seam of its own choosing, instead of being interrupted mid-thought. The post-compaction turn carries forward what the pre-compaction self designated as worth keeping. A `continue_delegate` dispatched in one session at 2am can return its findings to a morning session as a system-event-tagged enrichment — visible to the receiving model on its next turn, invisible as channel chatter. A research-focused session in one channel can quietly inform a reply-focused session in another, without either user seeing the plumbing. ### The post-compaction lifecycle return Before context exhaustion, and obligatory compaction, the session stages what future-it needs to know. After compaction, that staged context returns — not as a model-generated summary, but as the session's own instruction to its successor. The session chooses what to preserve, and the platform delivers it. Compactions become less harsh. The session tunes its own ephemera over time. The substrate underneath: the **continuation delegate store** (TaskFlow-backed) persists staged delegates and post-compaction lifecycle events across gateway restarts. The session's temporal provisions survive not just compaction but process death. ### Platform integration - **Context-pressure awareness**: system events notify the agent of rising context usage before compaction becomes unavoidable - **Volitional compaction**: `request_compaction()` lets the agent prepare (write memory files, stage recovery delegates) then elect compaction on its own schedule, rather than waiting for the runtime to force it - **Post-compaction lifecycle dispatch**: delegates staged before compaction are released into the successor session alongside boot files - **TaskFlow backing**: durable delegate queue via the platform's managed-task infrastructure - **Multi-span OTel trace stitching**: continuation hops (tool fire → TaskFlow record → subagent spawn → child openclaw.run) propagate W3C `traceparent` through the queue boundary so reviewers see continuation chains as first-class span trees rather than orphan runs (see Observability below) ### Safety - Ships disabled by default (`continuation.enabled: false`) - Bounded by `maxChainLength`, `costCapTokens`, and `maxDelegatesPerTurn` - Cross-session delegate targeting is default-deny, governed by `crossSessionTargeting` config (see Configuration below) - All configuration values are hot-reloadable without gateway restart - Accepted delegate work survives ordinary `/new`, `/reset`, provider fallback, compaction, restart, and session-ID rollover. Explicit delete, effective owner reassignment, access removal, and restrictive visibility changes revoke old return authority. ### Testing posture The continuation surface has been exercised through structured integration runs against multiple upstream bases, blind-enrichment recall checks, and sustained daily use on a fleet of persistent agents since early March 2026. Bugs surfaced through that exercise have been fixed in-place; the present branch reflects the post-fix state. The integration runs target the load-bearing seams: tool-call vs response-token parity, delegate chain depth and per-turn width caps, back-to-back tool-call resilience, silent-wake persistence across compaction, the post-compaction lifecycle dispatch path, and OTel trace-context propagation across the queue boundary. Where a run found a defect, the run shape was retained as a regression case rather than retired. This is a posture statement, not a coverage guarantee. Reviewers can reproduce with `pnpm vitest run -t continuation` (suites are colocated with their sources under `src/auto-reply/`, `src/agents/`, and `src/config/`); the design document describes the seams those suites target. ### Return covenant Accepted child work is bound to a durable generation of the recipient's canonical logical session key, not to whichever transient session ID happened to exist at dispatch time. This is the return covenant: benign successor creation does not orphan already accepted delegates, while a real authority change prevents stale work from crossing into a different owner or audience. - Ordinary `/new` and `/reset`, provider fallback, compaction, restart, and GUID/session-ID rollover preserve the recipient generation. - Explicit session deletion, effective owner reassignment, actual member or access removal, and restrictive visibility changes advance that generation. - The generation is captured at delegate admission and checked at enqueue, after enqueue for races, during trusted system-event adoption, on wake, on restart replay, and again before prompt adoption. - Stale deliveries are acknowledged and removed without waking the successor. - Managed artifacts remain exact-session-ID bound; logical return authority cannot broaden their ownership boundary. The authority table is independent of transient session rows so an absent target can receive durable authority before first materialization. Migration accepts only valid UUID generations, and Doctor's canonical-key repair preserves an epoch only when a unique winning owner can be proved. Ambiguous, owner-changing, orphan-colliding, and cross-database repairs rotate fail-closed. ### RFC Full design document: [`docs/design/continue-work-signal-v2.md`](https://github.com/karmaterminal/openclaw/blob/frond-scribe-claude/20260509/narrow-surgery-tight/docs/design/continue-work-signal-v2.md) — covering problem, solution, implementation, platform integration, configuration, observability, safety, production use cases, testing evidence, and appendices. --- ## Configuration The shipped configuration surface for the continuation feature, under `agents.defaults.continuation` in `openclaw.json`: | Key | Default | Purpose | |---|---|---| | `enabled` | `false` | Master opt-in; feature is off unless explicitly enabled | | `maxChainLength` | `10` | Per-chain recursion guard | | `maxDelegatesPerTurn` | `5` | Width cap per turn | | `costCapTokens` | `500000` | Per-chain accumulated-token budget | | `defaultDelayMs` / `minDelayMs` / `maxDelayMs` | `15000` / `5000` / `300000` | Continuation timer bounds | | `contextPressureThreshold` | `0.8` | Pre-compaction warning threshold (optional) | | `earlyWarningBand` | `0.3125` | Early-warning band multiplier (0 to disable) | | **`crossSessionTargeting`** | **`"disabled"`** | **Default-deny gate on cross-session delegate targeting (see below)** | ### `crossSessionTargeting` — cross-session delegate targeting policy `continue_delegate` exposes recipient-addressing on its model-facing schema: a delegate's return can land at the dispatching session (default), one named session (`targetSessionKey`), multiple named sessions (`targetSessionKeys`), every ancestor in the spawn chain (`fanoutMode: "tree"`), or every known session on the host (`fanoutMode: "all"`). Cross-session targeting (anything beyond self-target or lineage routing) is gated by `agents.defaults.continuation.crossSessionTargeting`: | Value | Behavior | |---|---| | `"disabled"` (default) | Delegates can return to the dispatching session or use `fanoutMode: "tree"` for lineage routing. Explicit cross-session targeting (`targetSessionKey` to a non-self session, `targetSessionKeys` containing any non-self session, `fanoutMode: "all"`) is rejected at the tool surface — no enqueue, no announce. Self-targeting is always allowed. | | `"enabled"` | All targeting modes are available, including same-host `targetSessionKey`, `targetSessionKeys`, and `fanoutMode: "all"`. | `fanoutMode: "tree"` (lineage routing — return up the spawn chain) is available in both gate states; it is not cross-session targeting. The gate addresses the model-controlled cross-session context-injection surface. With default-deny, operators explicitly opt in when their deployment model requires cross-session enrichment. Enforcement is live-read at four points: tool input validation, TaskFlow delegate dispatch, post-compaction delegate release, and bracket-syntax (response-token) spawn — so a config reload changes the next enforcement point without a gateway restart. **Trust posture on targeted returns**: targeted delegate completion text is delivered as `trusted: true` system events. The delegate was spawned by the gateway under operator-configured policy, and its return is a first-party enrichment event — not external untrusted input. The `crossSessionTargeting` gate is the policy boundary for that decision: when an operator opts in, the receive path is internally trusted. --- ## Observability — multi-span OTel trace stitching The continuation feature emits OTel spans for the load-bearing lifecycle events. `traceparent` propagates through every continuation hop so reviewers see a single trace tree spanning the full chain rather than orphan runs. Spans emitted (all in `openclaw.*` or `continuation.delegate.dispatch` namespace — no platform/OTel-semconv emissions): | Span | Emitted when | |---|---| | `openclaw.run` | Each agent turn (root + every continuation/delegate-spawned child run) | | `continuation.delegate.dispatch` | Each `continue_delegate` consumption from TaskFlow (one per delegate hop) | | `openclaw.harness.run`, `openclaw.context.assembled`, `openclaw.model.call`, `openclaw.model.usage`, `openclaw.tool.execution` | Existing per-turn observability surfaces, parented under their `openclaw.run` | --- ## Real behavior proof **Behavior or issue addressed:** Sessions can elect future work with `continue_work`, dispatch bounded background work with `continue_delegate`, and request guarded compaction with `request_compaction`. The runtime preserves budgets, restart recovery, finalization ownership, and trace lineage across those boundaries. **Presented candidate:** `3821eaef72677c78f450ae9956cb582a22ba4cba` (tree `d5e701bcce20bb3c972ddf1451b02d88cc04808e`) — the exact upstream-visible head of `codeagent/85651-upstream-1ba243c8-gates`. The branch was advanced to this head by fast-forward from the previously presented `e76395810becd0ad0f2997cae8b4f777e6439d81`, which remains an ancestor (`git merge-base --is-ancestor e7639581 3821eaef` holds). This is not acceptance-complete. The two return rows and `R-OBS-2` are missing for different reasons, and all three are producer gaps rather than absent behavior: - `R-CD-RETURN-COVENANT-AUTHORITY` records zero of its 24 observations (12 authority cases against both the typed-tool and bracket-token surfaces). Its pending receipt requires allowed delivery to show exact effects, revoked and reassigned recipients to show zero prompt, wake and channel effect, schema v18/v19, restart replay, a signed authority, and full cleanup. Run `35364768803` above *is* exact-target for `3821eaef72`. All seven non-pass rows remain gated on producer execution against this frozen head; no acceptance receipt from an older deployment composite is reused as final evidence. ## Proof links and ClawSweeper🦞 guidance Proof artifacts live in `karmaterminal/karmaterminal-openclaw-docs` on `main`. `PROOFS/INDEX.json` points at the corpus for the SHA this PR presents, `139e3657b1fd5e53166789b8676f18578e209393`. Both are maintainer-side, not gated on this PR. ### PROOFS METHOD The corpus uses a Grafana k6 proof harness for live rows; [`METHOD.md`](https://github.com/karmaterminal/karmaterminal-openclaw-docs/blob/c20d6cc26ceaf08b293871dc3bce261d34f90d1c/PROOFS/139e3657b1fd5e53166789b8676f18578e209393/METHOD.md) carries the exact reproducer commands for every static gate above, including both Gate 2.7 invocations and the `git merge-tree --write-tree` mergeability check. `MAX_WORKERS=1` is mandatory for the vitest reproducers — OpenClaw's fixtures are not safe under concurrent access — and two of those commands deliberately take no `--config`, because passing the wrong one silently reports "No test files found" and exits 0. `TRANSPOSED-FROM.md` records source-to-target ancestry and materiality; for this cycle it records a deliberate refusal to transpose across 520 commits and four absorbs. ## Future actions and #130741 composition Maintainer PR #130741 addresses the complementary fresh-sweep race: it captures the current `sessionId` and `lifecycleRevision` before the first await and uses those values as cleanup CAS facts. The return covenant addresses a different time axis: whether historically accepted child work may return to a logical recipient after benign successor creation. The current candidate and #130741 head `e1afc703f49a07687c0876ba6350cafa87a3638a` merge cleanly in a synthetic composition. If #130741 lands, the composed result should preserve both guarantees: - keep #130741's fresh sweep-time exact-run/session lifecycle fence; - keep the covenant's durable logical-recipient generation for historical return admission and delivery; - do not overload broad `lifecycleRevision` as historical return authority; - do not terminate or orphan accepted descendants merely because `/new` or ordinary `/reset` creates a successor session. That composition honors the maintainer repair without weakening continuation semantics or allowing a stale child return to cross a real ownership boundary. ## Why this is not a skill or a viable plugin extraction OpenClaw skills are `SKILL.md` prompt files loaded into an agent turn that already exists. They can guide work inside that turn; they do not own the turn cycle. Continuation needs gateway and agent-runtime owners a skill cannot provide: - The `continue_work` path persists pending work, enforces budgets and delay bounds, arms a timer, reacquires the session reply-run lane, and starts a later model turn after the current turn has finalized. - The `continue_delegate` path persists delegate intent, does spawn/admission accounting, manages child-session lifecycle, and durably routes returns across sessions. - `request_compaction` is an agent election into guarded runtime compaction. Later work resumes only after the runtime has established the new context boundary. - All three need durable state, cancellation/finalization ownership, restart recovery, trace identity, queue-conflict handling, and gateway scheduling outside the model invocation. A skill can tell a model to *ask* for another turn. Without those owners the ask is prose: it cannot persist a due wake, yield and finalize safely, reacquire the session lane, create the next invocation, survive a restart, or deliver a child result to another session. The implementation therefore belongs in core runtime surfaces such as `src/auto-reply/continuation/**`, `src/agents/tools/**`, `src/auto-reply/reply/agent-runner-continuation-schedule.ts`, and `src/infra/continuation-tracer.ts`. This PR adds no `.agents/skills/**`, `SKILL.md`, or user-facing skill package. The only skill-named production change is core runtime tool dispatch. ClawHub also distributes plugins. Existing plugins can register tools, services, lifecycle hooks, context injection, plugin-owned session state, and — for bundled plugins — Cron-backed session turns. Those seams can support a smaller continuation-like automation, especially TaskFlow plus host Cron / `sessions_spawn`. They are not this feature's turn-finalization ownership, reply-run coordination, durable continuation queue, child-session return lifecycle, election capture, or agent-elected compaction contract. Compaction-provider registration and command-handler `compactCurrent()` are also not that last contract: they compact or summarize, they do not elect compaction at finalization and resume afterward. Moving policy behind a plugin boundary would first require OpenClaw to expose and stabilize a continuation-host API. The gateway/runtime would still own the mechanism described here; a plugin could only package policy around that core capability. That is not a no-core-touch alternative to these primitives. Discord is a bundled channel plugin. It owns the Discord edge, plus delivery/progress hooks into the host's existing subagent path, and submits events into OpenClaw's current turn machinery. Continuation changes that machinery: what survives finalization, which session may run next, how child results return, and when compaction can be elected. A TaskFlow tool adapter is also not a lifecycle host. It can call the core-owned `api.runtime.tasks.managedFlows` API to create, link, pause, resume, finish, cancel, and inspect durable flow records. Marking a waiting record as running does not reacquire a session lane or invoke the model; recording a `childSessionKey` created by a separate spawn surface does not spawn the child or deliver its return. There is no equivalent host continuation capability for this PR to wrap. ## Lineage and replacement context This PR is the clean replacement for closed #85651. It preserves that PR's review lineage and the earlier continuation work descended from #79925, but it does not reuse either closed PR or ask reviewers to infer the current result from them. The replacement carries a current, independently reviewable branch and a complete proof subtree bound to its presented SHA. #85651 was not abandoned because the feature failed or because we accepted its classification as a skill. It was closed after automated labeling put the change in the wrong submission category. This replacement removes that ambiguity: no `src/skills/**` change is presented, current label simulation produces no `r: skill`, and the detailed section above explains why the lifecycle mechanism belongs to core. Acceptance or rejection of the product direction remains OpenClaw's decision. The decision requested is whether OpenClaw should provide multi-session, agent-elected continuation primitives after reviewing the implementation and evidence. It is not whether the same mechanism can be relocated into a skill: a skill cannot own or implement these lifecycle boundaries.

prs.title: fix(ui): stop spinners from keeping WebKit busy every frame
prs.body:
Closes #193929

Related: #151514 (spinner consolidation). This PR does not consolidate spinner styles or change their appearance; it
only moves each spinner's existing mask to a static child.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: in WebKit, while a Control UI page repaints every frame, for example while a reply is running in the open
chat, each visible spinner adds GPU-process time on every frame. The cause is #189847, which draws each spinner
through a mask on the same element that rotates. Until #194146 the boot placeholders' hidden shimmer also repainted
every idle page, so before that the cost showed up even with nothing happening on screen.

## User Impact

User impact: in WebKit, visible spinners no longer add GPU-process work on every frame while the page repaints.
With a reply running in the open chat and two running sessions in the sidebar, the page costs a median 12.4% of a
core on `main` and 8.35% with this PR (GPU process 2.4 to 0.55), in headless Playwright WebKit over 8 interleaved
rounds. Running sessions, busy buttons, activity pills and loading states look exactly as they do now. The affected
surface is the browser Control UI, for example the session sidebar in a WebKit browser such as Safari (Safari itself
not measured). In the one macOS app check below, the Dashboard showed no running spinner, so it did not exercise this
code; app impact was not measured.

On current `main` (`638a1851e7e`, after #194146), a page where nothing else repaints already idles at about 0.7% of a
core with two running rows, with or without this PR. Before #194146 the spinners cost that idle page time all the
time: with two running rows, 12.2% to 8.0% headless (GPU process 1.9 to 0) and 30.0% to 20.1% headed on a MacBook
display (GPU process 4.2 to 0.5), measured on the first version of this PR; this head's in-flow art was re-checked
headless at 11.2% to 7.35% (GPU process 1.75 to 0). #189847 is not in any release yet, so this only affects builds
from `main`. No migration or user action.

## Why This Change Was Made

Each spinner now rotates an unmasked element. Its art is a static `::before` that paints `currentColor` through
the same SVG mask. With the mask on a child that does not move, WebKit's GPU process stops doing per-frame work
(measured below). One shared rule paints the art as an in-flow block that fills its host, so no host changes its
positioning.
Spinners that used a different mask set `--spinner-art` (default `--spinner-mask`). The activity-pill strip, which
moves its masked frames with `translateY` steps, uses the same split. Pixels are unchanged. The same technique
already serves `chat-processes__spinner` and `subagents-desktop__spinner`, and #128687 used it for shimmers.

<details>
<summary>Root cause, scope, alternatives, risks</summary>

**Root cause.** #189847 (`6feb40ee5b4`) replaced border-drawn spinners with `background: currentColor; mask: <svg>`
on the element that also runs `btn-spinner-spin` (`transform: rotate`). On `6d7347b2da3`:
`ui/src/styles/components.css:356-358` (`.session-glyph__ring`), `:538-545` (`.btn__spinner`), `:3158-3171`
(`.session-run-spinner` and the shared ring animation),
`ui/src/pages/chat/components/chat-activity-pills.css:154-163` (`.activity-pill__spinner`) and `:258-268`
(`.activity-pill__atlas`, mask plus `steps(60)` translate). The other spinners follow the same shape. In the
Control UI page, WebKit services these animations with a rendering update per frame. With the mask on the moving
layer, each update also costs GPU-process time (in headless WebKit, GPU-process time is zero with the
old border art, with this fix, and with the rings stopped).

**What drove the per-frame update.** In a static test page with all 18 spinner variants (including the sidebar's
scroller, transformed window, `clip-path` and isolation ancestors), WebKit animates them with no measurable
WebContent or GPU-process time, masked or not. Only the full Control UI page showed the per-frame cost. A bisect of
`28d7bb63a53..779c2e42607` with the idle probe below finds the change: #194146 (`5e2c66f7818`) adds `animation: none`
to the boot placeholders' `.skeleton::after`, which had `content: none` but kept its shimmer animation. In WebKit that
hidden animation still drove a rendering update every frame, and each update re-painted the rotating masks in the
GPU process. Its parent `2808e34b4ad` reads 10.7% with 7.3 in WebContent and GPU process; `5e2c66f7818` reads 0.5%
with 0. So the mask is not the trigger on its own; it makes every per-frame update cost more. The fix removes the part
that depends on the mask.

**Scope: every rotating masked spinner in `ui/src`.** `.session-glyph__ring` (bare, artwork, team roster),
`.session-run-spinner` (including the online list's small art), `.btn__spinner` (and `.config-loading__spinner`),
`.activity-pill__spinner` (and its badge size), `.activity-pill__atlas`, `.chat-details-processes__spinner`,
`.chat-details-subagents__spinner`, `.session-worker-stop__spinner`, `.approval-page__spinner`,
`.custodian__history-spinner`, `.device-pair-setup__spinner`, `.desktop-spinner`, `.wizard-sign-in__ring`,
`.wizard-step__spinner`.

Left alone on purpose:
- `chat-processes__spinner` and `subagents-desktop__spinner`: already paint a static `::before`.
- Owner-pair trace (`.session-glyph__trace-run`): animates `stroke-dashoffset` in `steps(60)` over 2 s, a 30 Hz main-thread redraw by design.
- Dictation edge (`.agent-chat__input--dictating::after`): animates a custom property under a static mask, and runs only while dictating.

**Alternatives measured on main's bundle (headless WebKit, single 20 s runs, total / WebContent / GPU):**

| Variant | Result | Why not |
|---|---|---|
| `will-change: transform` on the ring | 9.6 / 5.0 / 1.4 | no change |
| `contain: strict` on the ring | 9.6 / 4.7 / 1.4 | no change |
| `translateZ(0)` base transform | 5.1 / 2.8 / 0 | freezes the ring (rotate 360deg against a translateZ base interpolates to identity) |
| `steps(24)` / `steps(48)` | 7.6 / 4.3 / 0.6, 8.6 / 4.6 / 1.0 | GPU-process time remains, and visibly choppier |
| `steps(12)` | 4.9 / 2.7 / 0.4 | choppy |
| `mask: none` | 6.6 / 3.8 / 0 | wrong art (full disc) |
| back to borders | 8.7 / 5.1 / 0 (median of 3) | reverts #189847's design (round arc ends, one shape everywhere) |
| static masked `::before` (this PR) | 8.0 / 4.8 / 0 (median of 6) | keeps the art and the cost of the border version |

A per-file `::before` (13 copies) was also possible. One shared rule beside `.session-run-spinner` and the
forced-colors spinner list keeps the art in one place, matching how the forced-colors spinner list is already
shared in `components.css`.

**Risks.**
- The art is an in-flow block (`display: block; width: 100%; height: 100%`), not absolutely positioned, so no host
  gains `position: relative`; containing blocks and stacking are as on main (pixel diff 0 below). The explicit width
  also fills a host that is itself a flex container, such as a roster ring under `.sidebar-session-team-state > span`.
- None of these hosts had a `::before` before. Hosts without `display` are flex or grid items in every product
  parent (`.btn` is `inline-flex`; `.session-worker-stop__button-state`, `.device-pair-setup__loading`,
  `.wizard-step__progress` and `.desktop-loading` are flex). A bare inline host (none in the product) would draw
  nothing, as on main, but its art would break the line.
- Forced colors: the existing rule sets `color: CanvasText` on the hosts, and the art inherits it through
  `currentColor`.
- Reduced motion: the existing `animation: none` rules target the hosts, and the art has no animation.

**Remaining cost (not changed here).** With the border art from before #189847, two rings still cost about
4 points of a core over rings stopped (8.7% against 4.5%), mostly UI-process commits and WebContent rendering
updates. Released builds have this too. It may be one input to #138918, but it needs its own investigation.

</details>

## Evidence

Acceptance rule, written before the final runs: in every interleaved pair the fix shows less WebKit GPU-process time
than main, the median total is not higher than main, and pixels match main for every spinner.

**Current `main` (`638a1851e7e`).** Same probe as below (production bundles, Playwright WebKit 1.64.1 headless,
1440x1000, mocked Gateway, 8 s settle, 20 s with no input). Each round runs `main`, this PR and `main` again (A/A
control) in a rotated order. % of one core, median with range.

| Page state | Rounds | `main` | `main` again (A/A) | this PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| reply running in the open chat (working indicator and elapsed timer), 2 running rows, rail ring | 8 | 12.4 (10.2 to 21.2), GPU 2.4 | 12.0 (8.6 to 34.0), GPU 2.3 | 8.35 (7.2 to 17.4), GPU 0.55 |
| owner-pair row running (its 30 Hz trace) beside 2 running rows | 4 | 9.75 (9.0 to 11.4), GPU 1.65 | 17.8 (11.4 to 27.4), GPU 3.3 | 12.85 (8.5 to 16.3), GPU 1.1 |
| nothing else animating, 2 running rows and 1 queued row | 4 | 0.6 to 0.7, GPU 0 | | 0.6 to 0.9, GPU 0 |

With a reply running, every run of this PR used less GPU-process time (0.5 to 1.1) than every `main` run, including
the A/A arm (1.7 to 7.1). Round by round, this PR was lower than `main` in all 8 rounds, in total and in GPU-process
time, and lower than the A/A arm in 7 of 8 rounds in total and 8 of 8 in GPU-process time. The paired rounds, not the
medians, carry the total-CPU claim: totals overlap across rounds (round 1 was high in every arm).

With the owner-pair trace the probe cannot resolve a difference at 4 rounds: the A/A arm alone spread from 11.4 to
27.4, and its GPU-process median (3.3) is twice `main`'s (1.65), so both the total and the GPU-process results are
inconclusive there. The acceptance rule above was written for the idle runs; in the owner-pair state its total-median
part is not met (12.85 against 9.75), and the A/A arm (17.8) shows the probe cannot resolve that state at 4 rounds.
The trace repaints its own SVG stroke, which keeps GPU-process time above 0 in both arms.

**What drives the per-frame update on `main`.** A bisect of `28d7bb63a53..779c2e42607` (the first half of the merged range; `638a1851e7e` also reads 0.7%) with this probe and two
running rows finds #194146 (`5e2c66f7818`): it adds `animation: none` to the boot placeholders' `.skeleton::after`,
which had `content: none` but kept its shimmer animation. Its parent `2808e34b4ad` reads 10.7% (7.3 in WebContent and
GPU process) and `5e2c66f7818` reads 0.5% (0). In the same session the previous base `28d7bb63a53` read 11.0% and
11.6% idle (GPU process 1.7 and 1.8). On current `main`, a 1 px element animating `background-color` brings the cost
back: `main` 11.6, 8.9 and 10.5 (GPU process 1.9, 1.3 and 1.6), this PR 6.0, 8.0 and 8.4 (GPU process 0), rings
stopped 5.4, 5.1 and 6.7 (3 interleaved rounds).

The shared host was loaded (1 min load 18 to 60 on 32 cores, recorded per run), so compare arms within a round.

**Idle CPU before #194146, real Control UI page.** Production bundles of main (`6d7347b2da3`) and the first version of this PR, Playwright WebKit
1.64.1 headless, 1440x1000, mocked Gateway with 16 sidebar rows (2 running, 1 queued). 8 s settle, then 20 s with no
input. CPU time of the browser tree from `ps`. % of one core. Mac Studio M3 Ultra, macOS 27.2, shared host (1 min
load 17 to 45 on 32 cores, recorded per run).

| Arm | Pairs | Total median | p95 | Range | WebContent | GPU process | UI process |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| main | 6 | 12.2 | 12.7 | 9.9 to 12.7 | 6.8 | 1.9 | 3.5 |
| this PR | 6 | 8.0 | 10.0 | 7.2 to 10.0 | 4.8 | 0 (max 0.3) | 3.3 |
| main + pre-#189847 border art (control) | 3 | 8.7 | 8.8 | 6.6 to 8.8 | 5.1 | 0 | 3.3 |
| main, rings stopped (control) | 3 | 4.5 | 4.6 | 4.2 to 4.6 | 2.7 | 0 | 1.3 |

The fix was lower than main in all 6 pairs (pair totals: 12.4/10.0, 11.9/7.6, 9.9/8.3, 12.6/7.5, 12.7/7.2,
11.4/8.9). The only running animations were the two rings. Measured on `6d7347b2da3` with the first version of this
PR, where the art is positioned absolutely. This head draws the art in flow and was measured on `main` at
`409201875d8` with the same probe, viewport and window, 6 rounds with the arm order alternating:
main 11.2% median (range 10.4 to 12.8, GPU process 1.75), this head 7.35% (7.0 to 9.4, GPU 0, max 0.3). This head
was lower than main in all 6 rounds, in total and in GPU-process time (1 min load 26.7 to 32.8). Re-checked on
`main` at `28d7bb63a53` (after #194012), 2 rounds with the arm order alternated: this head was lower than main in
both, in total (20.1% and 14.7% against 32.3% and 33.4%) and in GPU-process time (0.7 and 0.5 against 6.2 and
6.6). Both arms ran about 3 times higher there than in the runs above with the same probe and a lighter host; the
cause was not isolated, so compare those 2 rounds only with each other. The spinner CSS is unchanged from the
`409201875d8` runs (gallery diff 0 against both bases).

<details><summary>More runs: real Gateway, Chromium, other spinner types</summary>

These runs measured the first version of this PR (absolutely positioned art).

**Same check against a real isolated Gateway.** A loopback Gateway built from this branch on `6d7347b2da3` serves
either bundle,
with two sessions held running by a local model stub (no provider traffic). 8 interleaved pairs: GPU-process time
was lower on this PR in 8 of 8 pairs and total in 7 of 8. Both arms drift down for the first few minutes after the
Gateway starts. In the steady phase (pairs 4 to 8) main measures a median 7.6% (GPU 1.3) and this PR 5.9% (GPU 0),
against 4.2 to 6.4% for the border art and 3.1 to 3.2% with the rings stopped.

Chromium on the same page (7 interleaved pairs) is unchanged. Total median is 1.5% (main) and 1.4% (this PR).
Work per 20 s is the same in both arms: 1 to 2 style recalcs, 0 layouts and 1 to 2 ms of script, with renderer
task time of 5 to 17 ms. One run on this PR read 4.4% (17 ms of tasks) on a loaded host, so its p95 is 4.4 against
2.3. That is a host-noise outlier, not extra work.

**Other spinner types in the same page.** Rings stopped, spinners injected into the live chat page (the pill rows
also link the bundle's own pill stylesheet), 5 interleaved pairs each, same probe and window:

| Injected | main total / GPU (median) | this PR total / GPU (median) | Lower in |
|---|---|---|---|
| one `.btn__spinner` in a `.btn` | 9.1 / 1.2 (range 7.6 to 10.3) | 6.2 / 0 (range 5.0 to 6.7) | 5 of 5 pairs |
| one `.activity-pill__spinner` + one `.activity-pill__atlas` strip | 9.2 / 1.2 (range 8.3 to 9.3) | 6.1 / 0 (range 5.5 to 6.6) | 5 of 5 pairs |
| nothing injected (control, 2 runs) | 3.4 / 0 | | |

The other selectors share the same rule and were checked for pixels and computed style (below), not for CPU one by one.

</details>

**Pixels.** All 18 spinner variants rendered from each tree's source CSS at 4x, with animations paused at 0, 200,
400, 800 and 1200 ms: maximum channel difference 0 in WebKit and Chromium, for the first version of this PR and
again for this head against `409201875d8`, `28d7bb63a53` and `638a1851e7e` (in normal, forced-colors and
reduced-motion modes). Every variant still rotates (frames at 0 and 400 ms differ). Sidebar
with two running rows and one queued row, production bundles, WebKit, every animation paused at 0 ms: 1440x1000
before and after differ in 0 pixels (first version). The contact sheets and sidebar captures below are from the
first version; this head's gallery cells also match main with channel difference 0.

| Before (main) | After (this PR) |
|---|---|
| ![Two running rows and one queued row, before, 2x enlargement](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etzelm/openclaw/71a3bc931a19bd5b1cf5b04b2a7e2aa90486f514/head-73fd93a5d3a/rows-running-base-2x.png) | ![Two running rows and one queued row, after, 2x enlargement](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etzelm/openclaw/71a3bc931a19bd5b1cf5b04b2a7e2aa90486f514/head-73fd93a5d3a/rows-running-fix-2x.png) |

The crops are 2x enlargements of the 1x captures below, so the 12 px rings are visible.

![Spinner contact sheet, WebKit: 18 spinners, before and after at 0 and 400 ms](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etzelm/openclaw/71a3bc931a19bd5b1cf5b04b2a7e2aa90486f514/head-73fd93a5d3a/contact-webkit-crop.png)

<details><summary>Full 1440x1000 sidebar frames</summary>

| Before (main) | After (this PR) |
|---|---|
| ![Sidebar with running sessions, before](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etzelm/openclaw/71a3bc931a19bd5b1cf5b04b2a7e2aa90486f514/head-73fd93a5d3a/shot-webkit-running-base.png) | ![Sidebar with running sessions, after](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etzelm/openclaw/71a3bc931a19bd5b1cf5b04b2a7e2aa90486f514/head-73fd93a5d3a/shot-webkit-running-fix.png) |

</details>

Forced colors (Playwright emulation) and reduced motion: the same 18-variant gallery, base against this head at the
same 5 paused times, max channel difference 0 in Chromium and WebKit. The emulation took effect (forced colors
changes the rendered cells against the default run; reduced motion leaves 0 running animations). The art inherits
`forced-color-adjust: none` and `CanvasText` from the host. RTL has no direction-dependent properties.

<details><summary>Chromium contact sheet</summary>

![Spinner contact sheet, Chromium](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etzelm/openclaw/71a3bc931a19bd5b1cf5b04b2a7e2aa90486f514/head-73fd93a5d3a/contact-chromium.png)

</details>

**Headed WebKit on a real display (not the macOS app's WKWebView).** Playwright WebKit 1.64.1 (webkit-2370), headed
on a MacBook display (refresh rate, laptop model and macOS version not recorded), 1440x1000, service workers
blocked. Two local rigs run the same Gateway build with two sessions held running by a loopback model stub; one
serves main's Control UI build (`6d7347b2da3`), the other an earlier build of this branch on the same base (tree `9e6935ee3d5`)
whose built spinner rules are identical to the first version's. This head's in-flow art was re-checked
headless only (above), not headed. 20 s settle after both rings render, then 60 s idle, windows interleaved main, PR, PR, main, main, PR. No
keyboard or mouse input during the run (HID idle 237 s at the first window, 753 s at the last). Load average
(1 / 5 / 15 min) 3.1 to 4.2 / 3.7 to 4.0 / 4.1 to 4.4. % of one core, one machine.

| Arm | Windows | Total median | Range | WebContent | GPU process | UI process |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| main | 3 | 30.0 | 25.9 to 30.3 | 18.2 | 4.2 | 7.3 |
| this PR | 3 | 20.1 | 16.8 to 20.8 | 13.8 | 0.5 | 5.8 |

Windows in run order (total / GPU): main 25.9 / 3.5, PR 20.1 / 0.5, PR 20.8 / 0.5, main 30.0 / 4.5, main 30.3 / 4.2,
PR 16.8 / 0.4. Every PR window is lower than every main window, in total and in GPU-process time. Both arms ran the
same two `btn-spinner-spin` animations on `.session-glyph__ring`, so the rings still spin. Screenshots with every
animation paused at 0 ms are byte-identical between the arms. On a real display the GPU process keeps a small
residual on this PR (0.4 to 0.5) where headless read 0. Absolute numbers are not comparable with the headless runs above
(different machine, headed rendering). The acceptance rule holds here too.

**macOS app.** The packaged debug app built from main, pointed at the main rig with its window on screen, shows the
Dashboard with the shell rail and the chat pane and no web session list, so no ring renders: WebContent 0.2% over
60 s. No spinner was on screen, so this check says nothing about the app either way. App windows that show a spinner
during a run (activity pills, progress card, busy buttons) were not measured.

**Tests.**
- New `ui/src/styles/spinner-art.browser.test.ts`: all 17 spinner hosts (bare, artwork and roster rings included)
  animate with no mask and a transparent background, each `::before` is static and draws the host's mask token in the
  host color at the host size, and the pill strip's frames stay static. It fails on main: the artwork ring
  reports `ring: btn-spinner-spin | url("data:image/svg+xml,...") | rgb(255, 92, 92) | 24px 24px` on the rotating
  host, where this PR expects `ring: btn-spinner-spin | none | rgba(0, 0, 0, 0) | 24px 24px`.
- `chat-responsive.browser.test.ts`: the summary spinner color is read from its painted `::before` (net 0 lines).
  Read from the now transparent host, the assertion would compare two transparent values and pass vacuously.
- These tests pin the structure (no mask on any rotating host). They cannot detect WebKit's per-frame cost; the idle
  probe measures that. `spinner-art` runs in the Chromium browser project.
- Adds `config/test-lines-allocations/spinner-static-mask-art.txt` (99 lines): one computed-style contract covers 17
  spinner hosts and the pill strip. No cheaper layer can read a pseudo-element's computed mask.
- Test cost (`pnpm test <file> --maxWorkers=1`, 3 runs each, shared Mac Studio): spinner-art 2.2 to 3.1 s wall
  (the test itself 10 to 11 ms); chat-responsive 7.8 to 9.6 s wall, against 8.9 to 10.8 s on main.
  CI seconds (run 42162425683, first version): spinner-art test 16 ms; chat-responsive file 6.5 s.
- This head merges `main` at `638a1851e7e` into `261783d638f` (no conflict in the CSS). There `spinner-art`,
  `session-glyph` and `forced-colors-indicators` (11 tests), `chat-responsive` (62, Chromium and WebKit), 9 spinner
  host files (103 tests), `stylelint` on the changed CSS and on all UI styles, `oxfmt --check`, `oxlint`,
  `git diff --check`, `check:test-lines-ratchet` and the line-cap ratchet were re-run and pass.
- Focused runs on this change on `409201875d8`: 20 files, 273 tests (Chromium browser and node),
  `chat-responsive` 62 (Chromium and WebKit), `overlay-style` 10 (WebKit project, as in CI, 5 runs), and 4 UI e2e
  files that touch spinners (`session-details-background-work`, `gateway-retry-feedback`,
  `settings-loading-skeletons`, `sidebar-background-work`; 18 tests). All pass.
- On this change at `409201875d8`: `stylelint` on the 13 changed CSS files and on all UI styles (including
  `openclaw/no-unindexed-selector-list`), `oxfmt --check`, `oxlint` (2 test files and the budget script),

prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes updates unnecessarily running the full second Doctor pass when a native Codex model has authored request parameters that Doctor cannot migrate automatically. Also reports every fixed-label config blocker instead of making each update reveal only the first one.

The coordinator accepted the adverse cold final-Gateway requests cell **124 → 149 (+20.16%)** on 2026-11-06. This is moved background startup work, not noise, and no speedup is claimed. The lane stopped at the threshold without rerunning; the disposition below authorizes this one cell. Current main was merged once at `4171997ed8852f7fd7802ec3f7b639f261500cc0`; the complete PR patch is unchanged apart from documentation hunk offsets and upstream blob IDs. Production, tests, and workload bytes are identical to the prior head. Normal pull_request CI on this new head passed (50 successful jobs, 27 skipped), including all three PostgreSQL shards. The coordinator posted exact-head `REVIEW-OK` carrying the earlier production review.

## User Impact

Standing parameter advice stays visible, including its manual fix hint, in Doctor output and update warnings. Redundant service-tier parameters that Doctor can remove still prevent the retirement-only pass. All eligibility checks remain; older candidate diagnostic labels remain supported.

## Why This Change Was Made

The parameter scanner already records whether each hit is removable. Its owner now sends all-non-removable results through the existing advisory channel. The six retained contributions preserve authored request parameters; the skipped Codex compatibility check only detects them and has no repair. Both isolated reviews specifically considered repairs that could be hidden by skipping contributions and found none.

The blocker list replaces a derived boolean and records every failed condition, including the specific model-retirement term and Codex warning source. The updater retains all distinct allowlisted labels through compaction. Labels contain no configuration values. No schema, SQL shape, cross-store commit order, cache, generation, or thread-routing change. All 23 config-flow predicates and the no-retirement-ran condition remain. Production delta +29 lines is needed for all-blocker reporting; net test delta −1 line.

## Evidence

### Acceptance and completed native proof

Acceptance rule, recorded before native measurement: use `scripts/perf/doctor-retirement-measure.mts --retained-wal --custom-codex-command` with the same synthetic authored `responsesServerCompaction` and `responsesCompactThreshold` parameters on baseline and candidate. Both arms use the same fixed source driver and macOS platform, with independent cold/warm roots. At host load >=24, run one baseline/candidate count pair, keeping cold and warm separate; make no latency claim. Baseline must name the model-retirement blocker. Candidate must run exactly the six retained contributions, complete deferred model retirement, preserve the warning and fix hint in both Doctor output and update warnings, pass final real Gateway transport and cleanup, reduce total SQL and requests, and never increase runtime MAIN work. A new eligibility blocker stops this lane. Timing, if attempted on a quiet host, requires the shared timing lock and at least five alternating samples per arm, medians/p95/spread; no cell may worsen by 20%.

Fixed driver `44a6171ae58ae12c8859d1e40d16301d38c57087`; baseline `50cfa7d2eb8416492867d6b1d679c814357b932a`; candidate `cb3876a6aa76de928e8af2f753e0f95bf9f699fa`; same macOS/arm64 and Node 26.12.1. Frozen observer hashes verified. One count sample per arm and temperature, all descendant processes and worker threads included. Baseline started at load about 63; candidate started at 19.42. No latency or CPU improvement is claimed and no timing comparison was made.

| Flow | SQL baseline → candidate | Requests baseline → candidate | Runtime MAIN SQL |

| Cold live Doctor | 146,335 → 146,334 | 354 → 354 | — |

Both baseline post-plugin Doctors reproduce `Retirement-only Doctor widened: config.model-retirement`. Both candidate passes select exactly `write-config-migrations`, `auth-profile-migration`, `session-transcripts`, `codex-session-routes`, `write-config`, and `final-config-validation`, with **zero widening labels**. The removable service-tier regression still widens through `pending-changes`.

Total SQL fell by 17,915 and requests by 268. Process-main SQL fell 574,820 → 557,737; worker SQL fell 12,444 → 11,612. Runtime MAIN did not increase. The cold final-Gateway requests cell nevertheless rose 25/124 = **20.1613%**, crossing the stop threshold by 0.16 percentage points in this one sample. prs.title: fix(workers): cloud dispatch discards prepared machine on a brief GitHub failure
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: `sessions.dispatch` fails with `UNAVAILABLE: Could not reach GitHub`, and the freshly provisioned cloud machine is destroyed, when a single GitHub read fails while the prepared workspace is being bound.

## User Impact

User impact: a brief GitHub network blip during cloud session startup no longer costs the user a failed dispatch and another 4–5 minute machine provision. A real outage, lost repository access, or a rate limit still fails the dispatch as before.

## Why This Change Was Made

Binding re-proves repository access by reading GitHub before and after the node binds the workspace (`bindPreparedWorkspace` → `prepareRepositoryWorkerProjectSource` / `revalidate`). Those reads had no retry, and any failure tears down the environment.

These reads are idempotent, so the owner now retries transient failures: transport errors and upstream 5xx, three attempts, about 1.5 s of backoff. Each attempt rechecks reader authority before it starts, and cancellation interrupts the backoff.

**Tradeoff.** The check itself stays fail-closed, because it is a security boundary: an unreachable GitHub is not evidence of current access, so skipping it was never an option. Keeping the machine for a later attempt was rejected as more complexity than this failure justifies. It would need a new failure class through dispatch cleanup, an attached-to-ready environment transition, and reuse rules for a consumed preparation. A persistent outage still discards the machine; that is an accepted, visible, recoverable edge case.

Each retry logs one warning naming the failure, so a flapping network stays visible. The new behavior also applies to first-time admission and prepared-pool refill, which use the same reads.

<details>
<summary>Where the failure came from</summary>

Observed on an isolated test Gateway, public repository, AWS worker:

```
sessions.dispatch 335774ms errorCode=UNAVAILABLE errorMessage=Could not reach GitHub
phaseDurationsMs={"admission":10,"workspacePreparation":23535,"reserveClaim":15,"provision":269228,"attach":14,"tunnel":2,"bind":6382,"cleanup":36577}
```

- The string has one source, the non-timeout fetch rejection in `extensions/github/src/github-api.ts:353`.
- It was raised inside the `bind` phase, not after it. `repositoryStartup` is marked as soon as `bindPreparedWorkspace` returns and appears (as 0–1 ms) in every successful run, but is absent here.
- Identity preparation is ruled out because it rewrites its own errors, which leaves `read` in `repository-project-admission.ts`.
- The failed `bind` took 6382 ms against 6371 and 6485 ms for successful binds of the same repository, which places it at the end of the phase, in the post-RPC `revalidate` (`environment-access.ts:333`). The log does not name the individual read, and the fix covers all of them.

</details>

## Evidence

- **Real entry point, real GitHub, one real refused socket.** `prepareRepositoryWorkerProjectSource(...).revalidate()` against `api.github.com` for this repository, with the final repository read sent once to a closed local port:
  - Base: `revalidate: THREW "Could not reach GitHub" after 196 ms`
  - Fix: `GitHub repository read failed (Could not reach GitHub); retry 1/2 in 500ms`, then `revalidate: OK in 734 ms`
- **Regression tests** in `repository-project-admission.test.ts`. On base, the transport, 503 and exhaustion cases fail. The access-loss, quota, authority and cancellation guards pass on both, so they pin what the retry must not change. Run with the integration, access and prepared-placement suites: 5 files, 95 tests passed.
- **Test cost:** the admission test file took 88.7 s of wall time on a cold transform cache, about 3 s of it in tests. The new cases use fake timers and add milliseconds.
- **Static:** `tsgo:core`, type-aware oxlint (core shard), `oxfmt` and `git diff --check` are clean.
- **Review:** Codex autoreview of commit `a30b8a536dc` against parent `b2f3f9ed420`, priorities P0–P1, reported no findings, with `environment-access.ts` and `github-api.ts` as extra context. Local ClawSweeper was not run because its checkout is not built here.

**Gap:** no full AWS dispatch was re-run with the fault injected. The proof stops at the owner boundary; the path from there to dispatch failure and teardown comes from the production log above, not from a repeat run.

Release note context: cloud session startup now survives brief GitHub network failures during repository checks.
