prs.title: fix(config): get/set/unset cannot address mixed-case agents.entries keys by normalized id
prs.body:
Closes #193534

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: `openclaw config get/set/unset agents.entries.work...` cannot address an agent entry stored under a mixed-case key (`Work`) even though `openclaw agents list` shows it by its normalized id (`work`). `config get` reports the path valid but unset, `config set` tries to create a second `work` key and is declined with the duplicate-id error, and `config unset` reports the path not found.

## User Impact

User impact: the agent id that `agents list` prints now addresses the stored entry through `config get/set/unset/patch`, and the stored key keeps its spelling. Exact keys still win, hand-edited configs with casing-colliding keys keep their duplicate-id validation error, and ids that differ beyond casing (`work!`, `!!!`) remain unresolvable instead of silently hitting another agent.

## Why This Change Was Made

The config CLI used the `agents.entries.<id>` segment as a literal object key while the schema accepts keys case-insensitively and the runtime identifies entries by normalized id. `resolveStoredAgentsEntryKey` (in `config-cli-roster.ts`) rewrites the key segment to its stored spelling when the requested key is absent and exactly one stored key differs only by casing. The mutation runner resolves stored casing before checking whether a conditional write would redirect. If it would, the command rejects the write and leaves the config untouched. `config get` resolves the stored key before lookup while schema diagnostics use the authored path. A delete-then-write across casings in one patch still renames, because the second write only resolves when the stored key is gone.

## Evidence

- Integration tests in `src/cli/config-cli.roster.integration.test.ts`: `set`/`get`/`unset` through `agents.entries.work...` edit the stored `Work` entry in place (key spelling preserved, no duplicate id); `unset` of ids that differ beyond casing (`agents.entries["!!!"].name`, `agents.entries.work!.name`) still fails with the path-not-found error and leaves the config untouched. `node scripts/test-projects.mts src/cli/config-cli.roster.integration.test.ts` — 23/23 passing.
- Sibling suites: `config-cli.test.ts` (14), `config-cli.integration.test.ts` (25), `config-cli-input.test.ts` + `config-cli-path.test.ts` + `config-cli-runner.supplied-intent.test.ts` (91 combined) all passing.
- The current hosted [CI gate](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/42094185967/job/127503921692) passed.
- The 34 added test lines have a matching allocation in `config/test-lines-allocations/config-mixed-case-agents-entry-key.txt`.
- The gateway `agents.delete` sibling gap (#190496) is intentionally untouched; this PR scopes the fix to the config CLI surfaces named in the issue.


## Real CLI behavior proof

Run from source (`node --import tsx src/entry.ts`) with isolated `HOME`, `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`, and `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH` holding `{"agents":{"ownership":"explicit","entries":{"main":{},"Work":{"name":"Work Agent"}}}}`.

**Unpatched base, identical inputs:**

```
$ openclaw config get agents.entries.work.name
Config path is valid but unset: agents.entries.work.name. ...
$ openclaw config set agents.entries.work.name '"Renamed"' --strict-json
Config change declined. No settings were saved.
Config validation failed: agents.entries.work: agents.entries keys "Work" and "work" resolve to the same agent id "work"; ...
$ openclaw config unset agents.entries.work.name
Config path not found: agents.entries.work.name. Nothing was changed.
# saved agents.entries: {"main":{},"Work":{"name":"Work Agent"}}  (unchanged)
```

**This patch, identical inputs:**

```
$ openclaw config get agents.entries.work.name
Work Agent
$ openclaw config set agents.entries.work.name '"Renamed"' --strict-json
Updated agents.entries.work.name. Change will apply without restarting the gateway.
# saved agents.entries: {"main":{},"Work":{"name":"Renamed"}}   ← stored key keeps "Work"
$ openclaw config unset agents.entries.work.name
Removed agents.entries.work.name. Change will apply without restarting the gateway.
# saved agents.entries: {"main":{},"Work":{}}
$ openclaw config set agents.entries.work.name '"Renamed"' --strict-json --expect-current-json '"Work Agent"'
exit=1  conditional config set requires a direct, non-redirected config path
# config bytes verified unchanged (diff against pre-write copy)
```

`node scripts/test-projects.mts src/cli/config-cli.roster.integration.test.ts` — 24/24 passing on this head, including the redirected-conditional regression.

[Independent CLI reproduction](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/193610#issuecomment-6683286287)

prs.title: fix(plugins): uninstall leaves home-relative (~/...) load paths behind
prs.body:
Closes #193529

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: `openclaw plugins uninstall` keeps a home-relative `plugins.load.paths` entry (the documented `~/...` form) after removing a linked plugin, so the "uninstalled" plugin stays discoverable and shows up in `plugins list` as `disabled` / `record-missing`. The same path written absolute is removed correctly.

## User Impact

User impact: uninstalling (and package update/replace ownership checks for) a plugin whose load path uses the documented `~/...` form now removes that path like the absolute form does, so uninstalled plugins stop reappearing in `plugins list`.

## Why This Change Was Made

`loadPathMatchesInstallPath` in `src/plugins/uninstall-package-config.ts` compared paths without home expansion: `resolveRealpathOrAbsolute("~/plugins/demo")` treats `~` as a literal directory and falls back to `path.resolve(cwd, ...)`, which never equals the absolute install path. Discovery (`src/plugins/discovery.ts`) and the update helpers (`buildLoadPathHelpers` in `src/plugins/update-config.ts`) resolve load paths through `resolveUserPath`, so the uninstall/package-update comparison was the one that disagreed. Both sides of the comparison now expand through `resolveUserPath` before the canonical comparison, covering the three shared consumers (`removePluginInstallOwnerFromConfig`, `removePluginRuntimePolicyFromConfig`, `hasMatchingPluginLoadPath`).

## Evidence

- Regression tests in the new sibling file `src/plugins/uninstall-load-path-matching.test.ts` (uninstall.test.ts is over the line-cap ratchet, so the hook forbids growing it): a `~/plugin` load path resolving to the install path is removed with `loadPath` action reported; home-relative paths owned by other plugins are kept. `node scripts/test-projects.mts src/plugins/uninstall-load-path-matching.test.ts src/plugins/uninstall.test.ts` — 78/78 passing, plus consumer suites `plugin-package-update.test.ts` (9), `management-service.uninstall-ownership.test.ts` (14), `management-uninstall.source-cleanup.test.ts` (19), and `plugins-local-state.test.ts` (19) all passing.
- `pnpm check:changed`: typecheck core, typecheck core tests, lint core changed files, format, and all boundary guards pass. The only red lane is the pre-existing `deadcode` scan flagging `extensions/google/provider-policy.ts: normalizeGoogleServiceTier` and `scripts/e2e/lib/upgrade-survivor/config-recipe.mts: resolveScenarioConfigSteps` — exports in files this PR does not touch.
- The 49 added test lines have a matching allocation in `config/test-lines-allocations/plugins-uninstall-tilde-load-path.txt`.


## Real CLI behavior proof (head 9dbacc529f6c)

Run from source (`node --import tsx src/entry.ts`) with isolated `HOME` (fixture plugin at `~/plugins/demo-tilde`), isolated `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`, and a fresh config. Fixture plugin: minimal `openclaw.plugin.json` + `package.json` + `index.js`.

**Unpatched `origin/main` (480d5030538)** — after `plugins install --link --force --accept-capabilities ~/plugins/demo-tilde`, config `plugins.load.paths = ["~/plugins/demo-tilde", "/opt/shared-tools/plugin"]`:

```
$ openclaw plugins uninstall demo-tilde --force
Uninstalled plugin "demo-tilde". Removed: install record.
# config after: plugins.load.paths = ["~/plugins/demo-tilde", "/opt/shared-tools/plugin"]
#   → the home-relative path SURVIVES (the bug); uninstall kept the plugin discoverable
```

**This patch, identical steps and inputs:**

```
$ openclaw plugins install --link --force --accept-capabilities '~/plugins/demo-tilde'
exit=0  Linked plugin path: ~/plugins/demo-tilde
$ openclaw plugins uninstall demo-tilde --force
exit=0  Uninstalled plugin "demo-tilde". Removed: install record, load path.
# config after: plugins.load.paths = ["/opt/shared-tools/plugin"]
#   → home-relative path removed; unrelated absolute path and agents config preserved
```

**Package-update consumer (`hasMatchingPluginLoadPath` in `plugin-package-update.ts`)** — a real git-source plugin installed from a local two-tag repo, config `plugins.load.paths = ["~/.openclaw/state/git/git-c30035d65a579ddc/repo", "~/plugins/demo-tilde"]` (home-relative forms):

```
$ openclaw plugins update demo-git
exit=0  demo-git already at 1.0.0.
        Updates saved; they will load on the next Gateway start.
# config after: both home-relative load paths preserved verbatim; agents config preserved
```

**Data-model compatibility:** every run above started from or produced a config mixing home-relative and absolute load-path forms; installs, the update, and the uninstall all loaded the pre-existing config, preserved unrelated entries, and left the stored spellings unchanged. (Note: `plugins list` reports `provenance-invalid` for these synthetic local fixtures on both base and fix — a pre-existing trust finding for unverified sources, unchanged by this PR.)


## Review follow-up 2: package-replacement and release-state compatibility

**Data-model compatibility (verified):** state was created by the published release — `npx openclaw@2026.11.1 (4ffdd20) plugins install --link --force --accept-capabilities ~/plugins/demo-tilde` (exit 0) against an isolated `HOME`/`OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`, then the operator config was set to the documented tilde form `plugins.load.paths = ["~/plugins/demo-tilde", "/opt/shared-tools/plugin"]`. The patched source then ran the sanctioned migration (`openclaw doctor --fix`, exit 0, "maintenance release") and performed the uninstall on that release-created state:

```
$ openclaw plugins uninstall demo-tilde --force   (patched source, release-created + migrated state)
exit=0  Uninstalled plugin "demo-tilde". Removed: install record, load path.
# config after: plugins.load.paths = ["/opt/shared-tools/plugin"]  (tilde path removed; unrelated path and agents config preserved)
```

**Package replacement (attempted, blocked pre-existing):** a real two-tag git-source plugin (`git:file:///…@v1.0.0` → `@v1.0.1`, config-first tilde load path) fails during replacement with `Source snapshot no longer matches installed plugin demo-git` (exit 1, version stays 1.0.0) — **identically on unpatched `origin/main` (480d5030538) and on this head** (same error, same exit, same final state; logs `/tmp` ephemeral, command sequence documented above). The failure occurs in the installed-plugin-index snapshot verification before this diff's matcher runs and is out of scope for the six-line comparison change; the uninstall and `plugins update` flows above exercise the changed helper directly.

prs.title: fix(sessions): failed runs hide the provider safety-precaution explanation
prs.body:
Closes #189398

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: a request that stops on a provider misalignment refusal is reported as the bare "Your request couldn't be completed." when the transcript only retained the error code.

## User Impact

User impact: when a request is stopped as a safety precaution, the failed-run message now keeps that explanation instead of collapsing into a generic failure, so operators can tell a model-side refusal apart from a broken run.

## Why This Change Was Made

`formatProviderRefusalText` still produces the pre-diagnostics copy `The provider stopped this request as a safety precaution (misalignment).` for transcripts that only kept `errorCode`, but `isProviderRefusalNoticeText` matched only the two newer strings. The legacy copy then slipped past every remaining branch of the run-failure notice and was replaced by the generic fallback.

The matcher now recognizes that copy, and both sides read one shared constant so the producer and the matcher cannot drift apart again.

## Real behavior proof

`test/chat-history-legacy-refusal-notice.e2e.test.ts` runs the path against a Gateway started as its own process in the e2e lane (`test/vitest/vitest.e2e.config.ts`, `pool: forks`, `isolate: true`):

1. The isolated test home gets a session whose transcript keeps only `errorCode` — the older shape this regression is about.
2. The failure is recorded with the shipped recorder, using the text the shipped producer returns for that code (`formatProviderRefusalText({ errorCode: "misalignment_policy_violation" })`, asserted to be the legacy notice — not a literal copied into the test).
3. The Gateway process is started, a client connects over the websocket, and `chat.history` returns what a Control UI pane would render.

Both halves of the proof were produced by CI, not by a local harness.

prs.title: fix(infer): web search/fetch --provider rejects valid provider ids with different casing
prs.body:
Closes #193535

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: `openclaw infer web search --provider Brave` and `openclaw infer web fetch --provider Firecrawl` fail with "Unknown web_search provider" / "provider is not available" when the flag's casing differs from the lowercase plugin id, while the same commands work with `--provider brave`.

The explicit-selection guard and the fetch provider lookup compared the raw flag against lowercase plugin ids, even though the same command already lowercases the value for secret scoping and plugin loading, and `tools.web.search.provider` / `tools.web.fetch.provider` config is matched case-insensitively (#177836).

## User Impact

User impact: `--provider` accepts valid provider ids in any casing on both commands, matching config-key behavior; the error message keeps the caller's original casing when a provider genuinely does not exist.

## Why This Change Was Made

`src/web-search/runtime.ts` normalized the explicit id only for plugin loading (`normalizeOptionalLowercaseString`), then compared the raw value against `entry.id` in the unknown-provider guard and in the preferred-candidate ordering — so even with the guard patched alone, the explicit provider would lose priority ordering. `src/web-fetch/runtime.ts` used `options?.providerId` raw in its provider lookup. Both now normalize the explicit id once before comparing, matching the established config-selection behavior.

## Evidence

prs.title: fix(codex): settled-turn recovery rejects sessions containing a media-only user turn
prs.body:
Closes #185079

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: Codex settled-turn finalization repeatedly fails with `invalid_content` when the session history contains a legitimate media-only user turn — a message persisted with empty text plus ordered `__openclaw.media` facts (for example, a JPEG-only Telegram message) and no upstream-text fallback. The projection validated every earlier message before trimming, so one such historical turn kept rejecting every later finalization context capture on that session.

## User Impact

User impact: a verified historical media-only message no longer invalidates settled-turn recovery. It projects as a bounded, deterministic marker naming the attachment types, and finalization context capture succeeds for sessions that contain one. Empty messages without any well-formed media fact are still rejected, upstream text keeps winning over the placeholder, and current-turn evidence and pairing checks are unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

`projectUserMessage` required non-empty text and threw `CodexHistoryRejection("invalid_content")` for a blank user turn. The persisted representation for media-only turns is exactly that shape (empty `content`, media metadata under `message.__openclaw.media` — the documented "media-bearing user turns use ordered `message.__openclaw.media` facts" convention). The payloads themselves are not replayable through the text-oriented recovery projection, so the fix projects a deterministic `[User media attachment unavailable in this context: <types>]` marker — the same approach the projector already uses for image tool results (`[Image tool result: <mime>]`) — capped at the first eight entries with a `+N more` suffix, always inside the existing byte budgets.

## Evidence

- New regression tests in `extensions/codex/src/app-server/settled-turn-projection.test.ts`: against unpatched `origin/main`, exactly the two placeholder-projecting cases fail (media-only turn rejected with `invalid_content`); with the fix all 26 cases pass, including the guards for empty turns without well-formed media facts (still `invalid_content`), upstream-text precedence, and the placeholder cap.
- `pnpm test:extension codex` passes except two `transport-startup.test.ts` cases that fail identically on unpatched `main` on this machine (macOS native process inspection returns a permission error in this environment); the projection suites themselves are fully green.
- `pnpm check:changed` passes typecheck extensions, typecheck extension tests, and lint extension changed files. The only red lane is the pre-existing `deadcode` unused-export scan flagging three exports in files this PR does not touch.


**Remaining proof:** No end-to-end Gateway/Codex recovery run with persisted media-only history has been performed. The regression tests cover the projection boundary; they do not establish the full recovery and finalization flow.

Addresses the `withNodeRuntimePath` duplicate Windows PATH spelling item of #184894.

## What Problem This Solves

A direct call to `withNodeRuntimePath` with both `PATH` and `Path` retains directories only from the first spelling. This proposal concatenates both values before prepending the selected Node runtime.

## User Impact and Open Decision

If differently cased values reach this helper in a production Windows lifecycle, concatenation would retain both lists. That production scenario has not been demonstrated: review notes that the normal spawn caller normalizes duplicate aliases first, and that first-key precedence may be an intentional contract. This PR is a draft until a maintainer decides whether that behavior should change and a relevant Windows flow is demonstrated.

## Why This Change Was Made

The helper currently sorts PATH-keyed variables, reads the first value, and writes it to every spelling. The proposed change instead concatenates the values, retaining the first spelling's order and removing the duplicate runtime entry. Single-key behavior is unchanged.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes the missing work signal when a chat is waiting on subagents or still has task-owned background commands running.

prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

If a paired node disconnects during workspace Skill discovery, the Gateway can lose the read even when the same node reconnects. In source checkouts, loading the workspace handler on the first request can also consume its progress timeout.

## User Impact

Skill discovery and resource reads can recover on the same paired node without restarting the model turn. Writes, installs and subscriptions stay outside the retry path.

## Why This Change Was Made

For a recognized disconnect, the adapter opens a fresh authorized channel to the configured node and workspace. It retries at most twice, after one and two seconds, within the original 60-second read budget. Caller cancellation and permission denials still stop the read. The node prepares the shared handler before advertising a selected Skills or Memory command.

## Evidence

- On base `349859e0`, the wire test failed when the socket closed during discovery. On `321e5df0`, the same test passed locally on Node 24.22.1 and in hosted CI on Bun, each 1/1 with zero skips. The Gateway sent a fresh request to the same node and returned a Skill present only in its workspace. The QA runtime build and all 58 focused tests passed locally. Both hosted worker E2E jobs passed, although the overall run failed (138 jobs passed, 9 failed, 13 skipped). [Hosted reconnect job](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/42324733101/job/128257623538)
- On the main merge `6098e563`, all nine changed source files passed Node syntax checks and the diff check passed. Local autoreview covered all 11 changed files and 41 source contexts in `7ab0143f..6098e563` with no P0–P3 findings. The independent source review also found no P0–P3 issues.

prs.title: fix(onepassword): expire cached secrets on elapsed time
prs.body:
## Reopened

This PR reopens #193412 with the same patch and evidence. The previous PR's final re-review (2026-11-06) never landed: ClawSweeper acked "review queued" but the exact-review step ran as skipped, leaving the PR stuck at `status: needs proof` with zero formal reviews. The production code is byte-identical to the reviewed head (`d76c3b49efd`); only the base is refreshed so the test-line ratchet aligns with current `main`.

## What Problem This Solves

`OnePasswordBroker.get` caches a resolved secret for `cacheTtlSeconds` (default 300 s) so repeated reads do not hit `op`. Both ends of that window read the wall clock:

- freshness: `cached.expiresAtMs > Date.now()`
- write: `expiresAtMs: Date.now() + config.cacheTtlSeconds * 1000`

A backwards clock step on the Gateway host keeps the cached secret being served as fresh for the length of the step after a rotation, so an agent can keep using a rotated credential until the clock catches up.

## Why This Change Was Made

Secret-cache expiry now runs on elapsed time (`performance.now()`). The TTL, cache key (`slug`), target-fingerprint check, config-fingerprint invalidation, and audit rows are unchanged; behavior without a clock step is identical.

Standing grants and pending authorizations keep the wall clock on purpose: they are persisted safety windows (`grantTtlHours`), so an operator correcting the clock must not extend a persisted grant. Only this in-memory, per-process cache moves.

The module is a bundled extension and may only import `openclaw/plugin-sdk/*`, so it reads `performance.now()` directly. Bundled extensions ship with the host, so no compatibility path is needed.

This is **behavior-completing** for the elapsed-clock family (#191606, #192700, #193147, #193306).

## User Impact

A clock correction no longer extends a cached secret past its TTL. Without a clock step nothing changes: same TTL, same cache hits, same audits.

## Evidence

### Unit regression (mocked clocks and mocked `getItem`)

`extensions/onepassword/src/broker.test.ts` via the repository's Vitest entry (`node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/onepassword/src/broker.test.ts`) on Node v24.22.1:

| Test | BASE | HEAD |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `expires cached secrets on elapsed time when the wall clock steps backwards` | **FAIL** — the second read is a cache hit (one `getItem` call) | PASS |
| `rechecks grant expiry with cache TTL 300` / `7200` (existing) | PASS | PASS |

The existing harness already fakes `Date.now`; it now fakes `performance.now` with the same counter so both clocks advance together, and `advance(ms)` drives both. The new test steps `Date.now` back an hour while `performance.now` advances past the TTL.

### Real-boundary proof — committed reproducible test (real broker + real op-client + real CLI execution)

ClawSweeper asked for real-behavior evidence through the op boundary rather than mocked clocks and a mocked `getItem`. This proof drives the **shipped production classes end to end**: `OnePasswordBroker.get` → real `OpClient.getItem` → real `resolveTrustedOnePasswordCli` trust validation → real subprocess exec of an `op` CLI. A fake `op` executable (owned by the current user, non-writable, absolute-node shebang — passes the same trust validation the product runs) stands in for the 1Password CLI and logs every invocation to a counter file. The wall clock is stepped back one hour by overriding `Date.now` (the same rollback the fix targets); the process-local `performance.now()` is the real clock and its value at the second read (≈14.5s) far exceeds the 1s cache TTL.

This was previously a one-off driver script; it is now committed as `re-fetches a secret through the real op boundary after a backward clock step` in `broker.test.ts`, so it runs in CI. RED/GREEN verified locally:

```
# BASE (broker.ts reads Date.now)
 × re-fetches a secret through the real op boundary after a backward clock step
   → expected '1\n' to be '1\n1\n' // Object.is equality
# HEAD (broker.ts reads performance.now)
 ✓ re-fetches a secret through the real op boundary after a backward clock step 1323ms
 # counter file reads "1\n1\n" — op called 2×, secret re-fetched
```

The counter-file discriminator makes the stale-cache defect directly observable: BASE serves the pre-rollback cached value and logs one `op` invocation; HEAD re-fetches and logs two. BASE/HEAD differ only in `broker.ts`'s clock read (`Date.now` vs `performance.now`); everything else (real op-client, real trust check, real exec, same fake-op binary, same test) is identical. No production Gateway, session, token, vault, or real 1Password credential was touched; all CLI targets are local fixtures. The test is `it.runIf(process.platform !== "win32")`-guarded because the trusted-node fixture relies on a POSIX shebang.

HEAD full suite:

```
 ✓ extensions/onepassword/src/broker.test.ts (29 tests)
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  29 passed (29)
```

### Shipped-Gateway proof — real Gateway process, real plugin, real `op` subprocess, real wall-clock step

ClawSweeper asked for evidence through the isolated Gateway with a real agent and model rather than mocked clocks under Vitest. This run drives the **built `dist` for the reviewed head** (`d76c3b49efd`; this PR's head `9fd039bc3bc` has byte-identical production files — `broker.ts`, `broker.test.ts`, `openclaw.plugin.json`, `package.json` — the only delta is the refreshed base), and a base build that differs **only** in `broker.ts`'s clock read. It runs as a long-running Gateway and reaches the plugin's broker through the shipped `POST /tools/invoke` path — the same production entry the Control UI and channel adapters use:

```
Gateway process (dist build)
  └─ onepassword plugin register()  →  OnePasswordBroker (one instance, in-memory secret cache)
        ├─ before_tool_call policy gate (auto)       ← real
        ├─ OnePasswordBroker.get → cache lookup      ← the changed line
        ├─ OpClient.getItem → resolveTrustedOnePasswordCli
        └─ subprocess exec of a fake `op` CLI         ← real exec; logs every invocation
```

The fake `op` is a POSIX script owned by the invoking user, mode `0700`, with an absolute-node shebang, inside a `0755` directory chain — it passes the **same** `resolveTrustedExecutablePath` trust validation the product runs (an untrusted fixture is rejected with `1Password CLI executable is not trusted`, so the trust check is live, not bypassed). A Gateway token, no channel, no real vault, no real 1Password credential, no outbound endpoint: the fixture host is local.

Sequence, identical on both builds: **read #1** (populates the cache, TTL `cacheTtlSeconds: 1`) → step the host wall clock **back 1 hour** with `date -s` → wait **2 s** so elapsed time passes the 1 s TTL → **read #2**. The discriminator is the number of `op` subprocess invocations.

**HEAD (elapsed clock) — GREEN: the cache expires and the secret is re-fetched**

```text
[gateway] http server listening (2 plugins: memory-core, onepassword; 11.8s)
=== [HEAD] read #1 (populates the secret cache) ===
{"ok":true,"result":{"details":{"ok":true,"slug":"demo","value":"proof-secret-value","itemTitle":"Demo Item","fieldLabel":"credential"}}}
op subprocess invocations after read #1: 1

=== [HEAD] stepping the wall clock backwards 1 hour ===
before: 2026-11-06T04:46:33Z
after:  2026-11-06T03:46:33Z

=== [HEAD] waiting 2s so elapsed time passes the 1s TTL ===

=== [HEAD] read #2 ===
{"ok":true,"result":{"details":{"ok":true,"slug":"demo","value":"proof-secret-value","itemTitle":"Demo Item","fieldLabel":"credential"}}}

=== [HEAD] RESULT: the op subprocess ran 2 time(s) ===
--- op invocation transcript ---
2026-11-06T04:46:33.309Z
2026-11-06T03:46:35.748Z
```

**BASE (production file restored to `Date.now()`) — RED: the backwards step keeps the stale cache alive**

```text
[gateway] http server listening (2 plugins: memory-core, onepassword; 12.6s)
=== [BASE] read #1 (populates the secret cache) ===
{"ok":true,"result":{"details":{"ok":true,"slug":"demo","value":"proof-secret-value","itemTitle":"Demo Item","fieldLabel":"credential"}}}
op subprocess invocations after read #1: 1

=== [BASE] stepping the wall clock backwards 1 hour ===
before: 2026-11-06T04:28:23Z
after:  2026-11-06T03:28:23Z

=== [BASE] waiting 2s so elapsed time passes the 1s TTL ===

=== [BASE] read #2 ===
{"ok":true,"result":{"details":{"ok":true,"slug":"demo","value":"proof-secret-value","itemTitle":"Demo Item","fieldLabel":"credential"}}}

=== [BASE] RESULT: the op subprocess ran 1 time(s) ===
--- op invocation transcript ---
2026-11-06T04:28:22.624Z
```

BASE returns the **cached** secret on read #2 with **one** `op` invocation: after the host clock moved back an hour, `cached.expiresAtMs > Date.now()` is still true, so a rotated credential keeps being served. HEAD returns the same value but **re-fetches it** (two `op` invocations separated by exactly the 2 s wait and the clock step), because `performance.now()` advanced past the 1 s TTL regardless of the step.

Both reads returned `ok: true` and the value is the same, so the observable difference is purely the cache decision the fix changes — the proof does not depend on the secret's content, only on whether `op` is contacted again.

### Proof receipt

- Product head SHA: `9fd039bc3bc`; the shipped-Gateway dist proof above ran on `d76c3b49efd`, whose production files are byte-identical (`git diff d76c3b49efd HEAD -- extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts extensions/onepassword/src/broker.test.ts` is empty; `dist/extensions/onepassword/index.js` contains `cached.expiresAtMs > this.secretNow()`)
- RED baseline: same tree with **only** `extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts` reverted to `Date.now()` (two lines), rebuilt and run identically
- Production entry: shipped Gateway `gateway run` from `dist`; tool reached via `POST /tools/invoke` → `onepassword` plugin tool → `OnePasswordBroker.get`
- Recorder: fake `op` CLI appends one timestamp line per invocation; the line count is the discriminator
- Acceptance RED: BASE → 1 `op` invocation across the two reads after a −1 h clock step
- Acceptance GREEN: HEAD → 2 `op` invocations across the same sequence (repeated on a second HEAD build with the same result)
- Control: both builds return `ok: true` and the same secret value on both reads; the only variable is the cache-expiry decision
- Cleanup: the Gateway is stopped after the run and the host clock is restored immediately after read #2 (`restored:` timestamp in each log); the fixture op binary, token file, and state live under a private `0700` home directory and touch no real vault, channel, or credential

### Impact surface

| File:line | Risk |
| --- | --- |
| `extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts:183-184` | Elapsed clock for the secret cache only |
| `extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts:537,558` | Cache freshness read and write; grant/pending windows untouched |

### Not tested

- **Model-driven agent turn.** The last review asked for the same sequence driven by a real agent and model rather than `POST /tools/invoke`. I could not produce that here: the only model endpoint reachable from this contributor host is a local compatibility proxy that does not reliably emit tool calls for this plugin's full agent request. Across repeated runs on a real Gateway it either returned an empty assistant message or announced the call without producing a `tool_use` block (five consecutive attempts, zero `op` invocations — logs available on request). This is a limitation of the local model fixture, not of the patch: the same `OnePasswordBroker.get` line, the same `op` subprocess, and the same cache decision are already exercised above through the shipped Gateway. A maintainer with a standard hosted model can confirm the model-driven turn in minutes by asking the agent to read `demo` twice around the same clock step.
- No live 1Password account: the CLI boundary is a local fake `op` binary that passes the product's own trust validation. The proof exercises the cache decision, not the `op` HTTP client.
- Local `pnpm tsgo:core` cannot run on this contributor host (bundled `tsrs` needs GLIBC 2.29+); type checking is left to CI.

### Cleanup

Work happened in a detached worktree off `origin/main`; no user Gateway, session, token, or user config was touched. The proof's Gateway used an isolated state/config dir under a private `0700` home, was stopped after the run, and the host clock was restored immediately after read #2.

### Maintainer options

<details>
<summary>Land-ready or alternatives</summary>

Narrow single-owner change in one broker method pair plus its test; land as-is if the elapsed-clock direction is what you want here.

Alternatives rejected: moving grants and pending authorizations to the elapsed clock (persisted windows should follow the wall clock an operator sets); clamping instead of switching clocks (leaves existing entries frozen).

Scope: `extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts` and its test file.

</details>

prs.title: fix(gateway): agent.run can carry a fallback ladder so a pinned model no longer dead-ends on a quota 429
prs.body:
Closes #186418
Related: #151980, #141115, #181981

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: an automation caller that pins a model on the WebSocket agent.run request loses the agent's configured model-fallback ladder, so a quota-class 429 ends the run instead of advancing to the next candidate.

The request schema had no way to express a chain, so the only lever an automation caller had was to pin a model - which silently suppresses the configured ladder. Operators who configured a working fallback chain for the agent had no caller-side way to keep it alive.

## User Impact

User impact: automation callers can now send an explicit fallback ladder with their agent.run request, so a provider quota window on the pinned model no longer ends the run - the run advances to the next candidate the caller named.

This is opt-in and additive. A request that pins a model and sends no ladder behaves exactly as before: the pin stays strict and the configured chain stays suppressed, which is the contract #151980 asks to keep.

## Why This Change Was Made

The gateway already had the pieces to carry a run-scoped chain, but the wire protocol could not express one. Rather than relax the strict-pin contract, this change adds an explicit field so the caller states the chain it wants:

- agent.run accepts an optional fallbacks array of provider/model refs. Entries are trimmed, de-duplicated, and bounded to 16.
- The ladder is authorized exactly like a model override: a caller without the model-override scope is rejected with INVALID_REQUEST and a clear message.
- Every named model is checked against the agent's visible model set and the caller's operator authority before the run starts, so a caller cannot widen model access by naming extra chain entries.
- The chain travels with the run as a request-scoped override, so it is used for this run only and does not become session state.

The request-level pin remains the primary model; the ladder only adds candidates behind it.

## Evidence

Focused test runs, both green on this branch (rebased onto main at d2491817):

    node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.gateway.config.ts src/gateway/agent-turn/agent-request-preflight.test.ts
    -> Test Files 1 passed (1), Tests 33 passed (33)

    node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.agents-core.config.ts src/agents/agent-scope.test.ts
    -> Test Files 1 passed (1), Tests 44 passed (44)

Typecheck:

    pnpm tsgo:test:root -> exit 0 (all root shards)
    pnpm tsgo:test:packages -> exit 0

New coverage:

- src/gateway/agent-turn/agent-request-preflight.test.ts - a request that carries both a pinned model and a ladder keeps the ladder and reports it as request-scoped; a request with a ladder but no model-override scope is rejected; a request with no ladder leaves the override unset.
- src/agents/agent-scope.test.ts - a request-supplied ladder survives a pinned model during model selection, and a request-supplied chain that names a model the agent cannot use is rejected before the run starts.

Behavior with no fallbacks in the request is unchanged, so existing agent.run callers are unaffected.

prs.title: fix #188935: throw the typed schema-admission error at handle adoption
prs.body:
## Summary

- Problem: When an agent-database open loses the schema-admission race at handle adoption, the site throws an untyped `Error` ("Agent schema admission changed before handle adoption; retry the operation") instead of `AgentDatabaseSchemaAdmissionChangedError`, so no retry/replay path classifies it and a completed long turn ends with only "OpenClaw couldn't finish this reply" (#188935).
- Solution: Throw the existing typed `AgentDatabaseSchemaAdmissionChangedError` at the adoption site (keeping its exact message), so the transcript-commit replay classifier already in the tree treats the race as retryable.
- What changed: `src/state/openclaw-agent-db-validation-schema.ts` (typed throw), `src/state/agent-database-admission-error.ts` (optional custom message, default unchanged), strengthened race assertions in `src/state/openclaw-agent-db-validation-cache.test.ts`.
- What did NOT change: The typed error's identity, default message, and all publication-path behavior; the admission/adoption verdicts themselves; no retry logic was added — the fix only connects the existing throw to the existing classifier.

Fixes #188935

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** A session-turn Worker's agent-database open lost the publication race at handle adoption and threw an untyped `Error`, which `isReplayableWorkerTranscriptCommitError` could not classify, so the turn was terminated terminally instead of being retried.
- **Real environment tested:** This branch's worktree on Linux x64, Node v24.20.0, pnpm 12.15.0, driving the real `adoptOpenClawAgentDatabaseSchema` through the repo's concurrent-publication race fixture with a real SQLite agent database and the real replay classifier `isReplayableWorkerTranscriptCommitError`.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:**
  ```bash
  pnpm install
  OPENCLAW_TEST_FILE_LOG=1 node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run \
    src/state/openclaw-agent-db-validation-cache.test.ts
  ```
  (`OPENCLAW_TEST_FILE_LOG=1` keeps test file logs under the repo on this host; see "What was not tested".)
- **Evidence after fix:**
  ```text
  before (production files restored to unmodified main, same assertions):
    × schema: expected Error: Agent schema admission changed bef… to be an instance of SchemaAdmissionChangedError
    (the adoption race surfaced as a bare Error; the replay classifier did not own it)
  after (this patch):
    ✓ same race now throws AgentDatabaseSchemaAdmissionChangedError with the unchanged message
    ✓ isReplayableWorkerTranscriptCommitError(error) === true
    ✓ openclaw-agent-db-validation-cache.test.ts: 51 passed (51)
  worker transport replay (real session Worker, src/worker/worker.transcript-failure.test.ts):
    ✓ replays transient transcript failures and completes the run without duplicate messages
      — drives an actual AgentDatabaseSchemaAdmissionChangedError through the real worker
      transcript-commit transport: replayed requests equal the original, the run completes,
      and no duplicate messages are persisted (3 passed, exit 0)
  ```
- **Observed result after fix:** The adoption-race failure is now an instance of the typed error the transcript-commit replay path already classifies as retryable, so a raced open can be retried instead of discarding the turn; the same typed error is shown replaying through the real worker transcript transport to a clean completion without duplicate persisted messages (the pre-existing worker replay suite, re-run green on this head).
- **What was not tested:** The original 54-minute Feishu turn was not replayed (the race window requires a live long-running turn plus a concurrent memory-index publication; the repo's race fixture exercises the exact adoption path deterministically). The `core-runtime-infra-state` CI-like shard was attempted but this host's dist-fence guard refuses to run it (it cannot verify separation from managed Gateway artifacts; this is an environment restriction, not a test failure) — the affected validation-cache suite runs green standalone and CI lanes remain the shard guardrail. This host's `/` is world-writable without the sticky bit, so tests resolving the default rolling log path use the repo-supported `OPENCLAW_TEST_FILE_LOG=1` route, which CI does not need. tsgo could not run locally (GLIBC too old for the native binary); CI type lanes remain the guardrail.

## Regression Test Plan

- Coverage level: Unit test
- Target test file: `src/state/openclaw-agent-db-validation-cache.test.ts`
- Scenario locked in: the "schema" race in `distinguishes raced publication from malformed receipts even after revocation` now asserts the adoption failure is an `AgentDatabaseSchemaAdmissionChangedError` with the exact message and is classified replayable by the transcript-commit path.
- Why this is the smallest reliable guardrail: it fails on unpatched main with the precise defect from the issue (bare Error, unclassifiable) and pins both the type contract and the replay classification without touching unrelated races.

## Root Cause

- Root cause: the handle-adoption race site threw a bare `Error`, while the sibling publication-race site threw the typed `AgentDatabaseSchemaAdmissionChangedError`; the replay classifier keys on the type, so the adoption race fell through every retry path despite its message saying "retry the operation".
- Missing detection / guardrail: the race fixture asserted only the message text, never the error type or its replay classification, so the untyped throw compiled and passed review.

prs.title: fix(nodes): macOS node host version labeled ui instead of core in nodes describe/status
prs.body:
Closes #193527

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: `openclaw nodes describe` and `openclaw nodes status` label a headless macOS node host's version as `ui v...` instead of `core v...`; the same host on Linux or Windows is labeled correctly.

The legacy single-version formatter treats `darwin`, `linux`, `win32`, and `windows` as headless platforms, but a macOS node host reports platform `macos` (mapped from `darwin` by the gateway client platform identity), so it fell into the UI branch.

## User Impact

User impact: macOS headless node hosts show their version under the correct `core` label in `nodes describe` / `nodes status` and the companion Nodes menu; Apple app platforms (iOS, versioned macOS strings) remain on the `ui` label because matching stays exact.

## Why This Change Was Made

The formatter's headless platform list missed the `macos` identity that macOS node hosts actually report. The same list exists twice: `src/cli/nodes-cli/register.status.ts` and `NodeMenuEntryFormatter.isHeadlessPlatform` in `apps/macos/Sources/OpenClaw/NodesMenu.swift` (the sibling surface named in the issue). Both are updated.

## Evidence

- Regression tests in `src/cli/nodes-cli/register.status.test.ts`: a legacy single-version node is classified `core` for `macos`, `darwin`, and `windows`, and `ui` for `ios` (guarding exact matching). Full file: 16/16 passing (`node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.cli.config.ts src/cli/nodes-cli/register.status.test.ts`).
- The macOS Nodes menu change is one token on the same list; this machine currently has no full Xcode install (Command Line Tools only, which cannot load the SwiftUI SDK macro plugins), and repo CI skips the `macos-swift` job on `pull_request` events (the manifest computes `runMacos = !ordinaryPullRequest`; recently merged macOS PR #185529 shows the same SKIPPED checks). The Swift change therefore lands through the maintainer qualification dispatch or the post-merge main CI per docs/platforms/mac/dev-setup.md; the TS-side formatter change is fully covered by the tests above.
- The 31 added test lines have a matching allocation in `config/test-lines-allocations/nodes-macos-headless-version.txt`.



## Review follow-up (b5c6d52b8fc)

- Added the missing native regression: `apps/macos/Tests/OpenClawIPCTests/NodesMenuHeadlessPlatformTests.swift` covers `NodeMenuEntryFormatter.isHeadlessPlatform` (widened to internal) — `macos` classifies headless like `darwin`/`linux`/`win32`/`windows`, while `ios`, `iPadOS 18.2`, and `macOS 26.0` stay non-headless (exact matching preserved).
- On the requested Nodes menu screenshots: this machine has no full Xcode install (Command Line Tools only, which cannot load the SwiftUI SDK macro plugins), so the patched companion app cannot be built or screenshotted locally; repo CI also skips `macos-swift` on `pull_request` events (see the `runMacos = !ordinaryPullRequest` manifest gate; merged macOS PR #185529 shows the same SKIPPED checks). The Swift change remains a one-token addition mirroring the CLI predicate the reviewer already accepted as source-verified; native verification will land through the maintainer qualification dispatch or post-merge main CI per docs/platforms/mac/dev-setup.md.
- Red-on-base note for the CLI side: the issue body records the real-Gateway run on unpatched main showing `ui v2026.10.9` (reporter yetval, offending lines unchanged between 4e4342b9f82 and this base); this branch's `register.status.test.ts` asserts the fixed `core` label plus the `ui` guard cases.


## Review follow-up 2 (e6bcb6010b8)

- P3 addressed: `isHeadlessPlatform` is private again and the regression now drives the existing `detailRightVersion` entry point with legacy version fixtures — `macos`/`darwin`/`windows` render `core 2026.10.9`, while `ios`, `iPadOS 18.2`, and `macOS 26.0` render `ui 2026.10.9`. The test fails if the displayed label misclassifies a platform, not merely if the classifier changes.
- The Nodes-menu screenshot blocker stands as described above (no Xcode on this machine; `macos-swift` skips on `pull_request` events) — that proof will land through the maintainer qualification dispatch or post-merge main CI.


## Review follow-up 3 (f2b628f01d0)

prs.title: fix(auth): CLI clients refuse to start after a macOS reboot renumbers the state volume
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: `openclaw node run` and other CLI clients stop with "Client credential migration is incomplete or stale; run openclaw doctor --fix" after a macOS reboot, even though the shared state database did not change.

## User Impact

User impact: clients keep working after a reboot that renumbers the data volume. A node under a service manager no longer crash-loops until someone runs `openclaw doctor --fix` by hand (we observed one restarted about 32,500 times over four days). A shared database that was really replaced (new inode or new path) is still refused, as before.

## Why This Change Was Made

The local client credential receipt binds itself to the shared `state/openclaw.sqlite` with `{path, dev, ino}`, and readiness refused any mismatch, including `st_dev`. On macOS APFS, `st_dev` is assigned at mount time and can change across reboots. Some Linux mounts do the same. In the observed case the device number changed while the database kept the same path and inode, and every client start failed closed.

Path plus inode is the stable part of that identity. It is what detects a replaced database (restore, rename-over, new file). This change compares only path and inode, and treats a changed `dev` as the same file:

- **Canonical receipts:** writable admission rewrites the recorded `dev`, so the receipt heals itself. Read-only admission accepts the file and writes nothing.
- **Independent native receipts:** their `source.identity` embeds `<dev>:<ino>`, so only the inode is compared. Before this change, a writable admission after a renumbering also wiped the local derived rows and rebuilt them from the native source, which dropped tokens refreshed since the copy. Now an unchanged source keeps its rows, and only the receipt's identity and binding are refreshed.
- **Migration paths** that compare the same binding (fresh bootstrap, recovery, independent→canonical cutover) use the same comparison. Recovery still rewrites the receipt when only `dev` changed, so `doctor --fix` records the current device.

The restore and rewrite flows in `client-credential-restore.ts` still compare their captured identities exactly. They run inside one Doctor operation and are unchanged.

<details>
<summary>Why not a stronger identity signal, and what about the macOS app?</summary>

A generation stored inside the database would also survive a reboot. But canonical readiness deliberately does not open the shared database. A realpath'd path plus inode already distinguishes the replacement cases this guard exists for. What remains is a different filesystem, mounted at the same path, holding a file with the same inode. A whole-volume clone or restore is the realistic version of that, and it carries `client/credentials.sqlite` along with the shared database, so the pair stays consistent.

The macOS app's native check (`ClientCredentialReceipt.swift` `assertReady`) still compares the full binding. After this change, any CLI client admission on the profile refreshes the receipt, and that also clears the app's check. Relaxing the Swift comparison can follow separately.
</details>

## Evidence

The new tests fail on `origin/main` and pass with the fix. The inode-change guard tests pass on both.

- `client-credential-store.test.ts`: a receipt with a shifted `dev` and the same path and inode is admitted. Writable admission rewrites `dev`; read-only leaves the receipt untouched. A shifted inode still throws the `doctor --fix` error in both modes and leaves the receipt untouched.
- `client-credential-native-bootstrap.test.ts`: an independent receipt with a renumbered device keeps the locally refreshed token in both modes. Writable admission refreshes `source.identity` and `sharedFile`.
- `client-credential-bootstrap.test.ts`: rebinding the same anchor file after a `dev` change succeeds, records the current `dev`, and keeps local identities and tokens.
- `startup-client-credentials.test.ts` (the startup path `node run` uses): after a `dev` change, preparation finishes without entering Doctor maintenance, and credentials stay readable. Existing recovery tests that used a `dev` shift to force recovery now shift the inode, which still requires recovery.

Commands run locally:

- `pnpm exec vitest run src/infra/client-credential-*.test.ts src/infra/state-migrations.device-*.test.ts src/commands/startup-client-credentials*.test.ts src/state/openclaw-state-db.test.ts`
- `pnpm tsgo:core`
- `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs <touched files>` and `node scripts/run-format.mts --check <touched files>`

Results: 17 test files passed, 2 skipped (PostgreSQL-only suites with no local server). Typecheck, lint, and format are clean. An independent local review of the branch reported no actionable findings.

prs.title: fix(state): type the handle-adoption schema admission race for retry and replay
prs.body:
Fixes #188935

## What Problem This Solves

When a concurrent publisher revokes an agent database's schema proof during the worker's handle adoption, the guard in `adoptAgentValidationSchema` throws a plain `Error("Agent schema admission changed before handle adoption; retry the operation")`. In the report, the publisher is memory-core republishing after an index refresh. The same race at publication time throws the typed `AgentDatabaseSchemaAdmissionChangedError`, and that is the type the recovery code recognizes:
- `isReplayableWorkerTranscriptCommitError` treats it as a replayable worker transcript commit;
- the native open path treats it as `open-refused`, which leads to fresh admission;
- the bounded startup publication retry (#178577) retries it.

The plain error matches none of these. In the report, a completed 54-minute turn ended with only "OpenClaw couldn't finish this reply", even though the error text says "retry the operation".

## User Impact

Losing this race now goes through the existing retry and replay paths instead of discarding the turn's reply.

## Why This Change Was Made

ClawSweeper's next step on the issue: "Fix handle-adoption error classification". The adoption site now throws `AgentDatabaseSchemaAdmissionChangedError` with an optional stage name, so the message still says "before handle adoption" and the publication message is unchanged. No classifier changes: every existing `instanceof` check now applies to the adoption race too.

## Evidence

Windows 11 / Node 26.12.1.
- **Setup:** the production `adoptAgentValidationSchema(…, reuseIntegrity=true, required=true)` is driven with a schema proof that a concurrent publisher revoked (valid flag 0).
- **Check:** the thrown error goes to the production `isReplayableWorkerTranscriptCommitError`. The native-open column mirrors the `instanceof AgentDatabaseSchemaAdmissionChangedError` check in `openclaw-agent-execution-native.ts`; the harness does not call that code.
- **Variable:** same harness; only `agent-database-admission-error.ts` and `openclaw-agent-db-validation-schema.ts` differ between main 2908f7a and this branch.

![proof](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wr-web/openclaw/proof-assets/188935/proof-188935.png)

| | main 2908f7a | this branch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| message | `Agent schema admission changed before handle adoption; retry the operation` | same text |
| type | plain `Error` | `AgentDatabaseSchemaAdmissionChangedError` |
| worker transcript commit replayable | false (terminal) | true |
| native open failure kind | `native` | `open-refused` (fresh admission) |

The regression is the existing case in `src/state/openclaw-agent-db-validation-cache.test.ts`, "distinguishes raced publication from malformed receipts even after revocation" (race=schema). It now asserts the typed error instead of the message.
- **On main:** it fails with "expected error to be instance of SchemaAdmissionChangedError".
- **With this change:** it passes. The test line count goes down by one.

Other cases in that file: 47 pass. 4 fail on this Windows checkout with `EPERM` from `fs.renameSync` over an open SQLite file. Those cases replace the database file and are unrelated to this change. Command: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/state/openclaw-agent-db-validation-cache.test.ts`.

Not reproduced: the live memory-core publication race inside a long turn. It needs a publication to land inside the worker's adoption window, and the reporter saw it once.

Gates run locally: oxfmt, oxlint, `pnpm check:line-cap-ratchet`.

prs.title: fix(talk): stop voice claiming cancelled consult work finished
prs.body:
Closes #189070

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: realtime Talk keeps reporting a task as in progress, then as done, after Google Live cancels the `openclaw_agent_consult` call and OpenClaw aborts the run.

## User Impact

After a cancelled consult, the voice model is told the request was interrupted and its outcome is unknown. It stops claiming the work finished and checks what was done before running it again, since steps that ran before the cancellation are not undone.

## Why This Change Was Made

When Google Live sends `toolCallCancellation`, the relay already aborts the consult run (`cancelTalkRealtimeRelayProviderToolCall`). The Android client then submits `aborted` for that call, but the Google provider deliberately drops results for cancelled call IDs (`submitToolResult` early return, added in 5be95ad4bab). The model's last word on the call was "working" or nothing, and it never learns the work stopped.

The relay's `tool.call.cancelled` handler now sends one notice through the existing bridge `sendUserMessage` path, the same path forced consults use for their "checking" and result prompts. It fires only when the relay actually retired an uncompleted call, so replays and cancellations after an accepted result send nothing. The notice says the outcome is unknown rather than that nothing happened: cancellation aborts only the remaining steps, so an earlier file write may already have landed.

<details>
<summary>Why the default model is exposed</summary>

The default `gemini-3.1-flash-live-preview` gets no async function calling and no `willContinue` interim result (`supportsAsyncFunctionCalling`, `modelSupportsToolResultContinuation`), so the consult is declared blocking. Speech while it is pending is a likely cancellation trigger; the reporter did not confirm the trigger.

</details>

## Evidence

- `pnpm test src/gateway/talk/relay/cancellation-recovery.test.ts`: 14 passed. With the one `sendUserMessage` line removed, the new notice test fails with "Number of calls: 0"; the control (cancellation after an accepted result sends nothing) passes both ways.
- `pnpm test src/gateway/talk/relay`: all relay tests passed.
- Live run, partial: an isolated QA Gateway with real Google Live (`gemini-3.1-flash-live-preview`) and a real Gemini agent model. A client speaks generated audio through the same RPCs Android uses (`talk.session.create` on `gateway-relay`, `talk.session.appendAudio`, `talk.client.toolCall`, `talk.session.steer`, `talk.session.submitToolResult`). It asks for a 20-second wait plus a file write, interrupts after about 4 s, then asks for status. These trials ran the first wording of the notice ("cancelled … produced no result"); the delivery path is unchanged. Main is `upstream/main`'s `session-create.ts` swapped in with `dist` rebuilt.
  - Google cancelled the running consult in all 9 trials that reached it. Each showed `chat.aborted`, then `toolCallCancelled`, then the dropped `{"error":"aborted"}` submit.
  - Main, 6 cancelled trials: in 1, the voice model claimed success right after the cancellation. It said "the greeting file has now been created in your workspace. Protocol complete!", and no file existed. The other 5 made no such claim.
  - This branch, 3 cancelled trials: none claimed the work finished. No speech followed the cancellation before the user's next turn, so the notice was not spoken over the user.
  - Gaps: the sample is small because the bug is intermittent and free-tier Gemini quota rate-limited the remaining trials. Those trials were excluded (`reason=rate_limit` in the Gateway log). The notice's delivery to Gemini is not logged, so it is shown by the unit test, not by the live run. In 1 main trial and 2 trials on this branch, the voice model started a new consult, and that agent run reported saving `proofnote.txt`. That run checked only for `proof-note.txt`, so whether the agent's claim was true is unverified.

<details>
<summary>Live trial transcript (main, the false-completion trial)</summary>

```
+66.3s talk.toolCall          openclaw_agent_consult
+66.5s toolCall.ack           runId=talk-c684…
+70.6s user.speaks            "Actually, while you do that, what is two plus two?"
+71.9s chat.aborted           runId=talk-c684…
+71.9s talk.toolCallCancelled
+72.0s submitToolResult       {"error":"aborted"}   (dropped by the provider)
+81.0s assistant              "...2 + 2 is 4. And one moment... the greeting file has now been created in your workspace. Protocol complete!"
+129.4s artifact              proof-note.txt exists: false
```

</details>

Production delta +8/-0; test delta +38/-0.

Merge risk: two-way door; reverting restores the prior behavior with no state or config migration. Blast radius is relay Talk sessions whose provider emits `tool.call.cancelled` (Google Live today).

prs.title: fix(android): show retry instead of SHA-256 entry on TLS timeout
prs.body:
Closes #142528

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: Android asks for a SHA-256 certificate fingerprint when the first TLS probe to a Gateway times out, for example a Tailscale Serve endpoint whose handshake stalls.

## User Impact

A timed-out first connection now shows the connection recovery screen with Retry (and the Tailscale hint on tailnet hosts) instead of asking the user to fetch a fingerprint from the Gateway host.

## Why This Change Was Made

#142651 routed `ENDPOINT_UNREACHABLE` to the network recovery path; this does the same for `TLS_HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT` in `decideGatewayTlsTrust` and reuses `gatewayNetworkConnectError(timedOut = true)` in `NodeRuntime`, keeping the existing timeout text. No UI or string changes.

This changes the fallback order from #110976 on purpose. A timeout with no captured fingerprint means the server never sent a certificate within the probe budget, so a pasted pin has nothing to match. Manual entry stays for `TLS_UNAVAILABLE`, which `connect_enforcesAcceptedManualFingerprintAfterTlsProbeFailure` still covers. iOS already treats `.tlsHandshakeTimeout` as a timeout rather than manual entry (`GatewayConnectionSupport.swift`). This follows the ClawSweeper recommendation on the issue, without the separate advanced pin action, because that action cannot help a stalled handshake.

Accepted edge case: the probe budget is 13s and the real connection timeout is 20s. A server whose handshake consistently takes 13–20s previously connected through a pasted pin; it now gets Retry.

## Evidence

Draft: tests and device proof not yet captured.

- [ ] Main RED: the `GatewayTlsTest` and `GatewayBootstrapAuthTest` timeout cases fail with the fix lines reverted.
- [ ] Fix GREEN: `./gradlew :app:testPlayDebugUnitTest` for `GatewayTlsTest`, `GatewayBootstrapAuthTest`, `InitialOnboardingLayoutTest`, `FoldAwareDialogTest`; `./gradlew :app:ktlintCheck`.
- [ ] Device: main vs fix APK against a TCP listener that never completes a handshake, no saved pin — prompt (main) vs recovery screen (fix).

Production delta +9/-4; test delta +26/-19.

Merge risk: two-way door; reverting restores the prior prompt with no state or config migration. Blast radius is first-time Android connections whose TLS probe times out.

prs.title: docs(users): explain that personal profiles from a past sign-in remain
prs.body:
Related: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/164580

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: owners of a single-user Gateway cannot tell from the docs that a personal profile created by a past personal sign-in, such as Tailscale Serve identity, stays after that sign-in is turned off and cannot be removed or merged into the shared Owner profile.

## User Impact

User impact: `openclaw users` docs now say that this personal profile is durable, that token and password connections keep using Owner, and that a later sign-in with the same identity reuses it, so owners stop looking for a cleanup step that does not exist. Docs only; no behavior change. Affects single-user Gateways that had a personal sign-in at least once, for example with `gateway.auth.allowTailscale` (on by default with `tailscale.mode: "serve"` and token auth).

## Why This Change Was Made

The review on https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/164580 leaves the choice between standalone profile retirement and explicit retention documentation to a maintainer. This PR is the smaller alternative: it documents the current retention behavior in the `openclaw users` merge section, next to the existing statement that Owner cannot be merged. It does not add a retirement operation or change the Owner merge boundary, so the issue stays open for that decision (`Refs`, not `Closes`).

| Area | File | Lines |
|---|---|---|
| Docs | `docs/cli/users.md` | +7 |

## Evidence

Details: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/164580#issuecomment-6535154395

prs.title: fix: announce run_stopped for exact Stops of reserved, exec-only and worker runs
prs.body:
Related: #190906

## What Problem This Solves

`run_stopped` should fire once per explicit Stop, after the Stop's authority is confirmed and before its runs commit cancellation (`docs/plugins/hooks/reference.md`, "Explicit Stop"). A `chat.abort` with an exact `runId` fires it only when that run is a live, registered RPC source. Three accepted exact Stops cancel work and fire nothing:

- a reserved run, whose input has a session target but is not yet registered as an RPC source;
- an exec-only run, where only commands owned by the run are still live, such as a wake turn continuing an earlier request's commands;
- an admin's worker-only Stop of a run whose inference is on a worker environment.

A plugin that suppresses detached post-turn work on `run_stopped` misses these Stops, so the stopped run's follow-up work still runs.

## User Impact

Plugins listening to `run_stopped` now hear these three Stops. The event has the same shape as every other Gateway client Stop: `source: "client"`, one session, and `runIds: [runId]`. A rejected Stop still fires nothing. Cancellation, authorization and the `chat.abort` response are unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

Each of these Stops now calls `notifySessionRunStopped` the way the session-wide plan does (`chat-abort-session-plan.ts`): after every authority check, synchronously behind a live authority assertion, and immediately before the call that commits cancellation.

- **Reserved run:** after `authorizeRunTarget`, before `stopSession`. Preparing the run's session can await, so the Stop re-runs its source assertion first. Without that, a requester revoked during the await would be announced and then rejected. The event names the run's own session, as the live exact-run Stop does.
- **Exec-only run:** inside `beforeKill`, after `assertCurrent()` and the successor check, before `stopWithoutCapturedRun`. The event names the requested session.
- **Worker-only run:** after the admin check, before `cancelWorker()`. The last await was session preparation, so the Stop asserts current authority first. The event names the worker's own session when `resolveSessionTargetForRunId` resolved one, since that is the session whose inference `captureWorkerInferenceForSession` cancels; otherwise it names the requested session.

`runIds` is `[runId]` for the reserved and exec-only Stops. For the worker Stop it is `workerCancellation.runIds`, which is also `[runId]`, because the worker capture is filtered by `runId`.

`chat-abort-handler.ts` was at 698 of its 700 counted lines (the oxlint `max-lines` rule), and `config/max-lines-baseline.txt` accepts no new entries. So the reserved Stop moves unchanged into `stopReservedClientRun` in `chat-abort-exact-run.ts`, next to `stopExactClientRun`, which already owns the live exact-run Stop and its announcement. The handler is now at 686 counted lines.

**Why the exec-only Stop names the requested session and not its command owners' sessions.** A command owner can belong to another session. A turn inherits the owners of the events it continues, and an exec completion can be routed to another session (`resolveEventSessionKeyForPolicy`); the cascade test below stops exactly such a continuation. Every owner the Stop captures either matches the requested session itself (`execRequestMatches`) or belongs to a live turn whose identity matched the requested session and `runId`. In the second case the stopped turn runs in the requested session, and the original request's session holds no stopped run. Naming that session would make consumers cancel unrelated pending work there. The session plan does the same: it cancels the same owner capture and announces the requested session. This also keeps the documented one-session context for Gateway client Stops.

<details>
<summary>Files</summary>

- `src/gateway/server-methods/chat-abort-handler.ts`: announces the exec-only and worker-only Stops, the worker-only one behind an authority re-check; the reserved branch calls `stopReservedClientRun`
- `src/gateway/server-methods/chat-abort-exact-run.ts`: `stopReservedClientRun`, the reserved Stop moved out of the handler, plus its authority re-check and announcement
- `src/gateway/server-methods/chat.abort-authorization.test.ts`:
  - worker-only Stop with and without a resolved worker session
  - a reserved run: foreign, revoked and accepted Stops
  - no event from the existing revoked-authority fence cases
- `src/gateway/server-methods/chat.abort-cascade.test.ts`: the exec-only continuation Stop, rejected for a foreign client and then accepted
- `config/test-lines-allocations/run-stopped-exact-stops.txt`: the test-line allocation below

</details>

## Evidence

Each case asserts the exact event and its hook context:

| Stop | Main | With the fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| reserved run, accepted | no event | `{ source: "client", sessions: [main/main], runIds: [reserved-run] }` |
| reserved run, foreign or revoked requester | no event | no event |
| exec-only continuation, accepted | no event | the requested session, `runIds: [continued-command]` |
| exec-only continuation, foreign requester | no event | no event |
| worker-only, admin, worker session resolved | no event | the worker's session (`agent:main:worker`) |
| worker-only, admin, no worker session | no event | the requested session (`agent:main:main`) |
| worker-only, non-admin | no event | no event |
| any exact Stop whose requester or target authority changed (active, queued, pending-chat, agent, worker) | no event | no event |

- Red on main: with the production change reverted and the tests kept, 5 tests fail, each on the missing event (`expected [] to deeply equal [ Array(1) ]`); 49 pass.
- Mutants, each applied alone, all fail on an assertion: removing any of the three announcements, removing either authority re-check (the hook then fires for the revoked Stop), or announcing the requested session instead of the worker's.
- Each file with `pnpm test <file> --maxWorkers=1`:
  - `chat.abort-authorization.test.ts`: 32/32 (97s wall, 94% transform)
  - `chat.abort-cascade.test.ts`: 22/22 (53s wall)
- Abort and Stop regression suites: 17 files, 212/212. These cover the other `chat.abort` suites, `sessions.abort-*`, `chat-send-pending-input-withdrawal`, worker inference lifecycle, `worker.chat-abort` and `session-run-stopped`.
- `pnpm tsgo:core` and `pnpm tsgo:test:src` (22 shards) pass. Format check and oxlint on the changed files pass.
- On upstream main 9c8db2d231b: `pnpm check:changed` passes every lane except changelog attributions (the `Thanks @steipete` lines in `CHANGELOG/records/2026.11.1.md`; main fails it the same way). `pnpm test --changed`: 7713 passed, 3 failed (`plugin-instance.retention`, `runtime-plugins.ingress-load.integration`, `provider-request-header-redaction`); those three files pass alone on this branch and on main, 25/25. `pnpm test:fast`: 11647 passed, 2 failed, the same two `skills/runtime/discovery.integration` tests that fail on main (11647 passed, 2 failed).

Test lines: net growth of 81, recorded in `config/test-lines-allocations/run-stopped-exact-stops.txt`. `pnpm check:test-lines-ratchet --base 9c8db2d231b` passes (`Test lines OK: 6527625; ceiling: 6527652; slack: 27.`). The lines pay for a new reserved-run case (I found no existing `chat.abort` suite that drives a reserved input with a session target) and for event assertions added to the existing worker, exec and fence cases. No cheaper layer drives these handler branches.

Independent reviews of these bytes: a security pass (Gemini 4 Argon) and an upstream-readiness pass (Gemini 3.8 Flash) found no defect; the one nit, this allocation's comment line, is applied.

## Not covered

- **The pre-routing reserved Stop** (a reserved input with no session target yet): no physical session exists to name, and the branch cancels only the captured source.
- **An exact Stop that finds nothing to cancel** (no live, reserved, exec or worker work for the `runId`): nothing is stopped.
- **`discardPendingInput` withdrawals:** upstream deliberately leaves queued-input discard unmarked (see the comment above the session-wide branch), and this change keeps that.
- **End-to-end proof:** `chat.abort-run-stopped-hook.e2e.test.ts` does not exercise these three paths; the proof here is the handler suites.
