prs.title: fix: tell the turn after a user's Stop that the user stopped it
prs.body:
Related: #120315, #186073

## What Problem This Solves

After a person stops a run, the agent's next turn is never told. It hears nothing once the stopped run has settled, and "continue the unfinished work" when the next message arrives first, so it can pick the stopped work back up. This holds for the Control UI Stop button, a typed `/stop`, a channel `/stop` and the TUI's Stop.

## User Impact

After a person's Stop, the next turn reads: "Note: The user stopped the previous agent run. Do not resume or retry that work unless the latest user message asks for it; if what they want is unclear, ask." It replaces the interruption note, so a stopped turn never also reads "continue the unfinished work". Timeouts, restarts, watchdog stops, maintenance aborts and other non-user cancellations keep today's behavior.

## Why This Change Was Made

#186073 gave an explicit Stop a native fact: the abort reason's `userInitiated` flag (`isUserInitiatedAgentRunAbortReason`). This change carries that fact to the next turn, at the Stop kernel every explicit Stop passes:

- `stopSession` records a user-initiated Stop once its cancellation commits, as `userStoppedAt` + `userStoppedSessionId` on each stopped row. It counts commitments through its own commit callbacks, before adapter callbacks that can throw, and starts the record as the parent phase exits, so a Stop that committed records even when a later target, child or hook fails; one rejected before any commitment records nothing.
- A row records only when this Stop cancelled, on that row (its store, key and incarnation), the run that owns it: its admitted writer, else its live or last lifecycle run, the same ownership upstream's abort-target writers check. An operation's run ids are its native backend identity (`listOperationBackendRunIds`), which survives the backend detaching. A side run, a successor's writer, another owner's live run, a replaced incarnation, the same key, session and run ids in another store, and a newer Stop are all left alone. An idle channel `/stop` records only on the row its native abort mark applied to, and only while that row still matches the target the mark was guarded against (`matchesSessionAbortTargetOwner`), so a successor admitted in between is never marked.
- Each stopped operation fences its successor's admission until that record settles, so the very next turn reads the note. The record starts at commit, so the fence never waits on slow child or ACP cancellation, and it always settles, so a failed write never leaves a session fenced.
- Every reader asks one question, `resolveUserStoppedAt(entry)`: is this Stop this incarnation's? A fork, rotation or rewind that copies the row never inherits the note. The prompt claims the Stop before it says it: the durable row's serialized write retires it for exactly one caller (a deleted row retires nothing, so no prompt says it), so two turns prepared at once never both say it, and a turn that loses the claim never reads the Stop as an interruption to continue.

Server-side Stops a person typed now mark the reason the way the Control UI's button does: a channel `/stop` and a `/stop` sent through `chat.send`. The TUI's Stop sends `userInitiated: true`, stepping back for a Gateway older than the flag. The flag stays presentation and provenance only; authorization is unchanged.

<details>
<summary>Files</summary>

- `src/sessions/session-run-stopped.ts`: the receipt (store and incarnation, never shown to plugins), `recordSessionRunStopped` with its ownership proof, and `trackUserStop`
- `src/sessions/session-controller.stop.ts`: the kernel records a committed user Stop once and fences its successors
- `src/auto-reply/reply/abort-operation.ts`, `src/auto-reply/reply/commands-session-abort.ts`: the channel `/stop` reason marked user-initiated; the abort-target writers report whether their mark applied
- `src/gateway/server-methods/chat-send-pre-admission.ts`: a typed `/stop` is user-initiated
- `src/gateway/server-methods/chat-abort-session-plan.ts`, `chat-abort-exact-run.ts`, `chat-abort-handler.ts`: each passes its announcement's receipt with the stopped session's store and incarnation
- `src/config/sessions/types.ts`, `session-entry-numeric-snapshot.ts`, `src/plugins/session-entry-slot-keys.ts`: the `userStoppedAt` / `userStoppedSessionId` pair
- `src/config/sessions/terminal-status.ts`: `resolveUserStoppedAt`
- `src/auto-reply/reply/body.ts`, `get-reply-run-context.ts`, `abort-cutoff.runtime.ts`: the note, and retiring the Stop it stated (beside `clearAbortCutoffInSessionRuntime`)
- `src/agents/agent-command.ts`: a direct agent command clears the pair beside `abortedLastRun`
- `src/tui/tui-session-actions.ts`, `tui-backend.ts`, `gateway-chat.ts`, `gateway-chat-requests.ts`: the TUI's Stop sends `userInitiated`
- Tests: `src/sessions/session-run-stopped.test.ts`, `src/sessions/session-controller.stop.test.ts`, `src/auto-reply/reply/abort.test.ts`, `get-reply-run-context.user-stop.test.ts`, `body.test.ts`, `session.terminal-completion.test.ts`, `src/gateway/server-methods/chat.abort-run-stopped-hook.e2e.test.ts`, `src/tui/gateway-chat.test.ts`, `tui-session-abort.test.ts`
- `config/test-lines-allocations/user-stop-note.txt`: the test-line allocation below

</details>

## Evidence

End to end, `chat.abort-run-stopped-hook.e2e.test.ts` (an in-process Gateway and a held provider) now sends one more message after each explicit Stop and reads the prompt the provider receives:

| Stop | Main | With the fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `chat.abort` of one run, `userInitiated` (Control UI) | no Stop note | Stop note, no "continue" |
| `chat.abort` of the session, `userInitiated` | no Stop note | Stop note, no "continue" |
| `/stop` typed into `chat.send` | no Stop note | Stop note, no "continue" |
| run timeout (control) | no Stop note | no Stop note |

Focused suites (`pnpm test <file> --maxWorkers=1`), all passing: `session-run-stopped` 5, `session-controller.stop` 39, `get-reply-run-context.user-stop` 10, `abort` 28, `commands-stop-target` 8, `commands-session-store` 9, `body` 3, `session.terminal-completion` 3, `gateway-chat` 27, `tui-session-abort` 19. `pnpm tsgo:core` and `pnpm tsgo:test:src` pass. On upstream main 9c8db2d231b: `pnpm check:changed` passes every lane except changelog attributions, which flags the `Thanks @steipete` lines in `CHANGELOG/records/2026.11.1.md` and fails the same way on main (this change does not touch the changelog). `pnpm test --changed`: 7719 passed, 1 failed (`plugin-instance.retention.test.ts`, which passes alone on this branch and on main, 14/14). Each new guard was mutated on its own and its test went red: 20 of 20 mutants.

Test lines: net growth of 524 lines (`Test lines OK: 6528068; ceiling: 6528095; slack: 27.`), recorded in `config/test-lines-allocations/user-stop-note.txt`. It buys the recorder's ownership table, the kernel's commit/failure/fence matrix, the prompt's precedence and retirement cases, the TUI fallback, and the end-to-end prompt after each Gateway Stop; no cheaper layer proves the end-to-end row.

## Not covered

- An admin's worker-only Stop: its cancellation has no controller operation to fence, so it does not record yet.
- The TUI's embedded (local) backend aborts its runs directly, outside the Stop kernel, so neither `run_stopped` nor this note sees them.
- Native apps' Stop buttons, until they send `userInitiated` as the Control UI does.
- A turn that fails before its prompt is prepared, or claims the note and is then answered without the model (an unsupported thinking level, a runtime that fails to start), loses it: preparing the prompt claims it.
- A run-bearing effect whose interrupt throws after cancelling publishes no run, so its Stop has nothing to prove and records nothing; a run cancelled only as a standalone effect has no operation to fence, so a successor admitted before the record lands can miss the note.
- In each of these the next turn gets no note, exactly as on main today; none can mark a run that was not stopped.
- Restart: a graceful restart right after a Stop is unchanged here.

prs.title: fix(cron): keep one-shot finalization working on PostgreSQL 16
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes cron job finalization and enable/disable transitions failing on PostgreSQL 16 with `function json(unknown) does not exist`. Also repairs the existing PostgreSQL 18 cache conformance assertion for fractional EXPLAIN row counts.

## User Impact

Retained one-shot jobs can finish, and cron jobs can change enabled state, while preserving authored configuration and unrelated JSON fields. No migration or operator action is required. Cache eviction behavior is unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

The cron row writer passed bound JSON text through SQLite's `json(...)` syntax on every engine. The database expression owner now parses serialized JSON with an explicit PostgreSQL cast and retains SQLite's JSON subtype behavior. The JSON path mutation helper stays unchanged, preserving scalar extraction behavior in session callers.

The all-major baseline also exposed a test-only PG18 failure: the correct timestamp-index scan reports `rows=11.00` instead of `rows=11`. Accept zero fractional digits while retaining exactly eleven rows, one loop, the canonical index and no sequential scan. The loop boundary now also rejects `loops=10`. PostgreSQL documents the [fractional EXPLAIN output change](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/release-18.html#RELEASE-18-UTILITY-EXPLAIN).

Correct the PostgreSQL guide's existing CI cadence and the index checker's stale runtime-admission comment.

No SQLite schema version, DDL, migration, persisted format, public API, SDK, config/default, protocol, durability, recovery, or retention-policy changes.

Production delta: +14 lines, justified by the internal engine-owned JSON conversion boundary; net test growth: zero (one existing assertion changed); prose/comments: +4/-3. Replaces the cron writer's unconditional SQLite function expression; adds no fallback or parallel storage path. The existing store-level regression catches the runtime defect; no duplicate helper tests are added.

## Evidence

- [Completed baseline Linux PG16/17/18 matrix](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/42319946804) at `efb980423985b290f5c294ba7b13ad4c2bd074d8`: seven of nine jobs passed. PG16: 1,511 passed, 1 failed, 40 skipped; its sole failure is the repaired [cron regression](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/42319946804/job/128241801265). PG17: all three jobs passed, 1,512 tests passed, 40 skipped. PG18: 1,511 passed, 1 failed, 40 skipped; its sole failure is the repaired [EXPLAIN assertion](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/42319946804/job/128241800966). Counts mix actual PostgreSQL, SQLite sibling and unit/mock cases; the baseline remains failed.
- Repaired runtime source: existing `cron-runtime-row.postgres.test.ts` passed on PostgreSQL 16, 17 and 18, including its SQLite sibling each time: 2/2 tests per major. Covers retained one-shot finalization, true/false enablement, current scratch snapshots, queue reconciliation and opaque authored fields. Runtime file hashes remain unchanged in the final head.
- Repaired `manager-embedding-cache.postgres.test.ts`: all six tests passed on each of PG16/17/18. End-to-end runner wall time: 28.18s / 28.10s / 32.08s respectively; most time is worker compilation, actual cache test cases below one second per major. Retains bounded canonical-index eviction, composite identities, batching, rollback and preferred eviction coverage.
- Original `json-values.test.ts`: 3/3 passed, 1.61s runner wall; byte-for-byte unchanged from baseline. Retains scalar/opaque preservation, ordered projections and nested-array aggregation.
- Each major's schema conformance preflight passed: shared-state and agent catalogs, indexes, constraints, existing task-index migration and trigger parity; zero unexplained differences.
- Focused proof used Node 26.12.1 on macOS with isolated Docker PostgreSQL services and CI's digest-pinned images. Frozen dependency inputs and exact source hashes were verified. PG17 used its cached amd64 image under emulation. Testbox allocation queued and was stopped; no remote payload result is claimed. This is focused repaired-source proof, not a passing full Linux all-major matrix or shipped Gateway/model end-to-end proof.
- Fresh final local autoreview against `efb9804`, P0-P2: complete, no actionable findings. Independent owner/dependency/sibling, test-value and PG18 planner-contract reviews also completed. Kysely 0.29.7 emits named functions verbatim; the PG16 repair belongs in the engine expression owner.
- Pinned formatter, `pnpm docs:list`, `git diff --check` and the zero-growth test-line ratchet passed. The single assertion edit preserves test line count; no existing tests, baseline or allocation were removed.
- [Final-head PR CI](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/42326380913) passed at `98bfbca282cbe41fde4a72e0d91059c3dd65b44b`, including all three full PG17 conformance shards. [Exact-head build artifacts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/42326380864) also passed. The final check rollup has 64 successes, 58 intentional skips, one neutral result and no failures. Earlier failed/cancelled runs remain recorded separately.
- [Final-head ClawSweeper review](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/194384#issuecomment-6700289161) found no actionable correctness/security issues and no before-merge actions. The missing Gateway-level PG16 proof remains the named follow-up below; review scores do not replace execution evidence.
- Squash-merged as [7ab0143fc228](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/7ab0143fc2288251377d0b355b1c78a30c1b55ac).

Follow-ups: add a Gateway-level retained one-shot cron smoke on PG16 in PR CI; separately reconcile inherited one-line test-budget accounting debt in its CI owner. Neither changes this repair's schema boundary.

prs.title: feat(pairing): pair a browser with a short code approved on the host
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A browser with no Gateway credential has no way to ask for one. Today it needs a pasted token, or a one-time link from `openclaw dashboard` carried over from the host. On a headless Gateway reached over SSH, both mean moving a secret by hand.

## User Impact

- A browser can pair without a token, link or host browser. Approving its code on the host pairs it as an ordinary operator device with the Control UI's admin scopes. That is the same result as approving it with `openclaw devices approve`, so it appears in `openclaw devices list` and the Devices page, and `openclaw devices remove` ends its access.
- New CLI command `openclaw pair <code>` and a new public route, both documented in `/cli/pair` and `/web/control-ui/connect-and-pair`.
- A browser that is already paired with a revoked or narrowed operator token keeps that limit. Its code is refused, and the message names `openclaw dashboard` or `openclaw devices remove <id>` as the next step. The owner handoff stays with `openclaw dashboard` and onboarding.
- Pairing works when browser storage is blocked or full. The approved token is kept for the life of the page, as the browser's device identity already is, so the page still connects and **Forget this browser** still clears it. A reload in that state needs pairing again.
- When `gateway.roles` is configured, bootstrap connections need a verified identity, so code pairing is refused there the same way `openclaw dashboard` links are.
- **Known low-impact limit:** a network client that rotates its source address can keep the 32-row pending table full, so other browsers see "Too many pairing requests". State stays bounded and nobody can replace another browser's request. Token and `openclaw dashboard` sign-in keep working.
- On a plain `http://` address, anyone on that network can read Gateway traffic after pairing, as with any plain-HTTP Control UI.

## Why This Change Was Made

1. The login gate's sign-in card gains a **Pair with a code instead** link. It opens a card that holds only pairing. **Get a code** shows `openclaw pair ABCD-EFGH` and a Browser ID while the browser waits. The link is offered only when the selected Gateway URL matches the page's scheme (`ws:` for `http:`, `wss:` for `https:`), host and base path.

   ![Sign-in card with code pairing link](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/b0598b57-272f-4ea4-9d85-4c476a42c6e4)

   ![Pairing card waiting with command and Browser ID](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/f421e08d-c6a2-4cb1-807c-b0885c26c1aa)

   ![Pairing card waiting at phone width](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/d572f64c-71da-4a82-891a-edd473332bf0)

2. On the host, over SSH if needed, `openclaw pair` shows who is asking and waits for an answer:

   ```text
   A browser is asking to pair with administrator access to this Gateway.

     Code                34EL-ZNRU
     Browser (reported)  Mozilla/5.0 (Macintosh; Intel Mac OS X 10_15_7) ... Safari/605.1.15
     Address             127.0.0.1
     Page (reported)     http://127.0.0.1:18789
     Browser ID          e2de4320
     Requested           just now

   Approve only if you opened this page yourself and it shows this code and Browser ID.
   If someone sent you this code or command, answer no: approving gives their browser administrator control of this Gateway.
   Approve this browser? [y/N]
   ```

3. The waiting browser keeps its device token for that Gateway and connects with it.

   ![Control UI connected after approval](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/6952e4cd-4691-4d4f-81c0-fe40e85439ac)

### How it works

- **`POST <base>/__openclaw__/browser-pair/start`** is public and same-origin. Each filed request spends the source's pairing budget under the Gateway's auth rate limit. It takes a signature from the browser's device key and files one row in a new `device_pairing_browser_requests` table, returning a request ID and an eight-character code.
- **`device.pair.code`** requires `operator.admin`.
  - With `code`, it returns the request.
  - With `requestId` and `decision`, it settles exactly that request.
  - Approval files an operator pairing request for the request's key and approves it through the existing approval kernel, using the approving caller's scopes. The browser's own earlier pending requests are closed, not merged into the grant.
- **`POST .../collect`** returns the outcome only to a signature from the requesting key.
  - After approval it returns the paired device's operator token, read from the device record, until the request expires.
  - Collect has its own budget, spent only by invalid signatures and unknown requests, so filing requests cannot lock a waiting browser out of its answer.
- **Expiry and rotation:** the request deadline and the shared-auth generation are checked again when the database writer takes the approval. An approval that waited past expiry or a shared-secret rotation rolls back. Collect checks the deadline again right before it answers, so a collect that waited past expiry answers `expired`.

### Security properties

- The code names a request and is not a bearer secret.
- On the signed pairing and WebSocket paths, the device token works only with the requesting key. Treat it as a secret, like any operator token.
- Code-paired tokens carry the Gateway's shared-auth generation, so rotating the shared secret retires them, like tokens issued at connect.
- An administrator revoked while their approval waits is refused at the final effect, and nothing is issued.
- A collected token is handed out only while it is the token that approval issued; rotation, revocation or removal ends collection.
- Requests expire after ten minutes. At most 32 are pending. Filing and invalid collects are each limited per source.
- **Origin policy:** the route uses the Gateway's browser origin policy, including the check that a loopback page came from a loopback socket. It is a CSRF guard, not a network boundary; authority comes from host approval and the key proof.
- `Browser` and `Page` are marked `(reported)` because the requester chooses them.
- The request table is covered by the secret-table policy, so redacted backups omit it.
- Without a terminal the CLI approves nothing unless `--yes` is passed. The page never suggests `--yes`.

### Decisions for review

- **Ordinary operator pairing, not the owner handoff.** Approval goes through the same approval rules as `openclaw devices approve`. The result is a normal paired device, so the existing ways of listing it, narrowing its token and removing it all apply.
- **`tokenIssuer` approval option.** The approval kernel gains an optional `tokenIssuer`, so the issued browser token is bound to the current shared-auth generation. Without it, the existing token policy refuses issuer-less browser tokens while shared auth is configured.
- **Page-lifetime token fallback.** When storage rejects a write, the device-token store keeps a page-lifetime copy, as the device identity does. This applies to every user of that store, not only pairing.
- **Separate table for unauthenticated input.** Route input stays out of the list operators approve from, including `openclaw devices approve --latest`. Only an admin's decision turns it into a pairing.
- **One additive protocol method and one additive lazy table.** No protocol version change.
- **Test-line allocation.** `config/test-lines-allocations/browser-pair-code.txt` covers the net test lines this PR adds.

## Evidence

### Original implementation

The following records validation before the November 7 review follow-up. Current repair validation and remaining gaps are recorded below.

**Gateway suite** (`src/gateway/server.browser-pair.test.ts`, 20 cases): passes against a real Gateway. It covers:
- first-time pairing by code as an ordinary admin device, with the token refused over WebSocket for another key;
- refusing to restore a narrowed operator token;
- closing the browser's earlier pending request instead of widening the grant;
- expiry while the approval waits in the writer queue, and while a collect waits;
- a queued approval refused once its administrator is revoked through the Gateway's live revocation owner;
- rollback when authority ends at any check;
- callers holding only `operator.pairing`, `operator.read` or `operator.write`;
- a browser that still collects its approval after filing spent its source's budget (`maxAttempts=1`), while forged collects are still limited;
- rejection, unknown or expired codes, origin and key checks, and the start rate limit.

**Control UI** (223 cases across the pairing card, device-identity and device-token storage, device credentials and forgetting, the connection page, the login gate, gateway connect and the app root): passes. It includes a browser whose storage rejects writes: it still connects with its approved token through the real connect auth selection, and that token is listed and forgotten through the real forget path.

**Regressions proven:**
- The storage, forget, collect-budget, token-rotation, collect-expiry and incomplete-stored-identity tests fail without their fixes.
- With the expiry recheck, the narrowed-token refusal or the superseded-request cleanup disabled, its test fails.

**Static checks:** core, UI and the touched test typecheck shards, plus oxlint and oxfmt on changed files, are clean. The generated protocol validators, Kysely types and Postgres schema verify.

**Not covered:**
- the full suite;
- a live browser run on this head, including real blocked storage;
- a browser on a different machine from the Gateway;
- trusted-proxy and Tailscale Serve deployments;
- the Postgres state engine;
- an upgrade from the latest stable;
- translated strings, which `control-ui-locale-refresh` adds.

## Review follow-up — November 7

Pushed as [`26338b1`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/191513/commits/26338b121d8e9d93409caed8c0544c808715f4cf).

- Cancel now withdraws a pending request in the authoritative worker. Only confirmed removal reports cancellation; missing requests are terminal, and approval winning the race does not revoke the device or silently connect the browser.
- Direct browser-code pairing is hidden in OpenClaw ID remote/embedded contexts. Gateways with configured roles explicitly require normal identity-aware sign-in; approval rechecks current policy instead of issuing an unusable grant or bypassing role restrictions.
- The card identifies administrator access (not guest invitation), says to run the command on the Gateway host, and shows bounded reconnect/cancellation retry states while retaining the same request.

CI follow-up [`2c96e0d`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/191513/commits/2c96e0d36ebcec31594455be5200a3b3e99975fa) registers the new browser proof in the serial E2E inventory expectation. The three CI inventory failures were reproduced locally; all 15 inventory tests now pass (15.96s), with lint and formatting clean. This follow-up changes no production behavior.

**Repair validation:** 23 Gateway pairing tests, 2 HTTP tests, 3 worker tests, 66 UI tests (including 23 pairing tests), and 4 CLI tests pass. Regression checks fail against the pre-repair boundary/UI implementations. Core/UI and selected Gateway-test typechecks, targeted type-aware lint, formatting, and diff checks pass.

One real Chromium/source-Gateway scenario proves first-time approval, token connection/reload, interrupted polling, confirmed withdrawal preventing subsequent approval, and approval winning cancellation. Approval uses the real administrator RPC; packaged CLI launch was not qualified because its worker build required unavailable cross-platform downloads in the offline sandbox. Existing CLI behavior is covered separately by its unit suite.

Local runner durations: Gateway pairing 26.79s; focused UI pairing 1.18s; related UI suite 3.10s; real-browser lifecycle 108.36s. CI timings will be supplied by this head's CI run. The single longer browser scenario proves the HTTP/WebSocket/UI/persistence boundary that the fast tests cannot. A separate 520-line regression allocation covers the withdrawal, identity-policy, reconnect/remote-ingress, and real-browser proof additions; the shared baseline is unchanged.

[Inspected before/after screenshots and repair evidence](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/191513#issuecomment-6700537343). Independent review through P2 found only pre-repair index defects, all addressed by the reviewed working-tree repairs included in this commit.

Maintainer security approval is required for this head.

Related: #159660, #120768

prs.title: fix(matrix): polls show as unsupported events in Element X
prs.body:
Closes #191678

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: polls sent by the Matrix channel show as "Unsupported event" in Element X, so people on Element X cannot see or answer them.

## User Impact

User impact: polls the agent or `openclaw message poll` sends to Matrix render and can be answered in Element X as well as Element Web; votes cast by the `poll-vote` action are counted by Element X too. No config or migration.

## Why This Change Was Made

The channel sent poll starts as `m.poll.start` with the MSC3381 unstable content layout, and votes as `m.poll.response`. Element X (matrix-rust-sdk) renders polls only under the unstable names (`org.matrix.msc3381.poll.start` / `.response` / `.end`, kinds `org.matrix.msc3381.poll.disclosed` / `.undisclosed`); Element Web sends those names itself and reads both, which hid the problem. This PR sends starts and votes under the unstable names. The read side already accepts both namespaces, so existing polls in history keep parsing.

<details>
<summary>Details</summary>

- `poll-types.ts`: `buildPollStartContent` puts the poll under `org.matrix.msc3381.poll.start` with the unstable kind names; `ORG_POLL_START` / `ORG_POLL_RESPONSE` exported.
- `send.ts` / `actions/polls.ts`: send with those event types (vote content already carried both keys).
- `SPEC-SUPPORT.md`: poll rows updated (stable names parsed; unstable names sent).
- matrix-rust-sdk reference: `crates/matrix-sdk-ui/src/timeline/event_handler.rs` handles `UnstablePollStart` / `UnstablePollResponse` / `UnstablePollEnd`; ruma `poll/unstable_start/unstable_poll_kind_serde.rs` accepts only the `org.matrix.msc3381.poll.*` kind names.

</details>

## Evidence

- Live observation before the fix (2026.9.4): every poll sent by the channel was drawn in Element Web and shown as "Unsupported event" in Element X Android, in the main timeline and in threads.
- Focused tests on this branch (Windows, Node 24): `poll-types`, `actions/polls`, `actions/messages`, `poll-summary` under the extension-matrix config — 40/40 passed; `send.test.ts` under the extension-database-workers config — 46/46 passed. New test checks the outbound content shape and that it round-trips through `parsePollStart`.
- Targeted typecheck of the changed files: no new errors (only pre-existing core errors unrelated to this change, from the local Windows setup).
- `oxfmt --check` and `oxlint` clean on the changed files; pre-commit hook passed.
- Not run: the QA Matrix live lane (no Docker on this machine); no Element X re-test against this build yet.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

prs.title: fix(onepassword): expire cached secrets on elapsed time
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`OnePasswordBroker.get` caches a resolved secret for `cacheTtlSeconds` (default 300 s) so repeated reads do not hit `op`. Both ends of that window read the wall clock:

- freshness: `cached.expiresAtMs > Date.now()`
- write: `expiresAtMs: Date.now() + config.cacheTtlSeconds * 1000`

A backwards clock step on the Gateway host keeps the cached secret being served as fresh for the length of the step after a rotation, so an agent can keep using a rotated credential until the clock catches up.

## Why This Change Was Made

Secret-cache expiry now runs on elapsed time (`performance.now()`). The TTL, cache key (`slug`), target-fingerprint check, config-fingerprint invalidation, and audit rows are unchanged; behavior without a clock step is identical.

Standing grants and pending authorizations keep the wall clock on purpose: they are persisted safety windows (`grantTtlHours`), so an operator correcting the clock must not extend a persisted grant. Only this in-memory, per-process cache moves.

The module is a bundled extension and may only import `openclaw/plugin-sdk/*`, so it reads `performance.now()` directly. Bundled extensions ship with the host, so no compatibility path is needed.

This is **behavior-completing** for the elapsed-clock family (#191606, #192700, #193147, #193306).

## User Impact

A clock correction no longer extends a cached secret past its TTL. Without a clock step nothing changes: same TTL, same cache hits, same audits.

## Evidence

### Unit regression (mocked clocks and mocked `getItem`)

`extensions/onepassword/src/broker.test.ts` via the repository's Vitest entry (`node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/onepassword/src/broker.test.ts`) on Node v24.22.1:

| Test | BASE | HEAD |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `expires cached secrets on elapsed time when the wall clock steps backwards` | **FAIL** — the second read is a cache hit (one `getItem` call) | PASS |
| `rechecks grant expiry with cache TTL 300` / `7200` (existing) | PASS | PASS |

The existing harness already fakes `Date.now`; it now fakes `performance.now` with the same counter so both clocks advance together, and `advance(ms)` drives both. The new test steps `Date.now` back an hour while `performance.now` advances past the TTL.

### Real-boundary proof — committed reproducible test (real broker + real op-client + real CLI execution)

ClawSweeper asked for real-behavior evidence through the op boundary rather than mocked clocks and a mocked `getItem`. This proof drives the **shipped production classes end to end**: `OnePasswordBroker.get` → real `OpClient.getItem` → real `resolveTrustedOnePasswordCli` trust validation → real subprocess exec of an `op` CLI. A fake `op` executable (owned by the current user, non-writable, absolute-node shebang — passes the same trust validation the product runs) stands in for the 1Password CLI and logs every invocation to a counter file. The wall clock is stepped back one hour by overriding `Date.now` (the same rollback the fix targets); the process-local `performance.now()` is the real clock and its value at the second read (≈14.5s) far exceeds the 1s cache TTL.

This was previously a one-off driver script; it is now committed as `re-fetches a secret through the real op boundary after a backward clock step` in `broker.test.ts`, so it runs in CI. RED/GREEN verified locally:

```
# BASE (broker.ts reads Date.now)
 × re-fetches a secret through the real op boundary after a backward clock step
   → expected '1\n' to be '1\n1\n' // Object.is equality
# HEAD (broker.ts reads performance.now)
 ✓ re-fetches a secret through the real op boundary after a backward clock step 1323ms
 # counter file reads "1\n1\n" — op called 2×, secret re-fetched
```

The counter-file discriminator makes the stale-cache defect directly observable: BASE serves the pre-rollback cached value and logs one `op` invocation; HEAD re-fetches and logs two. BASE/HEAD differ only in `broker.ts`'s clock read (`Date.now` vs `performance.now`); everything else (real op-client, real trust check, real exec, same fake-op binary, same test) is identical. No production Gateway, session, token, vault, or real 1Password credential was touched; all CLI targets are local fixtures. The test is `it.runIf(process.platform !== "win32")`-guarded because the trusted-node fixture relies on a POSIX shebang.

HEAD full suite:

```
 ✓ extensions/onepassword/src/broker.test.ts (29 tests)
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  29 passed (29)
```

### Shipped-Gateway proof — real Gateway process, real plugin, real `op` subprocess, real wall-clock step

ClawSweeper asked for evidence through the isolated Gateway with a real agent and model rather than mocked clocks under Vitest. This run drives the **built `dist` for this exact head** (`d76c3b49efd`, and a base build that differs **only** in `broker.ts`'s clock read) as a long-running Gateway, and reaches the plugin's broker through the shipped `POST /tools/invoke` path — the same production entry the Control UI and channel adapters use:

```
Gateway process (dist build)
  └─ onepassword plugin register()  →  OnePasswordBroker (one instance, in-memory secret cache)
        ├─ before_tool_call policy gate (auto)       ← real
        ├─ OnePasswordBroker.get → cache lookup      ← the changed line
        ├─ OpClient.getItem → resolveTrustedOnePasswordCli
        └─ subprocess exec of a fake `op` CLI         ← real exec; logs every invocation
```

The fake `op` is a POSIX script owned by the invoking user, mode `0700`, with an absolute-node shebang, inside a `0755` directory chain — it passes the **same** `resolveTrustedExecutablePath` trust validation the product runs (an untrusted fixture is rejected with `1Password CLI executable is not trusted`, so the trust check is live, not bypassed). A Gateway token, no channel, no real vault, no real 1Password credential, no outbound endpoint: the fixture host is local.

Sequence, identical on both builds: **read #1** (populates the cache, TTL `cacheTtlSeconds: 1`) → step the host wall clock **back 1 hour** with `date -s` → wait **2 s** so elapsed time passes the 1 s TTL → **read #2**. The discriminator is the number of `op` subprocess invocations.

**HEAD `d76c3b49efd` — GREEN (elapsed clock): the cache expires and the secret is re-fetched**

```text
[gateway] http server listening (2 plugins: memory-core, onepassword; 11.8s)
=== [HEAD] read #1 (populates the secret cache) ===
{"ok":true,"result":{"details":{"ok":true,"slug":"demo","value":"proof-secret-value","itemTitle":"Demo Item","fieldLabel":"credential"}}}
op subprocess invocations after read #1: 1

=== [HEAD] stepping the wall clock backwards 1 hour ===
before: 2026-11-06T04:46:33Z
after:  2026-11-06T03:46:33Z

=== [HEAD] waiting 2s so elapsed time passes the 1s TTL ===

=== [HEAD] read #2 ===
{"ok":true,"result":{"details":{"ok":true,"slug":"demo","value":"proof-secret-value","itemTitle":"Demo Item","fieldLabel":"credential"}}}

=== [HEAD] RESULT: the op subprocess ran 2 time(s) ===
--- op invocation transcript ---
2026-11-06T04:46:33.309Z
2026-11-06T03:46:35.748Z
```

**BASE (production file restored to `Date.now()`) — RED: the backwards step keeps the stale cache alive**

```text
[gateway] http server listening (2 plugins: memory-core, onepassword; 12.6s)
=== [BASE] read #1 (populates the secret cache) ===
{"ok":true,"result":{"details":{"ok":true,"slug":"demo","value":"proof-secret-value","itemTitle":"Demo Item","fieldLabel":"credential"}}}
op subprocess invocations after read #1: 1

=== [BASE] stepping the wall clock backwards 1 hour ===
before: 2026-11-06T04:28:23Z
after:  2026-11-06T03:28:23Z

=== [BASE] waiting 2s so elapsed time passes the 1s TTL ===

=== [BASE] read #2 ===
{"ok":true,"result":{"details":{"ok":true,"slug":"demo","value":"proof-secret-value","itemTitle":"Demo Item","fieldLabel":"credential"}}}

=== [BASE] RESULT: the op subprocess ran 1 time(s) ===
--- op invocation transcript ---
2026-11-06T04:28:22.624Z
```

BASE returns the **cached** secret on read #2 with **one** `op` invocation: after the host clock moved back an hour, `cached.expiresAtMs > Date.now()` is still true, so a rotated credential keeps being served. HEAD returns the same value but **re-fetches it** (two `op` invocations separated by exactly the 2 s wait and the clock step), because `performance.now()` advanced past the 1 s TTL regardless of the step.

Both reads returned `ok: true` and the value is the same, so the observable difference is purely the cache decision the fix changes — the proof does not depend on the secret's content, only on whether `op` is contacted again.

### Proof receipt

- Product head SHA: `d76c3b49efd` (dist built from this commit; `dist/extensions/onepassword/index.js` contains `cached.expiresAtMs > this.secretNow()`)
- RED baseline: same tree with **only** `extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts` reverted to `Date.now()` (two lines), rebuilt and run identically
- Production entry: shipped Gateway `gateway run` from `dist`; tool reached via `POST /tools/invoke` → `onepassword` plugin tool → `OnePasswordBroker.get`
- Recorder: fake `op` CLI appends one timestamp line per invocation; the line count is the discriminator
- Acceptance RED: BASE → 1 `op` invocation across the two reads after a −1 h clock step
- Acceptance GREEN: HEAD → 2 `op` invocations across the same sequence (repeated on a second HEAD build with the same result)
- Control: both builds return `ok: true` and the same secret value on both reads; the only variable is the cache-expiry decision
- Cleanup: the Gateway is stopped after the run and the host clock is restored immediately after read #2 (`restored:` timestamp in each log); the fixture op binary, token file, and state live under a private `0700` home directory and touch no real vault, channel, or credential

### Impact surface

| File:line | Risk |
| --- | --- |
| `extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts:183-184` | Elapsed clock for the secret cache only |
| `extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts:537,558` | Cache freshness read and write; grant/pending windows untouched |

### Not tested

- **Model-driven agent turn.** The last review asked for the same sequence driven by a real agent and model rather than `POST /tools/invoke`. I could not produce that here: the only model endpoint reachable from this contributor host is a local compatibility proxy that does not reliably emit tool calls for this plugin's full agent request. Across repeated runs on a real Gateway it either returned an empty assistant message or announced the call without producing a `tool_use` block (five consecutive attempts, zero `op` invocations — logs available on request). This is a limitation of the local model fixture, not of the patch: the same `OnePasswordBroker.get` line, the same `op` subprocess, and the same cache decision are already exercised above through the shipped Gateway. A maintainer with a standard hosted model can confirm the model-driven turn in minutes by asking the agent to read `demo` twice around the same clock step.
- No live 1Password account: the CLI boundary is a local fake `op` binary that passes the product's own trust validation. The proof exercises the cache decision, not the `op` HTTP client.
- Local `pnpm tsgo:core` cannot run on this contributor host (bundled `tsrs` needs GLIBC 2.29+); type checking is left to CI.

### Cleanup

Work happened in a detached worktree off `origin/main`; no user Gateway, session, token, or user config was touched. The proof's Gateway used an isolated state/config dir under a private `0700` home, was stopped after the run, and the host clock was restored immediately after read #2.

### Maintainer options

<details>
<summary>Land-ready or alternatives</summary>

Narrow single-owner change in one broker method pair plus its test; land as-is if the elapsed-clock direction is what you want here.

Alternatives rejected: moving grants and pending authorizations to the elapsed clock (persisted windows should follow the wall clock an operator sets); clamping instead of switching clocks (leaves existing entries frozen).

Scope: `extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts` and its test file.

</details>

## What Problem This Solves

Repeated dates crowded automation and approval rows, truncating the useful names beside them.

## User Impact

Today's timestamps show only the time in the viewer's locale and hour cycle. Explicit dates from this year omit the year; older dates retain the caller's fields. One-shot session automations keep “Tomorrow at …” and dated future labels. Approval history keeps its full-date tooltip.

## Why This Change Was Made

A shared compact formatter reuses the existing timestamp formatter and its invalid-value fallback. The session one-shot formatter returns the time directly for today, so the unused English “Today” key is removed through the normal translation workflow. Existing local-zone and render-time clock semantics remain intact.

The correction updates the one failing automation-row assertion to require the exact time-only result. No production behavior or passing tests changed in that correction. Whole PR: production +69/-31 lines; tests +1/-1, with no new test allocation.

prs.title: ci: give release watchers a stable workflow identity
prs.body:
Related: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/190941
Stacked on https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/193499.

## What Problem This Solves

Full Release Validation runs from immutable `release-ci/` refs. A workflow-restricted Boat runner group needs a stable, explicitly admitted workflow version for its twelve-hour watcher jobs.

## User Impact

Release operators can restrict the Boat runner group to Full Release Validation Nightly at `refs/heads/main` and Full Release State Watcher at `80d330dfe6d79833a6d5abffcad7478ec1b28b86`. The group, App permission, published Crabbox client, and live runner proof remain prerequisites before enabling Boat. This PR stays a draft.

## Why This Change Was Made

Move Release Decision and Diagnostic Drain into one reusable workflow pinned to its reviewed definition. It preserves the caller's run identity, pinned tooling, admitted verifier, artifacts, outputs, timeouts, and decision-only fail-fast behavior. Both CLI observers recognize the nested job names while continuing to read historical runs.

The duplicate watcher job bodies are removed. The shared workflow and its input/output contract add 57 net production lines; the existing regression suites grow by 72 lines. Updating the watcher version requires updating the caller pin and runner-group allowlist together.

## Evidence

- Independent local reviews: no actionable findings in the extraction or the immutable-pin correction.
- 21 focused native checks passed across six files, covering both CLI observers, caller admission, artifact ownership, timeout budgets, and the strict full-SHA action guard.
- Both new nested-job regressions failed against the base observer source while all three legacy controls passed; all five pass with this change.
- The earlier complete nightly/admission run passed all 13 cases. Unchanged guard and no-push coverage from the broader run is retained; the two affected assertions passed in the focused replay. The full package-admission suite is not claimed complete.
- Tooling typecheck, touched-test lint, workflow validation (actionlint/zizmor), formatting, and whitespace checks passed after the correction.
- GitHub's pinned workflow blob matches the reviewed local definition exactly. No runner-group access or backend setting is changed by this PR.

- Dedicated-app follow-up: all six provisioning/cleanup callers now use `BOAT_RUNNER_APP_ID` and `BOAT_RUNNER_APP_PRIVATE_KEY`. The dedicated private OpenClaw Boat Runners app is not yet provisioned; creation, installation, credentials, and live runner proof remain pending before enabling this route.
- Local ClawSweeper reviewed `f1860e117d4c3c3d9d7dd8c803bc8a600e17a38e` → `9bc30ad20917fa696639c3bd1730c74e60f553c7` (high reasoning, 208.784s): no actionable correctness or security findings. Earlier whole-change review evidence remains applicable.
- The dedicated-app delta passed 12 focused tests (5 runner lifecycle and 7 nightly workflow cases) plus formatting, scoped actionlint/zizmor, and whitespace checks in the parent native checkout. New-head hosted CI and refreshed native preparation remain pending; both PRs stay drafts.

prs.title: fix(ci): preserve worker reuse when test caches grow
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The compiler input snapshot traverses the CI-owned Vitest transform and Node bytecode caches. A new Vitest metadata file changes the discovered input namespace and rejects an otherwise valid compiled-worker seed.

## User Impact

CI can reuse an identical verified worker build after its test caches grow. The compiler no longer scans those generated cache trees. Test selection, source validation, output verification and process isolation are unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

Exclude the two exact checkout-relative cache roots owned by the Node setup action, alongside the existing local Vitest cache exclusion. Nested workspace paths and installed dependencies still participate in discovery. Explicitly captured inputs are still byte-hashed, even inside an excluded root.

## Evidence

Acceptance: creating CI transform metadata must preserve a warm executable seed; neither cache tree should be read during namespace preparation; actual captured input changes and corrupt output must still reject reuse.

- Before: adding `slots/project/0/_metadata.json` under the CI Vitest cache makes the existing worker-cache restore return no seed. After: the same executable bytes are restored and execute successfully.
- All 40 compiler-input and worker-cache tests pass, including explicit captured files in both roots, installed dependency changes, real source changes, incompatible presets and corrupt output rejection.
- Another 15 artifact-cache and lint-lifetime tests pass.
- Root-tooling typecheck, scoped lint, formatting and diff checks pass.
- Independent source review and the full committed-range local review found no actionable correctness or security findings.

This fixes one demonstrated false cache invalidation. It does not attribute all historical cache misses to this bug or claim measured Blacksmith savings yet. No benchmark workflow or additional remote test allocation was used.

prs.title: ci: keep twelve-hour release watchers on Boat VMs
prs.body:
Related: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/190941

## What Problem This Solves

The release decision, diagnostic drain, and nightly qualification watcher allow twelve hours, beyond Boat native CI's six-hour limit.

## User Impact

When the Boat backend is selected, these three jobs run on separate regular Boat VMs with ephemeral organization runners. Existing job bodies and 720-minute budgets stay intact. A dedicated `BOAT_RELEASE_RUNNER_GROUP` keeps hosted runner selection unchanged.

**Draft; do not enable or merge yet.** This needs a published Crabbox release containing https://github.com/openclaw/crabbox/pull/3046, the corresponding managed-client pin, verified organization runner-group/App access, https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/193509 for the stable watcher identity, and a controlled live run. The client capability check runs before VM creation.

## Why This Change Was Made

Short hosted jobs own VM provisioning and cleanup. Each role gets a unique workflow-attempt label and a requested 24-hour lifetime; provisioning rejects an insufficient granted deadline. Same-run outputs carry only public VM identity and the exact Actions registration. Cleanup attempts deregistration and VM deletion independently.

Boat 1.0.89 is downloaded from its versioned upstream asset with a fixed SHA-256. No account credentials or private Crabbox claims are exported as outputs. A hard interruption before outputs reach GitHub can still prevent automatic cleanup; provider expiry bounds compute lifetime but does not prove data deletion.

## Evidence

- Both official and versioned Linux x64 downloads returned identical bytes and the pinned SHA-256; ELF architecture is x86-64.

prs.title: feat(agents): expose configured descriptions in agents_list
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Agent configuration accepts descriptions, but `agents_list` omits them. A requester choosing an allowed subagent cannot see the operator-authored capability summary. Fixes #7490.

## Why This Change Was Made

Expose bounded, nonblank descriptions only in on-demand discovery. Preserve the complete authorized roster, ordering, resolved model/runtime metadata, and existing child-agent restrictions. Each description is limited to 512 UTF-16 units without splitting a surrogate pair, with a shared 4096 CJK-aware weighted-unit budget. Later description text may be shortened or omitted; agent rows remain.

## User Impact

Names, descriptions and existing model/runtime metadata remain available together. Documentation at the current per-agent-entry and subagent-discovery owners describes model visibility and excludes secrets or tenant-sensitive material. There is no new configuration, authorization, persistence, provider, or automatic prompt-roster mechanism.

Existing nonblank descriptions would become model-visible to already-authorized discoverers after upgrade without an operator editing configuration. That disclosure choice requires the maintainer decision below; the spawn allowlist alone does not establish prior operator expectations.

prs.title: fix(agents): stop warning that documented core tool groups need a plugin (#161245)
prs.body:
Closes #161245

## Summary

### What Problem This Solves

Fixes: the warning that documented built-in `group:*` allowlist entries require a plugin. The final bundled-tool policy pass intentionally inspects no core tools, but the diagnostic classifier recognizes only individual core tool IDs.

### User Impact

Canonical core groups no longer produce a missing-plugin warning in that pass. Genuinely unknown entries still warn. Tool expansion, filtering, and grants are unchanged.

## Root Cause

### Why This Change Was Made

`applyToolPolicyPipeline()` classifies `resolved.unknownAllowlist` before applying unavailable-core warning suppression. A canonical group without an available member was incorrectly classified as a plugin entry, so the caller's existing suppression could not apply.

## Changes

The repair recognizes individual core IDs and own keys of `CORE_TOOL_GROUPS` in both diagnostic branches. Two existing red-first regressions protect classification and the suppressed bundled-tool pass.

### Current integration

Integrated main `f4b9e811416` without rewriting contributor ancestry; follow-up head `3bf492b9e1fc417efeb8dfcb4b8311ca168afeac` keeps the run-granted tool contract and consolidates warning tests without deleting cases. The current head has no merge-tree conflict and differs from that main parent in two files, +37/-19 lines.

## Current blocker status (November 7, 2026)

Head `3bf492b9e1fc417efeb8dfcb4b8311ca168afeac` resolves the prior merge conflict and consolidates the same 25 focused tests so the test-line delta falls from +21 to +11. The previous head failed hosted test-line ratchets by 10 lines; current-head hosted test-line ratchet passed. An authorized security reviewer must still approve this sensitive change on the new head. The prior local changed-file run failed only `check:changelog-attributions` on unchanged upstream release-owned files (`git diff upstream/main -- CHANGELOG/` is empty); the current-head local changed-file rerun failed only the pre-existing, unchanged release-changelog attribution gate. Real-process proof below belongs to its identified earlier head.

## Evidence

### Real Behavior Proof

#### Fresh built-process comparison

Ran the shipped `dist/mcp/plugin-tools-serve.js` processes with an actual JSON-RPC client, isolated synthetic homes and configuration, and explicit agent/session context. Each process completed MCP initialization, returned `tools/list`, and exited 0 after stdin EOF.

The bridge intentionally had no plugins enabled: this exercises its production core-absent policy pass, rather than mocking policy classification.

| Input | Historical main `3894c957b62e` | Integrated candidate `d4d349e16fb` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `group:fs`, `group:web` | 1 false core-group warning | 0 core-group warnings |
| Same groups plus `group:proof_unknown` | Core groups and unknown group warned | Only the unknown group warned |
| Returned plugin tools | 0 in both inputs | Same 0 in both inputs |
| MCP handshake, tool listing, process exit | Successful; exit 0 | Successful; exit 0 |

This is a fresh built-process comparison. The before build is the identified historical main revision, not a claim that it is today's latest main.

#### Retained Gateway proof

The original proof used a real isolated Gateway, a stdio MCP probe, and a local OpenAI-compatible mock provider. The seven reported core groups plus one bundled MCP tool produced one false warning before the repair and none afterward. An unknown-group control still produced one warning. All three turns exited 0 with `ok`, and the provider received the same 12 tools.

Those Gateway runs predate this integration. They are retained behavior evidence, not new current-head Gateway executions. Agent identifiers are omitted here.

The existing discussion also includes obviyus's independent Gateway confirmation.

### Test (supporting)

- Head `3bf492b9e1f`: 25 focused tool-policy tests, `pnpm tsgo:core:test`, formatting, and main-relative `git diff --check` passed. Fresh merge-base-scoped independent P0–P2 review found no actionable finding. `pnpm tsgo:core` and `pnpm build` passed on its production-identical parent `541389573ac`.
- At current head `3bf492b9e1f`, `check:changed` failed only at the unrelated unchanged release-changelog attribution gate; all other applicable changed-file gates passed.
- Six existing owner/caller suites passed: 88 tests across policy classification, plugin-only allowlists, effective bundled policy, bundled-tool preparation, the MCP bridge, and Gateway effective-tool inventory. Total wall time: 79.69 seconds; the directly changed suite took 3.46 seconds.
- `pnpm tsgo`, targeted repository lint, and changed-file `oxfmt --check` passed.
- `pnpm build` and the main-relative `git diff --check` passed.
- Fresh independent Codex P0-P2 review: no actionable findings, complete scope. Its frozen candidate tree `cd207b7279ababa2d173e90e5d36fe28902c7f35` exactly matches the published merge tree.

Current-head hosted test-line ratchet passed; refer to the live checks for other gates. Sensitive-path maintainer approval remains pending.

## Risk

Diagnostics only. Canonical-group expansion and tool filtering are untouched. The unknown-group controls and existing grant/filtering regressions remain passing. Upstream's bounded warning deduplication is preserved.

The tool-policy path still requires an authorized maintainer's sensitive-path approval on the current revision. This contribution does not bypass that gate.

## Changelog

User-facing fix notes are recorded here; `CHANGELOG.md` and release changelog files are release-owned.

## Notes

AI-assisted: yes. Prior-head built MCP and Gateway behavior proof is labeled above; current head passed focused tests, test typechecking, formatting, and merge-base-scoped review. Full build passed on the unchanged production tree at its parent head.

prs.title: fix(gateway): scope image capability discovery
prs.body:
## Summary

- scope attachment image-capability fallback to the selected provider instead of rebuilding every provider catalog
- keep runtime-only models by using the existing request-scoped live catalog path
- retry the complete Gateway projection when its published runtime owner is replaced during scoped discovery

## Root cause and owner

Attachment admission first reads the lifecycle-published catalog. When a selected runtime-only model is absent or has provisional text-only metadata, current main falls back to `readOnly: false`, which rebuilds the full cross-provider catalog inside the request. The provider-scoped catalog machinery exists, but this Gateway caller did not use it.

The canonical owner is the Gateway catalog projection. The second read now carries the selected provider into the existing prepared request-scoped live catalog. The projection checks the published owner before and after the asynchronous scoped read and reacquires the full owner on replacement, so catalog, config, agent identity, and auth projection never mix generations.

## ClawSweeper findings

- Early owner replacement: fixed by retrying at the Gateway projection boundary; the regression replaces the owner during scoped discovery and proves only the replacement catalog returns.
- Final provider I/O fence: the old branch tried to turn generation liveness into a public provider-auth revocation contract, but that was incomplete and added a large cross-plugin surface. This port removes that contract. Published-generation liveness governs whether results may publish; it does not retroactively revoke already-started provider requests. Results from a retired generation are discarded and the owner is reacquired.
- Runtime-only models: retained. An independent P1 review caught and rejected an intermediate static-only rewrite; the final branch uses the existing scoped live mode.
- Test-cost evidence: recorded below for the new image-capability file and the combined focused Gateway set.

## Scope

Seven Gateway files changed against integrated main: 222 insertions and 60 deletions. Reuses the existing scoped catalog owner; no provider/plugin implementation changes, new configuration, or cache.

## Validation

- Integrated main: `1f01f4944d45eb265081f8bfbf8d3e8e54ff4266`; resolved conflicts while retaining current static-capability and projection owners.
- Three focused Gateway suites: 86 tests passed (image capability, catalog projection, session utilities).
- Core production typecheck and targeted lint passed; `git diff --check` clean.
- Fresh autoreview against integrated main, P0–P2: no actionable findings in the seven-file candidate diff. Surrounding loader implementations were not included in the isolated reviewer bundle; integration assurance also relies on focused tests and source inspection.
- Previous validation counts and hosted evidence were for the old head and are not current-head proof.
- No new real-channel/live-provider proof was run.
- CI follow-up: the new catalog mock now accepts the loader's optional argument. The affected Gateway-server test-type leaf passed; 16 catalog tests passed. Current head: `8a7567d2df5d`. Replacement exact-head CI is pending, not claimed green.

Russian docs localization is wired up but nearly empty: `docs/.i18n/glossary.ru.json` was 21 entries (1.2 KB) against 107 KB for `zh-CN`, and `ru-navigation.json` did not exist at all, so the Russian sidebar fell back to English while the pages themselves were already 75% translated.

This PR fills in the two files that drive the Russian locale:

- `glossary.ru.json`: **21 → 250 entries** (1.2 KB → 18.6 KB). Existing entries and their order are preserved; 6 target terms were corrected for consistency with the pages: Compaction → Сжатие контекста, Gateway → Шлюз, Node → Нода, Plugin → Плагин, Skills → Скиллы, Webhook → Вебхук. Deliberately kept in English: Active Memory, Cron, Dreaming, Heartbeat, Loopback, Markdown, Self-hosted.
- `ru-navigation.json`: **created from scratch — 12 tabs, 55 groups** (8.6 KB), mirroring the English navigation structure.

No page content, no build scripts, no English strings touched: two data files only.

## Verification

- Every path in `ru-navigation.json` was checked against the repository tree (1,385 `.md` files): 0 broken links, 55 unique anchors.
- Rendered through the real `composeDocsConfig()` from `scripts/docs-sync-publish.mjs`: 12/12 Russian tabs, 55/55 groups, pages resolve as `ru/index…`.

- Note: `check-docs-i18n-glossary.mts` only validates `zh-CN` today, so this file is not CI-gated — I verified it manually as described above.

## Why

The Russian locale is the largest non-English audience for OpenClaw docs and currently has English headings over Russian text. These two files are the smallest, highest-leverage change: no translation work, but the sidebar and the inline glossary switch to Russian immediately.

## Visual proof

Rendered through the real `composeDocsConfig()` from `scripts/docs-sync-publish.mjs`, locale `ru`, same tree, only `docs/.i18n/ru-navigation.json` added.

prs.title: fix(browser): skip live listeners when allocating a CDP port
prs.body:
Closes #194236
Related: #194250, #194295

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: `browser create-profile` (without an explicit `cdpPort`) hands out a port that another gateway on the same host is already listening on. The allocator derived its candidate range from the gateway control port and only excluded ports claimed by this gateway's own profiles, so neighbouring gateways with close control ports never saw each other's live CDP listeners.

## User Impact

User impact: profile creation now skips ports that a live loopback listener already holds and assigns the next actually-free candidate, so two gateways on one host no longer receive each other's CDP ports; when every candidate in the range is occupied — by config claims or live listeners — creation fails with the existing explicit `no available CDP ports in range` error instead of handing out a conflicting port.

## Why This Change Was Made

`allocateFreeCdpPort` walks the same candidate range and per-candidate exclusion as before, and additionally binds a temporary `127.0.0.1` listener per candidate (`node:net`, released before the port is reported), handing out only ports that are genuinely bindable. The probe binds the same loopback address Chromium's DevTools server uses (the repo never passes `--remote-debugging-address`), and any bind error resolves the candidate as occupied, so an unbindable port can never be handed out. The now-unused pure allocator was removed; the range walk's skip/probe order is covered by unit tests with an injected probe, and a test binds a real listener on a port inside the candidate range with no profile claiming it and asserts the allocator skips it.

## Review status

The [review](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/194270#issuecomment-6692350818) requests shipped `browser create-profile` evidence and follow-up on the regression fixture and test-line check. #194250 and #194295 address the same allocation defect; #194295 includes an isolated Gateway CLI reproduction for its own change. This draft preserves the patch and focused tests while those PRs are open.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/test-projects.mts extensions/browser/src/browser/profiles.test.ts extensions/browser/src/browser/profiles-service.test.ts` — 7/7 and 13/13 passing, including the real-listener skip test and the service-level create flow (which runs the real bind probe through its mocked `mutateConfigFile`).
- `pnpm check:changed`: all lanes pass except the two pre-existing red lanes on `main` untouched by this diff (the `changelog attributions` records lane and the `dead export scan` flagging `extensions/codex/src/app-server/thread-prompt.ts` exports).
- The `checks-fast-baseline-ratchets` test-lines lane fails on this PR because `main` itself is currently over the ratchet ceiling (measured on `origin/main`: tree 6551670 vs ceiling 6551618, over by 52 with net delta 0 — non-growing trees pass with a notice). The ratchet does not forgive inherited debt, so any positive net test-line growth fails until the baseline is folded on `main`; this PR's 53 net added lines carry a matching `config/test-lines-allocations/browser-cdp-port-probe.txt` record (credit 53 = net growth 53, verified: removing the record moves the ceiling by exactly 53).
- The `check-prod-types` and `checks-ui-e2e` lanes also fail on a fresh `main` merge: `extensions/deep-research/browser/` gained a research pane whose `./client.js` module was missing on the base tested by that run (TS2307 in `index.tsx`/`pane.tsx`); another PR touching only control-UI scripts (#194265) shows the same failure. Neither lane is touched by this diff.
- Independent review of the commit found no P0/P1 findings. Both raised test-level P2s are fixed in this commit (the real-listener test caps its range at 65535 and asserts the assigned port differs from the listener instead of assuming a specific neighbour, and duplicate invalid-range coverage was merged). A documented residual limitation: a port persisted by another gateway whose Chromium has not launched yet is still invisible to the probe; the deterministic fix would be port 0 allocation, which is a larger behavioral change outside this issue's scope.

prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a problem where maintainers cannot refresh secret-backed native translations for review without also creating and arming an auto-merge generated PR.

## Why This Change Was Made

Adds an explicit non-publishing dispatch mode that runs the existing bounded locale matrix and validation, then uploads an allowlisted binary patch artifact. The default publishing path remains unchanged.

Secret-backed non-publishing runs execute only from the trusted `main` workflow. The operator supplies an exact source SHA; that SHA must be the current head of one open, non-draft PR targeting `main` with GitHub's current review decision `APPROVED`. Each locale worker revalidates the exact PR head and current approval immediately before the translation-secret step. Branch-selected preflight support was removed: guards inside branch-controlled YAML cannot independently guarantee secret isolation. Manual runs use the trusted main workflow definition.

## User Impact

No direct user-facing change. Maintainers gain a review-only native translation refresh path that cannot push, open a PR, or enable auto-merge, while non-publishing source selection requires current exact-head review approval.

## Evidence

### November 2 review-readiness repair

- Removed the branch-selected preflight mode and restored the main-only dispatch contract, addressing the P1 workflow-boundary finding without adding another execution path.

### CI integration repair

## What Problem This Solves

Interrupting `infer image describe` while its image URL is still downloading leaves the download running until the launcher forces the process to exit.

Related: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/194391

## User Impact

Interrupted image downloads close promptly and preserve exit status 130 without starting provider work or emitting late output. Existing execution-enabled media and document reads use the same cancellation path.

## Why This Change Was Made

Pass each read's existing cancellation signal through the attachment owner into its existing fetch/retry and file-write machinery. Cancellation does not become cache-wide state or clean up another borrower's files. The repair adds 27 net production lines; two shared-owner regressions and updated revocation assertions add 33 net test lines, funded by an exact allocation.

## Evidence

The repair exits 130 in 41.8 ms with an explicit model and 49.6 ms with the configured model; GET closes in 1.5/1.7 ms. The repaired cases also verify transport cancellation and a later successful read on the same cache. The four scoped CLI/cache/runtime/document suites pass in 54.80 s. prs.title: fix(codex): retain native thread reasoning effort
prs.body:
## Summary

- retain Codex App Server's effective reasoning effort from thread start, resume, and fork responses
- update the same live and durable binding from matching `thread/settings/updated` notifications
- report the effective native setting through the existing `turn_starting.effort` diagnostic when a supervised turn intentionally has no per-turn collaboration override

## Root cause and canonical fix

OpenClaw's manual response types and durable session binding omitted Codex's response-backed reasoning effort. The notification controller also discarded settings notifications emitted before `turn/start` returned a turn id. Supervised attempts therefore reported a null effort even when the native thread had an effective setting.

The repair records the fact where Codex owns it: start/resume/fork responses initialize it, and `thread/settings/updated` changes it. All binding writers carry the same nullable field. Existing generation and thread guards prevent stale clients from moving live or durable state.

This current-main rewrite does not add `thread_ready.reasoningEffort` or another event field. It fills the long-standing `turn_starting.effort` field only when the per-turn request intentionally omits an override. The live harness independently verifies the effective native effort and the absent collaboration override.

## Dependency contract

The integrated plugin pins `@openai/codex` 0.164.0. The sibling Codex source was inspected directly at commit `fdf23b4097bf19adf2286c64316da2d2a9fedae6`: `codex-rs/app-server-protocol/src/protocol/v2/thread.rs` defines response-backed nullable `reasoning_effort` for thread start/resume and `ThreadSettings.effort` for settings updates. Native thread facts remain separate from per-turn overrides.

## Coverage and change shape

Regressions cover response capture across start/resume/fork and supervised materialization, pre-turn settings updates, durable-owner rejection, effective turn-start diagnostics, and the live supervised/native assertion boundary.

No new configuration surface, schema migration, protocol version, fallback, or parallel path. The positive production delta propagates one native fact through the existing binding writers; notification writes use the connection's current authority.

## Validation

- Current head: `ae1b83e6b0bd`; integrated main: `1f01f4944d45`.
- 89 tests passed across three affected files during conflict repair.
- After the final current-authority adaptation: all three reasoning-effort regression cases passed; extension production types and targeted lint passed.
- Fresh autoreview against integrated main, P0–P2: no actionable findings in the supplied candidate diff; unchanged surrounding source was unavailable to the isolated reviewer.
- `git diff --check`: clean.
- No fresh credentialed live Codex run. Historical CI and hosted review are not current-head evidence.
- Exact-head CI pending after publication; not claimed green.

prs.title: improve: Doctor flags cron failure alerts that could not be delivered
prs.body:
Related: #186990

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes the Doctor gap behind #186990: when a scheduled automation fails and its failure alert cannot be delivered (for example on a gateway with no messaging channel configured), the delivery failure was recorded only in the job's state fields, and `openclaw doctor` never surfaced it.

## User Impact

User impact: operators running `openclaw doctor` now see which automations have an undeliverable failure alert, the recorded reason (such as "Channel is required (no configured channels detected)"), and what to do next: configure a messaging channel for the Gateway or set an explicit delivery target on the job. No behavior changes outside Doctor output, and the check is read-only.

## Why This Change Was Made

Doctor already reports chronic failures, auto-disabled jobs, and in-flight markers, but it did not read the settled alert-delivery result. This adds a finding next to those, driven by `lastFailureNotificationDeliveryStatus` and `lastFailureNotificationDeliveryError`.

Scope follows the agreement in the issue thread:
- Only `not-delivered` warns. `delivered`, `not-requested`, `unknown`, and absent fields stay silent, so an unsettled delivery is never reported as a failure.
- The recorded reason is sanitized before display (control characters stripped, whitespace collapsed, capped at 200 characters).
- Repair-brief wording and deduplication of repair requests are deliberately untouched. Current source already has a repair-per-streak marker and an owner-directed fallback, and the reporter is running the bounded repro to settle those separately. This PR uses `Related:` rather than `Closes` for that reason.

<details>
<summary>Implementation notes</summary>

- Detection lives in `inspectCronJobHealth` and runs for enabled and disabled jobs, so it is placed before the early `continue` that only the auto-disabled path needs.
- Tests are in a new `index.failure-alert.test.ts` because `index.test.ts` is already at the repo's file-length cap.
- `docs/cli/doctor/checks.md` lists the new check beside the other cron reports.

</details>

## Evidence

- New tests (3 passed) cover: a channel-less failed alert produces the warning with job name, recorded reason, and fix hint; a delivered alert produces no warning; `not-requested`, `unknown`, and missing fields produce no warning. These match the verification criteria the maintainer set on the issue.
- `pnpm tsgo:core` passes.
- Existing `index.test.ts`: 27 of 28 pass, and the one failure (`reports a moved partition, refuses --yes guessing...`) also fails on unmodified `upstream/main` on Windows. The message embeds the store path JSON-escaped, so the raw-path match fails. It is unrelated to this change.
- Docs file passes `oxfmt --check`.
- On my Windows machine the local pre-commit hook cannot launch `pnpm` (`spawn pnpm ENOENT`), so I ran the docs checks manually and relied on CI for the rest.

prs.title: improve(auto-reply): name each failed model in the fallback notice
prs.body:
Related: #187011

## What Problem This Solves

When several fallback candidates fail before one answers, the fallback notice names only the first failure and hides the rest behind "(+N more attempts)".

## User Impact

User impact: the fallback notice names each failed model with its reason, up to three, so users can see which models failed and why without opening logs. A single failed model reads exactly as before.

## Why This Change Was Made

OpenClaw already formats a per-attempt summary (`attemptSummaries`) for the lifecycle `fallback` event. When two or more attempts failed, the visible notice and the persisted reason now use that same formatter, capped at three hops plus the existing "(+N more attempts)" tail. Each model reference gets its own 40-character budget, shortened in the middle, so a long reference (a Bedrock inference-profile ARN runs past 100 characters) cannot push the reason out of the 80-character hop. References of 40 characters or fewer read as before, on the event too. Zero or one failed attempt keeps today's text.

The second and third failed models show the same error preview the first one already shows.

## Evidence

- `pnpm test src/auto-reply/fallback-state.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`: 22 passed. Against unchanged `main`, the 4 new behavior cases fail (names every hop, caps at three, keeps the reason for a long model reference, truncates each long reason) and the 2 regression guards pass (single-attempt notice unchanged, no repeated notice for the same chain).
- The same-chain repetition test stays, though ClawSweeper suggested removing it: it is the only test that pins the persisted multi-hop reason. Persisting only the first attempt's reason while the notice shows the chain (`reason: buildFallbackReasonSummary(params.attempts.slice(0, 1))` in `resolveFallbackTransition`) fails that test alone; the other 21 pass.
- `pnpm check:changed --base upstream/main` with `OPENCLAW_CHECK_CHANGED_SKIP_DEADCODE=1`: passed (typecheck core and all 27 core test graphs, lint and format of the changed files, every guard). The dead-export scan, run on its own, reports 7 exports in 4 files this change does not touch (`scripts/pr-lib/cache-lifetime.mjs`, `extensions/knowledge/src/conversation-access-view.ts`, `src/gateway/worker-environments/workspace-manifest-comparison.ts`, `src/state/openclaw-agent-execution-cleanup.ts`); this change adds no exports.
- Live, real providers: an isolated Gateway built from `main` and from this branch, the TUI as the client. The chain's first two candidates are the real OpenAI and xAI endpoints given an invalid key (both answer 401), and the third is Claude Haiku through the `claude-cli` backend, which answered. Text-only change, so a terminal capture rather than a screenshot:
