prs.title: fix(matrix): recover cached sessions and missing device keys
prs.body:
## Description

Fixes #8365. Password-authenticated Matrix channels log in again on restart. If a homeserver loses a device's encryption keys while the local crypto store marks them as shared, startup does not restore the keys and the channel can appear healthy while decryption fails.

Adapt session recovery to main's native Matrix plugin and per-instance `channel_state/matrix` storage. Reuse a session only for the same homeserver, login identity, device and password, then verify its canonical user/device pair with `whoami`. Fall back to password login only for `M_UNKNOWN_TOKEN`; preserve explicit tokens and main's atomic state writes, device locks and state migration. Retain the scope-based crypto database and trust-file names, read-only legacy copying, identity-mismatch handling and cross-workspace handoff.

Reconcile E2EE device keys at startup and re-upload a missing identity from the existing SQLite crypto store, preserving sessions. Refuse conflicting remote keys and distinguish query failure from deletion. Retry transient startup key-query failures up to three times, with a ten-second limit per query and a one-second interruptible delay. Permanent authorization failures and conflicting remote keys fail without retry. Run ongoing health probes in a separate background task once per minute, report failed key health to the plugin host, and keep routine sync/send maintenance independent of that result. Log the first undecryptable event at error level.

## Security considerations

Use PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 with 600,000 iterations and the session token as salt for the password fingerprint, with an explicit format version. Legacy fast-hash fingerprints cannot authorize cache reuse and require a fresh password login. Passwords are not persisted. Conflicting remote identities are never overwritten.

## Evidence

Validated on Linux/Python 3.11 after merging main `e00511b0`, using matrix-nio **0.26.0**, vodozemac **0.10.0**, local aiohttp homeserver fixtures and persisted SQLite crypto stores. `nio.crypto.ENCRYPTION_ENABLED` was checked as `True`.

```text
pytest tests/unit/channels/test_matrix.py tests/unit/channels/test_matrix_recovery.py tests/unit/channels/test_matrix_state.py -q
61 passed
```

The combined suites cover cached-session reuse, expired-token fallback, explicit tokens, credential changes, missing/conflicting server keys, bounded retries and health probes, continued device-message delivery, scope-based database/trust filenames, read-only legacy migration, identity mismatches, device locks and cross-workspace handoff. The main-suite homeserver fixture now retains uploaded device keys and returns them from key queries, so its crypto-store restart test exercises the new startup validation too.

`state.py` only adds the two optional auth-cache fields to `save_auth`; main's migration and lock implementation is retained. English/Chinese Matrix notes include both recovery behavior and main's migration/dependency guidance.

All applicable pre-commit hooks on the six PR files and `git diff --check` pass.

prs.title: feat: adapt dynamic-mcp skill and implement per-session tool persistence
prs.body:
## Description

**Fix: Persist dynamically loaded MCP connections across session turns**

This PR addresses a critical issue in the `CoPaw` framework where dynamically registered MCP tools (e.g., via a `dynamic-mcp` skill) are lost after each interaction. 

**Root Cause:** The `Runner` creates a new `CoPawAgent` instance for every request. While the conversation memory is persisted, the `Toolkit` state (including dynamically added MCP clients) is ephemeral and destroyed along with the agent instance at the end of the request.

**Solution:** 
- Implemented **session-scoped state persistence** for MCP connection parameters.
- Added `_dynamic_mcp_connection_params` to `CoPawAgent` and registered it using AgentScope's `register_state` mechanism.
- Added a `restore_dynamic_mcp_connections` method to `CoPawAgent` to automatically re-establish connections using saved parameters.
- Updated `Runner.query_handler` to trigger the restoration process immediately after the session state is loaded.

This ensures that once a user/agent connects to an MCP server, those tools remain available for the duration of the session, even though the agent instance is recreated.

**Related Issue:** Relates to the need for runtime extensibility of tools via MCP.

**Security Considerations:** Connection parameters are stored within the standard session JSON files. Only command/URL parameters used during the initial `connect_mcp` call are persisted.

prs.title: fix(console): keep reset chats empty after reopening
prs.body:
## Description

After `/clear`, reopening a chat or refreshing the Console restored the cached command as a user bubble even though the backend history was empty. That synthetic bubble hid the empty-state greeting. A successful `/new` could leave the same stale cache.

When an idle chat has empty history and its pending input is `/clear` or `/new`, discard the pending entry instead of synthesizing a user card. This uses the existing history reconciliation shared by direct submissions and background queues, and cleans up both canonical Chat IDs and local draft aliases, including legacy sessionStorage entries. Running commands, nonempty histories, ordinary pending messages, and other chats keep their existing behavior.

The preload-result cache now follows pending-message reconciliation too: submitting an input invalidates prior preloads under both supplied Chat IDs, and a preload with unconfirmed pending input is not reused on selection. Canonical history reads include the known local Chat ID when reconciling pending storage, so opening either alias removes the reset command after the backend clears it.

**Related Issue:** Fixes #8596

**Security Considerations:** Frontend-only cleanup of the affected chat's existing pending-message cache. No backend history, authentication, permissions, or API changes; runtime session aliases are not used as shared storage keys.

- Regressions cover running-command preload → idle backend → A → B → A within the preload-cache lifetime, opening through canonical/local IDs, and submitting a reset after a completed-history preload.
- Installed-SDK integration tests use the real session loader and message state to verify the preload race, navigation A → B → A, and remount after both reset commands.

prs.title: fix(matrix): preserve Windows ADS data during legacy migration
prs.body:
## Summary
Fix legacy Matrix crypto migration on Windows with Python 3.11 by explicitly
copying identity-based database and trust-state files to their scoped names.
This resolves the Windows test failures introduced by the interaction between
the non-destructive legacy migration in #8558 and the scoped crypto filenames
in #8584.
## Root Cause
Legacy Matrix filenames contain the full user ID, for example:
```text
@bot:example.com_qwenpaw-worker.db
```
On Windows, the colon causes the database content to be stored in an NTFS
alternate data stream attached to the base file `@bot`.
The migration flow first copied the legacy directory with `shutil.copytree()`
and then attempted to rename the copied files to their scoped names. With
Python 3.11, `copytree()` copied only the base file and omitted the alternate
data stream. The subsequent migration could not find the legacy database, so
the target `<scope>.db` was never created.
A later attempt to repair the same workspace could then fail with
`MATRIX_CRYPTO_STORE_CONFLICT` because the target directory contained residual
files but no valid scoped database.
Python 3.13 uses `CopyFile2`, which preserves alternate data streams. This
explains why the same tests could pass locally with Python 3.13 while failing
in the Windows Python 3.11 CI job.
## Changes
- Add a shared crypto-store copy path used by both:
  - `_migrate_previous_state()`.
  - `_copy_crypto_for_existing_owner()`.
- Explicitly read the legacy paths for:
  - The SQLite database.
  - Trusted devices.
  - Blacklisted devices.
  - Ignored devices.
- Write those files directly to their scoped filenames in the staging
  directory.
- Use temporary files and atomic replacement for the migrated files.
- Keep the legacy source directory unchanged.
- Remove copied legacy alternate data streams from the staging directory when
  newer Python versions preserve them, avoiding duplicate old/new state.
- Continue to reject source directories containing both legacy and scoped
  versions of the same state file.
- Preserve existing non-E2EE fallback and staging cleanup behavior.
## Tests
Added regression coverage for legacy/scoped filename conflicts and verified
that conflicts do not modify either source file.
Existing failing scenarios now pass, including:
- Legacy directory migration.
- Matching-identity crypto and sync migration.
- Account switching and workspace reuse.
- Existing-owner crypto repair from the legacy directory.
Validation results:
- Windows with Python 3.13:
  - `test_matrix_state.py` and `test_matrix.py`: **27 passed**.
- Windows with Python 3.11:
  - `test_matrix_state.py`: **12 passed**.
  - Focused legacy Matrix migration test: **1 passed**.
- Black, Flake8, Mypy, and `git diff --check`: passed.
- Pylint: no E/F errors.

issues.title: [Feature]: Validate the OIDC browser-flow redirect_uri against a configured dashboard origin instead of trusting the Host header

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: gateway
labels.description: Auto scope: src/gateway/** changed.

labels.name: security
labels.description: Auto scope: src/security/** changed.

labels.name: topic:identity-access
labels.description: Authentication, OIDC, principal isolation, and authorization; former milestone #17.

issues.body:
When a browser login starts, the gateway tells the identity provider where to send the user back, and it builds that address from whatever host name the request claims. The code trusts the identity provider to refuse unknown addresses, but many providers are set up loosely and accept wildcards. An attacker could then start a login pointing back to their own server, trick a real user into logging in, catch the user's login code, and use it to get that user's token or dashboard session.

### Summary

Add a configured public origin (or Host allowlist) for the OIDC browser flow and refuse Host values that are not a bare host[:port].

### Problem statement

`callback_uri` in `crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/api_oidc.rs:518-556` builds the redirect_uri from the request's Host header, with the scheme from the TLS state or from X-Forwarded-Proto when `trust_forwarded_headers` is on. Nothing checks the host against a configured value; the design note relies on the identity provider rejecting unregistered URIs. Many providers are configured with wildcard or prefix redirect rules, and a loose rule turns a spoofed Host into a working redirect.

### Proposed solution

Add an optional `[gateway] public_url` (or `dashboard_sign_in.origin`) and build the redirect_uri from it whenever it is set. When it is not set, accept only a Host that parses as `host[:port]` with no userinfo or path, and refuse anything else before a flow starts. Use the same configured origin for the dashboard sign-in's own-Origin and Secure-cookie decisions in PR #11965.

### Non-goals / out of scope

No change to how the identity provider validates redirect URIs. No change to the device grant, which has no redirect. No change to the CLI loopback listener, which already uses a fixed 127.0.0.1 redirect.

### Alternatives considered

Keep trusting the provider's registration, which is today's design and fails only when the provider is misconfigured. Pin the redirect host to the configured `[gateway] host`, which breaks reverse-proxy deployments. Derive the origin from the first request after startup, which is still attacker-influenced.

### Acceptance criteria

A flow started with a Host that does not match the configured origin is refused with 400 and nothing is sent to the provider. A Host such as `zc.example.com@evil.example` or `localhost:1@evil.example` is refused. Existing deployments without the setting keep working for plain `host[:port]` values, and the docs explain the setting.

### Architecture impact

One additive config field in `zeroclaw-config`. A small change in `api_oidc.rs` where the redirect_uri and the loopback checks are built. No RPC or wire change.

### Risk and rollback

The risk is a stricter Host check refusing a legitimate but unusual proxy setup; the error should name the fix. The setting is optional, so leaving it unset keeps today's behaviour apart from the stricter parse. Rollback is removing the setting or reverting the change.

### Expected routing

Should attach to an existing roadmap/tracker issue

### Next decision surface

Part of #8289 (stage 5, browser flow). It should land before or with PR #11965, where the same Host value also decides the session cookie's Secure flag and the binding cookie does not stop the attack. A maintainer should decide between a configured origin and a Host allowlist.

### Breaking change?

No

### Data hygiene checks

- [X] I removed personal/sensitive data from examples, payloads, and logs.
- [X] I used neutral, project-focused wording and placeholders.

### Recommended action

Add the configured origin, prefer it over Host whenever it is set, and reject any Host that is not a bare host[:port] in both the relay and the dashboard sign-in. Review PR #11965's loopback check so that `localhost:1@evil.example` no longer counts as loopback. Document that the identity provider should still register the exact redirect URI.

### Affected component
channel

### Severity
S1 - workflow blocked

### Current behavior

When a channel conversation's cached turns contain a `role=tool` message immediately followed by a
`role=user` message, `normalize_cached_channel_turns()` appends the user turn's text to the tool
message instead of keeping it as its own turn:

```text
{"tool_call_id":"call_x","content":"...","attachments":[]}

upgrade the host packages
```

The tool message's content is therefore no longer valid JSON. In the OpenAI-compatible adapter
(`convert_messages_for_native`, `crates/zeroclaw-providers/src/compatible.rs`) the
`message.role == "tool" && serde_json::from_str(...)` branch no longer matches, so the message falls
through to the generic branch and is serialized as `{"role":"tool","content":"..."}` with no
`tool_call_id`. Strict providers reject the whole request:

```text
422 Unprocessable Entity: Failed to deserialize the JSON body into the target type:
messages[23]: missing field `tool_call_id`
```

zeroclaw classifies this as a non-retryable `client_error` and the operator sees the generic
"The selected model provider rejected the request".

Because the corrupted pair is part of the persisted transcript, **every later turn in that
conversation rebuilds the same invalid request**: that conversation is permanently dead while other
conversations keep working. Retrying, switching provider/model, and restarting the daemon do not
help; the only recovery we found is deleting the duplicated `user` row by hand (see Workaround).

The persisted shape that triggers it is produced by the runtime itself when a tool round is cut
(`tool_loop_exhausted`, the 10-iteration cap): the transcript ends up as
`... assistant(tool_calls) -> tool(last result) -> user(re-persisted request text) -> assistant(summary)`.

### Expected behavior

- `normalize_cached_channel_turns()` must never rewrite a `role=tool` message. Its content is a
  structured tool-result envelope, not prose.
- A `user` turn that follows a `tool` turn should be pushed as a separate turn
  (`... assistant(tool_calls) -> tool -> user ...` is accepted by every provider we tried), or the
  dangling tool turn dropped — not concatenated.
- As a second line of defence, the provider adapter should not put a `role=tool` message on the wire
  without an id: read the id from the leading JSON envelope (tolerating trailing bytes), or borrow
  the preceding assistant tool-call id, or skip the message — instead of sending a body that a
  strict server rejects.

### Steps to reproduce

End-to-end on a daemon with any channel that keeps tool turns in its cached history
(`keep_tool_context_turns`):

1. Let a turn run a tool loop that is cut by the iteration cap (`tool_loop_exhausted`, 10 rounds).
2. Confirm the persisted transcript ends with `assistant(tool_calls) -> tool -> user` (the turn
   re-persists the user's request after the last tool result).
3. Send the next message in that conversation. The request carries the merged tool envelope and the
   provider answers 422 `missing field tool_call_id`; the turn fails.
4. Every following message in that conversation fails identically.

The corruption itself is a pure function of the input — a local `webhook` channel instance (same
orchestrator path, no chat platform involved) reproduces it deterministically:

```rust
let turns = vec![
    ChatMessage::user("upgrade the host packages"),
    ChatMessage::assistant(r#"{"content":null,"tool_calls":[{"id":"call_1","name":"shell","arguments":"{}"}]}"#),
    ChatMessage::tool(r#"{"tool_call_id":"call_1","content":"sync output","attachments":[]}"#),
    // the tool-capped turn re-persists the user's request after the last tool result
    ChatMessage::user("upgrade the host packages"),
];
let normalized = normalize_cached_channel_turns(turns);
// normalized[2].content == "{...}\n\nupgrade the host packages"  -> invalid envelope
```

### Impact

- Affected users: any channel whose cached history keeps tool turns (`keep_tool_context_turns`) and
  where a turn is interrupted or hits the tool-iteration cap right after a tool result — QQ /
  Telegram / Discord / Matrix / etc. all use the same code path.
- Frequency: deterministic once such a pair is written to the transcript.
- Consequence: that conversation is permanently unusable; every later message fails with a
  non-retryable provider 4xx while other conversations work, which reads like a credentials or
  model problem to the operator. Restarts and provider/model switches do not clear it.
- On lenient providers the same corruption degrades silently (tool result and user text squashed
  into one message) instead of failing loudly, so it is not caught early.

### Logs / stack traces

Provider: DeepSeek official API (`https://api.deepseek.com`, OpenAI-compatible wire, model
`deepseek-flash`) — no proxy, gateway or third-party router in front of it.

Provider rejection (redacted):

```text
WARN  providers: API error
      status=422
      body={"error":{"message":"Failed to deserialize the JSON body into the target type:
            messages[23]: missing field `tool_call_id` at line 1 column 13638 ...",
            "type":"invalid_request_error"}}
WARN  Non-retryable error, moving on
      error_kind=client_error error_phase=http_response
WARN  Exhausted retries, trying next model_provider/model
WARN  llm_response
      error=All model providers/models failed after 1 failure event(s): event 1 (retry 1/3):
      non_retryable; kind=client_error; phase=http_response
```

The same turn's `llm_request` event (request-payload capture, redacted) shows the merged message:

```text
[22] role=assistant  {"content":null,"tool_calls":[{"id":"call_x","name":"shell",...}]}
[23] role=tool       {"attachments":[],"content":"... package db sync output ...","tool_call_id":"call_x"}

                     [<timestamp>] upgrade the host packages
[24] role=assistant  <summary of the truncated turn>
```

### ZeroClaw version

0.8.7 (99bd353c7). The two functions named below are unchanged on master (checked 2026-11-02), so
this is not already fixed there.

### Rust version
rustc 1.99.1 (58cf8f9c3 2026-10-13)

### Operating system
Arch Linux (Linux 7.2.14-arch1-1)

### Regression?
Unknown — the merge behaviour landed with #1056 / #1057 (2026-02-20), but it only corrupts once
channel cached turns can contain tool results, so it has most likely been latent since then.

### Pre-flight checks
- [X] I reproduced this on the latest master branch or latest release.
- [X] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content.

### Root cause analysis (extra context for triage)

- `normalize_cached_channel_turns()` (`crates/zeroclaw-channels/src/orchestrator/mod.rs`): the
  `(_, "tool") | (true, "user")` arm pushes the tool turn and sets `expecting_user = false`, so a
  following `user` turn matches `(false, "user")` and is merged into `normalized.last_mut()`.
  That merge was introduced by #1057 (fixing #1056, "interrupted channel turns can drop latest user
  context"); its tests cover `user+user` and `assistant+assistant`, not `tool+user`.
- `convert_messages_for_native()` (`crates/zeroclaw-providers/src/compatible.rs`): only the branch
  that parses the whole content as JSON writes `tool_call_id`; a tool message whose content no
  longer parses reaches the generic branch with `tool_call_id: None`.
- Related, but different mechanisms: #843, #5268 (compressor fast-trim), #8219 (Groq null id).

### Proposed fix

1. `normalize_cached_channel_turns()`: a `user` turn whose predecessor is `role=tool` must be pushed
   as its own turn (`(false, "user") if last.role == "tool"` guard ahead of the merge arm).
2. `compatible.rs`: recover the id from the leading JSON value of the tool content
   (`serde_json::Deserializer::into_iter`, tolerating trailing bytes) and fall back to the most
   recent assistant tool-call id; keep a warning when neither is available.
3. Tests: `normalize_cached_channel_turns_keeps_tool_envelope_when_user_follows_tool`, plus a
   helper test for the id recovery; the existing `user+user` / `assistant+assistant` merge tests
   must stay green (they do).

### Verification

Local, on a `webhook` channel instance against DeepSeek's official API (`https://api.deepseek.com`,
model `deepseek-flash`, OpenAI-compatible wire) — no chat platform, proxy or router involved:

- Before the fix, one request logged, in causal order, the merge into the tool turn
  (`target_chars_before=82`, `incoming_chars=54`), the envelope going invalid
  (`chars 82 -> 138`, `valid_json true -> false` — exactly the appended `\n\n` plus the user turn),
  `role=tool` serialized without `tool_call_id`, and then the 422 above.
- With the fix applied, the same transcript (still containing `tool -> user`) returns 200; the tool
  message keeps its envelope and `tool_call_id`, the user turn is delivered as its own message, no
  such warnings are emitted, and the regression tests plus the two pre-existing merge tests pass.

### Workaround

For an affected conversation, remove the duplicated `user` row that directly follows a `tool` row
and restart the daemon (the restart drops the poisoned in-memory cache):

```sql
-- find it
SELECT s.id, s.role FROM sessions s
WHERE s.role = 'user'
  AND (SELECT role FROM sessions p
       WHERE p.session_key = s.session_key AND p.id < s.id
       ORDER BY p.id DESC LIMIT 1) = 'tool';
-- then: DELETE FROM sessions WHERE id = <that row's id>;
```

issues.body:
### Affected component

gateway/api

### Severity

S2 - degraded behavior

### Current behavior

After every chat turn the gateway replaces the whole session transcript in SQLite, and the replacement stamps **every** row with the same `created_at` (the time of the replacement). As a result `GET /api/sessions/{id}/messages` returns one single `created_at` for all rows of a session, including messages from earlier turns, and the original per-message times cannot be recovered.

Call chain, read on `74362c2d6bfeaa81cc611e75cd07b7f3afd52d64` (`master` as of 2026-10-01):

1. `crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/ws.rs:2185` (`Ok(outcome)` branch of the turn): `persist_agent_conversation_state(backend.as_ref(), session_key, agent);`. The error branch (`:2360`) and the cancellation branch (`:2126`, via `replace_conversation_state_unless_deleted(`) persist the same way.
2. `ws.rs:1099` `fn persist_agent_conversation_state` builds `zeroclaw_providers::durable_chat_messages(agent.history())` and goes through `replace_conversation_state_unless_deleted` (`:1069`) to `backend.replace_conversation_state_if_exists(...)`.
3. `crates/zeroclaw-infra/src/session_sqlite.rs:943` `fn replace_conversation_state_if_exists` calls `Self::rewrite_messages_on(&tx, session_key, messages)` (`:963`).
4. `session_sqlite.rs:237` `fn rewrite_messages_on` runs `DELETE FROM sessions WHERE session_key = ?1`, then `let now = Utc::now().to_rfc3339();` (`:246`) and `for message in messages { Self::append_on(conn, session_key, message, &now)?; }`: one `now` for the whole batch.
5. `ChatMessage` only has `role` and `content` (`crates/zeroclaw-api/src/model_provider.rs`), so the replacement has no original time to keep.
6. Read side: `load_with_timestamps` (`session_sqlite.rs:865`) and `handle_api_session_messages` (`crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/api.rs:1840`, `"created_at": m.created_at.map(...)`) expose the column as is. The dashboard renders it per message (`web/src/pages/Dashboard.tsx:1445-1451`, `formatLocalDateTime(m.created_at)`).

The same function is reached by other production writers that I read but did **not** execute: the chat RPC (`replace_rpc_chat_conversation_state`, `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/rpc/dispatch.rs:12713`, called at the end of a turn and when restoring with a trim) and the channels orchestrator after a history trim (`crates/zeroclaw-channels/src/orchestrator/mod.rs:4054` and `:16298`). The ACP store has the same pattern (`acp_session_store.rs` `replace_messages_inner`: `DELETE FROM acp_messages` plus one `now`), but nothing reads `acp_messages.created_at` today.

It was introduced by #9713 (`d6db0b273`). Before it, the turn appended only the new messages (`persist_conversation_messages` -> `backend.append(...)`), so each row got its own time.

### Expected behavior

`created_at` of a row should stay the time that message was first persisted. Rewriting the transcript (history trim, sync with `agent.history()`) should not change `created_at` of rows that did not change. At minimum, messages from different turns must keep different, ordered times after the next turn.

Contract note: the comments say "RFC 3339 timestamp recorded when the row was persisted" (`web/src/types/api.ts:313`) and "the row's `created_at` column" (`session_backend.rs:63-65`). Read literally, a re-inserted row was "persisted" at the replacement, so the text does not promise the original time; the expectation comes from how the field is used (per-message time in the dashboard) and from the previous append behavior. Maintainers may prefer to document "time of last replacement" instead; this report assumes "time of first persistence".

### Steps to reproduce

```bash
# --- A. Unit test (deterministic; no LLM, no gateway) -------------------------------------
# Needs Rust >= 1.96.0. Use a throwaway copy: the next step edits session_sqlite.rs.
mkdir ~/zc-repro && git -C <repo> archive 74362c2d6bfeaa81cc611e75cd07b7f3afd52d64 | tar -x -C ~/zc-repro
cd ~/zc-repro
F=crates/zeroclaw-infra/src/session_sqlite.rs
sed -i '$ d' "$F"            # drop the closing brace of `mod tests` (last line of the file)
cat >> "$F" <<'EOF'

    #[test]
    fn rewrite_keeps_created_at_of_unchanged_rows() {
        let tmp = TempDir::new().unwrap();
        let backend = SqliteSessionBackend::new(tmp.path()).unwrap();
        backend
            .replace_conversation_state(
                "k",
                &[ChatMessage::user("q1"), ChatMessage::assistant("a1")],
                false,
            )
            .unwrap();
        let first = backend.load_with_timestamps("k");
        assert_eq!(first.len(), 2);
        std::thread::sleep(std::time::Duration::from_millis(50));
        backend
            .replace_conversation_state(
                "k",
                &[
                    ChatMessage::user("q1"),
                    ChatMessage::assistant("a1"),
                    ChatMessage::user("q2"),
                    ChatMessage::assistant("a2"),
                ],
                false,
            )
            .unwrap();
        let rows = backend.load_with_timestamps("k");
        assert_eq!(rows.len(), 4);
        assert_eq!(rows[0].created_at, first[0].created_at); // FAILS on master
        assert!(rows[0].created_at < rows[2].created_at);
    }

    #[test]
    fn rewrite_if_exists_keeps_created_at_of_unchanged_rows() {
        // Same, but the second write goes through `replace_conversation_state_if_exists`,
        // the path used by the gateway and the RPC chat.
        let tmp = TempDir::new().unwrap();
        let backend = SqliteSessionBackend::new(tmp.path()).unwrap();
        backend
            .replace_conversation_state(
                "k",
                &[ChatMessage::user("q1"), ChatMessage::assistant("a1")],
                false,
            )
            .unwrap();
        let first = backend.load_with_timestamps("k");
        std::thread::sleep(std::time::Duration::from_millis(50));
        let wrote = backend
            .replace_conversation_state_if_exists(
                "k",
                &[
                    ChatMessage::user("q1"),
                    ChatMessage::assistant("a1"),
                    ChatMessage::user("q2"),
                    ChatMessage::assistant("a2"),
                ],
                false,
            )
            .unwrap();
        assert!(wrote);
        let rows = backend.load_with_timestamps("k");
        assert_eq!(rows.len(), 4);
        assert_eq!(rows[0].created_at, first[0].created_at); // FAILS on master
        assert!(rows[0].created_at < rows[2].created_at);
    }
}
EOF
cargo test -p zeroclaw-infra --locked --lib keeps_created_at -- --nocapture --test-threads=1
# Expected: both tests pass.  Observed on 74362c2d: "2 failed" (see Logs).

# --- B. End to end through the gateway ------------------------------------------------------
# The turn only enters through the WebSocket (`/ws/chat`, crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/lib.rs:2376);
# curl can only read the transcript.
zeroclaw daemon                       # or: zeroclaw gateway start
# 1. In the web chat of an agent send "one" and wait for the full answer
#    (or connect a WebSocket client to ws://127.0.0.1:<port>/ws/chat?agent=<alias>&session_id=<id>,
#     send {"type":"connect"} and then {"type":"message","content":"one"}).
# 2. Wait at least 60 seconds.
# 3. Send "two" and wait for the full answer.
# 4. Read the transcript (replace <TOKEN> and the session key, e.g. gw_<session_id>):
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>" http://127.0.0.1:<port>/api/sessions/<session_key>/messages
# Expected: the first two rows carry the time of the first turn (>= 60 s before the last two).
# Observed (executed with a scripted WebSocket client, a local OpenAI-compatible mock instead of a real
# provider, pairing disabled and 10 s between turns): all four rows carry the same created_at.
```

### Impact

Affected users: anyone on the SQLite session backend (the default) who reads `created_at` through the API: the dashboard "Sessions" view, custom clients, and the web chat if it starts using `created_at`.
Frequency: on every turn of a gateway WebSocket session; executed on the second turn of a session, and by code reading for later turns (each turn ends in the same replacement). The chat RPC does the same per turn by code reading (not executed); channel sessions and restores only when the history is trimmed, and that trim drops messages from the start of the history.
Consequence: per-message time is flattened and cannot be recovered; existing histories are flattened on their next turn. A client that starts reading `created_at` per message (for example the frontend change in the draft #9504) would show wrong, identical times until the backend keeps them.

### Logs / stack traces

No error or crash: this is a data result. Output of the unit test on `74362c2d` (WSL2, Ubuntu 24.04.4, rustc 1.98.1):

```text
test session_sqlite::tests::rewrite_if_exists_keeps_created_at_of_unchanged_rows ... IF_EXISTS PRIMERA: [Some(2026-10-02T01:33:36.514717237Z), Some(2026-10-02T01:33:36.514717237Z)]
IF_EXISTS SEGUNDA: [Some(2026-10-02T01:33:36.565942891Z), Some(2026-10-02T01:33:36.565942891Z), Some(2026-10-02T01:33:36.565942891Z), Some(2026-10-02T01:33:36.565942891Z)]
assertion `left == right` failed
  left: Some(2026-10-02T01:33:36.565942891Z)
 right: Some(2026-10-02T01:33:36.514717237Z)
test session_sqlite::tests::rewrite_keeps_created_at_of_unchanged_rows ... PRIMERA LECTURA: [Some(2026-10-02T01:33:36.595161730Z), Some(2026-10-02T01:33:36.595161730Z)]
SEGUNDA LECTURA: [Some(2026-10-02T01:33:36.646112447Z), Some(2026-10-02T01:33:36.646112447Z), Some(2026-10-02T01:33:36.646112447Z), Some(2026-10-02T01:33:36.646112447Z)]
assertion `left == right` failed
  left: Some(2026-10-02T01:33:36.646112447Z)
 right: Some(2026-10-02T01:33:36.595161730Z)
test result: FAILED. 0 passed; 2 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 311 filtered out
```

(Output trimmed: the `panicked at` lines are omitted. The `PRIMERA`/`SEGUNDA` lines (Spanish for "first"/"second") come from two `eprintln!` calls I used while reproducing and are not part of the test above; they print `created_at` after the first and the second write.)

End to end (gateway on `74362c2d`, two turns 12 s apart, `GET /api/sessions/gw_repro1/messages`); the session itself was created at `01:33:40.299`:

```text
user       2026-10-02T01:33:52.657649735+00:00
assistant  2026-10-02T01:33:52.657649735+00:00
user       2026-10-02T01:33:52.657649735+00:00
assistant  2026-10-02T01:33:52.657649735+00:00
rows: 4  distinct created_at: 1
```

The same end-to-end run on `5eb6bfa640500c315d66292672d65809ba855110` (parent of `d6db0b273`) gives four different values (`01:52:00.888330692`, `01:52:00.888781019`, `01:52:12.192018690`, `01:52:12.192250209`).

`zeroclaw doctor`, run in an isolated HOME with the test config and without the daemon or the mock running: `Summary: 20 ok, 6 warnings, 2 errors`. The two errors come from that test setup, not from this bug: `state file not found: <home>/.zeroclaw/state/daemon_state.json — is the daemon running?` and `custom.mock: Custom model list request failed: http://127.0.0.1:18080/v1/models`.

### ZeroClaw version

`zeroclaw 0.8.5 (unknown)` (debug build from `git archive` of `74362c2d6bfeaa81cc611e75cd07b7f3afd52d64`, `master` on 2026-10-01; `(unknown)` because the archive has no git metadata).

### Rust version

rustc 1.98.1 (48a229cea 2026-09-01), cargo 1.98.1 (`rust-version = "1.96.0"` in `Cargo.toml`)

### Operating system

WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS (kernel 6.6.87.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2) on a Windows 11 host. The defect is SQLite persistence logic and should not depend on the OS; I did not try macOS or native Windows.

### Regression?

Yes, it worked before

Executed: the same end-to-end run gives four different `created_at` values on `5eb6bfa6` (parent of `d6db0b273`) and a single value on `74362c2d`. In the parent, the turn is persisted with `persist_conversation_messages(backend.as_ref(), session_key, &outcome.new_messages)` (`ws.rs:1673` there), which calls `backend.append(session_key, message)` per message; that commit has no `rewrite_messages_on` or `replace_conversation_state`. Caveat: there are more commits between `5eb6bfa6` and `74362c2d` than `d6db0b273`. I did not build `d6db0b273` itself; attributing it to #9713 rests on `git blame` / `git log -L` of those lines.

### Pre-flight checks

- [x] I reproduced this on the latest master branch or latest release.
- [x] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content.

issues.title: [Bug]: cron update --agent reports success but never reassigns the job's agent
issues.body:
### Affected component

runtime/daemon

### Severity

S2 - degraded behavior

### Current behavior

`zeroclaw cron update <id> --agent <alias>` accepts the flag, validates that the alias exists (`require_configured_agent`), prints the success block (`cli-cron-updated`, next run, payload confirmation) — but the job keeps executing under its previous agent. The reassignment is silently dropped.

Root cause: `CronJobPatch` (`crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/cron/types.rs`) has **no `agent_alias` field**. The CLI handler (`src/cron/mod.rs`, `CronCommands::Update`) builds the patch with `..CronJobPatch::default()` and passes `agent_alias` only to `update_shell_job_with_approval`, where it names whose *risk profile validates a shell command* — it never reaches the stored row. So for prompt-only updates the flag is a pure no-op, reported as success.

We hit this operationally: attempted to reassign a weekly job to a different agent via the documented flag; CLI reported success; the job kept running under the old agent until the DB row was edited directly.

### Expected behavior

Either:
1. `cron update --agent <alias>` reassigns the job's executing agent (add `agent_alias` to `CronJobPatch`, persist it in `update_job`, emit a confirmation line naming the new agent), **or**
2. if reassignment is intentionally unsupported, the CLI rejects the flag with a clear error instead of reporting success.

Option 1 matches the flag's documented intent; option 2 is the minimal honest fix.

### Steps to reproduce

```bash
# 1. Create an agent cron job under agent A
zeroclaw cron add-agent '0 6 * * 1' 'do the weekly thing' --agent agent-a
# => created, id <id>

# 2. Reassign it to agent B
zeroclaw cron update <id> --agent agent-b
# => prints "updated", schedule, next run — looks successful

# 3. Check who actually owns it
zeroclaw cron list
# => agent_alias is still agent-a; the job ran (and will run) as agent-a
```

### Impact

Affected users: operators reassigning cron jobs between agents (e.g. moving a scheduled task to a secretary agent with different tools/skills).
Frequency: always — the update path has no field to carry the assignment.
Consequence: silent configuration drift; the operator believes a delegation took effect while the old agent keeps executing the job. In our case it required direct DB editing to recover.

### Logs / stack traces

No error is logged — the command exits 0 and prints the standard success block. Code references (v0.8.7, current master):

- `src/cron/mod.rs` — `CronCommands::Update` arm: `agent_alias` used only for `require_configured_agent` and `update_shell_job_with_approval(config, &agent_alias, &id, patch, false)`; the `CronJobPatch` literal uses `..CronJobPatch::default()`.
- `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/cron/types.rs` — `pub struct CronJobPatch` has no `agent_alias` field (the stored `CronJob.agent_alias` exists and is mutable only via direct DB writes).

### ZeroClaw version

v0.8.7 (reproduced on current master, commit 683d10139b)

### Rust version

rustc 1.97.1

### Operating system

Any — reproduced on Windows 11 (Windows Service install); the code path is platform-independent.

### Regression?

Unknown — the `CronJobPatch` struct appears to have never carried `agent_alias`, so this likely never worked, but we only discovered it now.

### Pre-flight checks

- [x] I reproduced this on the latest master branch or latest release.
- [x] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content.

issues.title: [Bug]: delegated agents don't load TOOLS.md (delegate prompt uses its own file list, not PERSONALITY_FILES)
issues.body:
### Affected component

runtime/daemon

### Severity

S2 - degraded behavior

### Current behavior

When an agent is reached through the `delegate` tool, its system prompt is built by a separate builder in `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/tools/delegate.rs` that appends a hard-coded list of workspace files:

```rust
let identity_files = [
    "AGENTS.md",
    "SOUL.md",
    "IDENTITY.md",
    "USER.md",
    "BOOTSTRAP.md",
];
```

(v0.8.7: `tools/delegate.rs` ~L4644; current master: ~L5012.)

The normal prompt path loads `PERSONALITY_FILES` from `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/agent/personality.rs`:

```rust
pub const PERSONALITY_FILES: &[&str] = &[
    "SOUL.md", "IDENTITY.md", "USER.md", "AGENTS.md",
    "TOOLS.md", "HEARTBEAT.md", "BOOTSTRAP.md", "MEMORY.md",
];
```

So a delegated target never sees its own `TOOLS.md` (and also not `HEARTBEAT.md` / `MEMORY.md`), even though the same agent sees them when addressed directly on a channel. The delegate list also skips the `MAX_FILE_CHARS` (20,000) per-file cap and uses a different file order than the normal path.

### Expected behavior

A delegated agent should get the same workspace context files as when it is addressed directly, ideally by reusing `PERSONALITY_FILES` (and the same truncation) rather than a second hard-coded list, so the two can't drift.

`MEMORY.md` may be an intentional exception: `personality.rs` notes that isolated sessions withhold `MEMORY.md` from the prompt. If a delegated run counts as isolated, keeping `MEMORY.md` out is fine, but it would be clearer to derive that from the shared list (minus the isolated-session exclusion) than to omit it implicitly. `TOOLS.md` has no such exclusion.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Configure two agents, `front` and `specialist`, with `[agents.front] delegates = [{ agent = "specialist", mode = "independent" }]`, `delegation_policy = { mode = "allow" }` on front's risk profile, and `agentic = true` on the specialist's runtime profile.
2. Put a distinctive instruction only in the specialist's workspace `TOOLS.md`, for example `When asked for the magic word, reply "pineapple".`
3. Ask the specialist directly on a channel: "What is the magic word?" It can answer "pineapple" (TOOLS.md is in the normal prompt).
4. Ask `front` to delegate the same question to `specialist`. Per the delegate prompt builder above, the delegated specialist's system prompt contains AGENTS/SOUL/IDENTITY/USER/BOOTSTRAP but not TOOLS.md, so it cannot know the magic word.

(Found by source inspection while debugging a two-agent setup; steps 3-4 describe what the code does rather than a captured run.)

### Impact

Operators naturally put tool-usage guidance in `TOOLS.md` (that is what the file is for). In a front-door + specialist setup, most of the specialist's traffic arrives via `delegate`, so that guidance silently never applies. There is no warning, and the agent docs (`docs/book/src/agents/multi-agent-setup.md`, filesystem/anatomy pages) describe the normal load set without noting that delegated runs differ.

### Logs / stack traces

N/A (prompt-composition difference; no error is raised).

### ZeroClaw version

v0.8.7 (same code on current master)

### Rust version

1.96.0

### Operating system

Linux (Docker, official v0.8.7 image)

### Regression?

Unknown

### Pre-flight checks

- [x] I reproduced this on the latest master branch or latest release. (Verified by reading the v0.8.7 source and current `master`; both have the same hard-coded list.)
- [x] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content.

issues.title: [Bug]: Empty canvases are never removed, stay in the viewer list and count toward the 100-canvas limit
issues.body:
### Affected component

tools

### Severity

S3 - minor issue

### Current behavior

`CanvasStore` (`crates/zeroclaw-tools/src/canvas.rs`) never removes an entry once it exists, so empty canvases pile up.

- **Viewing creates entries.** `subscribe()` (L148) creates an empty entry when the ID doesn't exist, and `/ws/canvas/{id}` calls it on every connection (`crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/canvas.rs` L214). The viewer connects to `default` on mount and to any ID typed into Switch, so just looking at a canvas creates one.
- **Clearing doesn't remove.** `clear()` (L126) empties the current frame and history and sends a `clear` frame, but keeps the entry. Both the tool's `clear` action and `DELETE /api/canvas/{id}` (the viewer's trash button, `handle_canvas_clear`) end there.
- **Listing includes empties.** `list()` (L166) is documented as "List all canvas IDs that currently have content" but returns every key. The viewer polls `GET /api/canvas` every 5 s (`web/src/pages/Canvas.tsx` L111–118), so cleared or merely viewed IDs stay in the list. On a `clear` frame (L86) the viewer resets its display but not the list.
- **Empties count toward the limit.** `render()` and `subscribe()` refuse new IDs once the store holds `MAX_CANVAS_COUNT` (100) entries, empty or not. The tool's `render` and `eval` errors (L292, L360) and `POST /api/canvas/{id}` (gateway `canvas.rs` L132) say "Clear unused canvases first.", but clearing doesn't free a slot. The WS refusal (gateway L219) says only "Maximum canvas count reached". Today only a restart frees slots, because the store is in memory.

Nothing evicts, expires or prunes entries.

### Expected behavior

- `list()` returns only canvases with content, as its doc comment says.
- An entry with no content and no connected viewers is removed, so it stops using a slot. That includes a canvas cleared from the viewer's trash button once the viewer moves on.
- The "Clear unused canvases first" advice works.

### Steps to reproduce

Steps 1–3 were observed on a v0.8.7 server. Step 4 was not reproduced; it follows from the source (the limit checks in `render()` and `subscribe()`).

```text
1. Open the dashboard's Canvas page. The `default` canvas now exists (empty).
2. Type `test-1` into the canvas ID box and click Switch. The viewer's canvas list now shows `default` and `test-1`, both empty.
3. Have the agent render something to `test-1`, then click the trash button twice to clear it.
   The canvas is emptied but `test-1` is still listed, and stays listed after switching away.
4. (Not reproduced, from source.) Repeat with new IDs. Once 100 IDs exist, the tool's render to a new ID fails with
   "Maximum canvas count (100) reached. Clear unused canvases first.", and a viewer connecting to a new ID gets
   "Maximum canvas count reached" over the socket and is dropped (the viewer just shows Disconnected).
   Clearing existing canvases doesn't make room. Only a restart does.
```

### Impact

The canvas list fills with empty IDs that can't be removed without a restart. In a long-running daemon, viewing and clearing canvases slowly uses up the 100 slots, after which the agent can't create new canvases, and the error's advice doesn't help.

#11428 (open, approved) makes canvases persist across restarts and already covers part of this: its `clear()` drops an entry nobody is subscribed to. Three cases remain on that branch:
- Clearing from the viewer keeps the entry, because the viewer itself is subscribed to the canvas it's showing.
- Entries created only by `subscribe()` stay after the last viewer disconnects (until a restart, where #11428 reloads only saved frames).
- `list()` still returns empty entries.

A possible follow-up on top of #11428: filter `list()` to entries with a current frame, and remove an entry with no current frame when its last subscriber disconnects (in the `/ws/canvas/{id}` handler, or through a drop guard on the receiver).

### Logs / stack traces

_No response_

### ZeroClaw version

v0.8.7 (steps 1–3 observed); source checked on master `03b29bcc6`, where these files are unchanged from v0.8.7

### Rust version

_No response_

### Operating system

Linux server (amd64)

### Regression?

Unknown

### Pre-flight checks

- [x] I reproduced this on the latest master branch or latest release.
- [x] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content.

issues.title: [Bug]: Shell approval depends on an "approved" value the model writes itself, so prompts appear inconsistently

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

issues.body:
### Affected component

tools

### Severity

S2 - degraded behavior

### Current behavior

For an agent on risk_profile = "default" (shell not in auto_approve), whether a shell command stops for an approval prompt appears to depend on an "approved" value inside the model's own tool-call arguments.

ZeroCode shows the model-generated input for each shell call:

  ▶ [tool: shell]
    input: {"approved":true,"command":"python ~/.zeroclaw/agents/<agent>/workspace/<script>.py answer --answer …

Most calls showed "approved":true and ran with no prompt. Occasionally the model emitted "approved":false for the identical command, and an "Approval Required" box appeared (120 s timer):

  approved: false, command: python ~/.zeroclaw/agents/<agent>/workspace/<script>.py ans…

So the same command sometimes prompts and sometimes doesn't, depending on the model's output rather than the configuration.

### Expected behavior

Whether a shell command needs approval should depend only on the risk profile (auto_approve, allowed_commands, always_ask) and the user's approval choices, never on a value in the model's tool-call arguments. Identical commands under the same profile should behave identically every time.

If the "approved" argument is already ignored for permission decisions, please document how shell approval is decided and avoid exposing a model-facing argument that looks like it controls approval.

### Steps to reproduce

```bash
1. Configure an agent with risk_profile = "default" (shell not in auto_approve).
2. Instruct it (via SOUL.md) to run the same local script through the shell tool on every user turn, e.g.:
   python ~/.zeroclaw/agents/<agent>/workspace/<script>.py answer --answer "A"
3. Start a chat: zerocode -a <agent>
4. Trigger that command many times in one session (we used a 20-question quiz: one call per answer).
5. Watch the tool-call input lines: the model emits "approved":true on most calls and "approved":false on some, and the Approval Required prompt appears only on the latter.
```

### Impact

Moderate. Workflows that call a script many times get interrupted at random, and users can't predict when a prompt will appear. If the model-supplied value does influence approval, the model can effectively approve its own commands, which undermines the risk-profile model.

Current workaround: move the agent to a profile with shell in auto_approve plus an allowed_commands list. That is broader than needed: allowing "python" permits any Python script.

Related requests (happy to split into separate issues):
- A way to allow one exact script path or command pattern per agent.
- "Always allow" only changes the running config (the dashboard then shows "1 path differ from on-disk: risk_profiles.default.auto_approve"). The prompt could offer to save the choice to config.toml, or say that it won't be saved.

### Logs / stack traces

```text

```

### ZeroClaw version

V0.8.7

### Rust version

rustc 1.99.1

### Operating system

CachyOS Linux (Arch-based), x86_64; ZeroClaw running as a systemd user service; [runtime] kind = "native", shell = "sh". Model: LM Studio (OpenAI-compatible provider), unsloth/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it-qat.

issues.title: config validate: warn on dead delegate grants (delegates roster unreachable under delegation_policy.mode = forbidden)
issues.body:
## Situation

An agent can carry explicit delegation grants:

```toml
[agents.projects_assistant]
risk_profile = "worker_project"

[[agents.projects_assistant.delegates]]
agent = "demiurge"
mode = "independent"
```

while its risk profile forbids delegation outright:

```toml
[risk_profiles.worker_project.delegation_policy]
mode = "forbidden"
```

`Config::validate()` accepts this silently, but the grant can never fire: `delegate.rs::policy_for_target_from_config` refuses any caller invocation on `!delegation_policy.permits()` **before** target reachability (`Config::delegate_target_mode`) is consulted. The runtime error message is good (it names the remediation), but the operator only sees it at first call time — the config looked valid and the roster looked wired.

In our deployment this produced a debugging session across two independent filters (the grant was also missing the `"delegate"` entry in `allowed_tools`, which fails even earlier): the config *comment* claimed "the grant overrides the mode", the code rightfully disagreed, and every layer passed validation individually.

## Ask

A `validate()`-time warning (not an error — the configuration is coherent, just useless) when:

- an agent has a non-empty `[[agents.X.delegates]]` roster, AND
- the resolved risk profile's `delegation_policy.mode` does not `permits()`,

e.g. `warning: agents.projects_assistant has 1 delegate grant(s) but risk profile "worker_project" delegation_policy.mode = "forbidden" makes them unreachable`.

Optionally the same class of check for `"delegate"` missing from the profile's `allowed_tools` when any agent on that profile has delegate grants.

## Why a warning, not an error

The triple contract (grant + `allowed_tools` key + `mode = "allow"`) is deliberately layered; forbidding the combination outright could break valid transitional configs. Surfacing the dead grant at load time is enough to stop the silent footgun.

issues.title: [Task]: show retired environment-variable warnings in zeroclaw config migrate
issues.body:
### Task

Make `zeroclaw config migrate` show the warning for a retired `ZEROCLAW_*` environment variable, as every other command does.

### Context

Follow-up from the review of #11218 (schema V4), raised by Greptile on that PR's `src/main.rs`.

At startup, `main.rs` prints the load's `migration_notices` unless the command is `config migrate` (`reports_own_migration`), because that command reports its own notices as changes it wrote. But `ConfigCommands::Migrate` then prints only `report.notices` from `migrate_file_in_place`, which come from the file. A `MigrationNotice::IgnoredEnvOverride` is raised at load time from the environment (`crates/zeroclaw-config/src/env_overrides.rs`), not from the file, so `config migrate` never mentions it. That includes the "already at the current schema" branch.

Nothing is written incorrectly, and the variable has no effect either way. But `config migrate` is the command an operator runs to see what still needs cleaning up, and it's the one command where this warning is missing.

`MigrationNotice::changes_file()` already separates the two kinds: it is false only for `IgnoredEnvOverride`.

### Acceptance criteria

- With a retired `ZEROCLAW_*` variable set, `zeroclaw config migrate` prints its warning once, both when the file is migrated and when it is already current.
- File-change notices are still printed once, by the migrate command itself, not twice.
- `config migrate --json` includes the environment notice in its `notices` output, or the issue records why it should not.
- A test covers the already-current case with a retired variable set.

### Likely files or areas

- `src/main.rs`: the `reports_own_migration` block in startup, and the `ConfigCommands::Migrate` arm.
- `crates/zeroclaw-config/src/migration.rs`: `MigrationNotice::changes_file`.

### Contributor fit

good first issue candidate

### Mentor, reviewer, or contact

@tidux

### Risk notes

Low. Output only: no config is read or written differently. Keep the warning text on its existing Fluent path.

issues.title: [Task]: don't treat a forwarded loopback address as local in SOP cancel authorization
issues.body:
### Task

Make `authorize_sop_cancel` decide "local" with the same rule the rate-limit key uses: a request is local only when its peer is loopback and no forwarded header says otherwise. A forwarded loopback address must never count as local.

### Context

Follow-up from the review of #12114, which fixes #12052 for the limiter keys.

`crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/api_sop_author.rs` `authorize_sop_cancel` calls `forwarded_client_ip` directly when `gateway.require_pairing` is off and `gateway.trust_forwarded_headers` is on. If the result is loopback, it grants `ApprovalPrincipal::cli` and lets the request cancel a SOP run. Otherwise it refuses with "Remote SOP cancellation requires gateway pairing ... or call from localhost."

#12114 changes `forwarded_client_ip` to prefer the rightmost non-loopback `X-Forwarded-For` hop, which already closes the appending-proxy case (on master, a client-supplied leading `127.0.0.1` passed as local). But when the forwarded value is loopback-only, `forwarded_client_ip` still returns `127.0.0.1`, and this check still treats it as local. In the same PR, `client_key_from_request` treats exactly that value as spoofed and never gives it the loopback exemption.

It's reachable when the client's `X-Forwarded-For` reaches the gateway unchanged with trust on: an `X-Real-IP`-only proxy that doesn't clear the list (the setup the #12114 docs warn against), or `trust_forwarded_headers` enabled with no proxy at all. It requires pairing to be off, so the exposure is narrow, but this route is one of the few with an extra locality guard in that posture.

### Acceptance criteria

- With `trust_forwarded_headers` on, a request whose forwarded address is loopback-only, or whose `X-Forwarded-For` contains only loopback hops, is not treated as local by `authorize_sop_cancel`.
- A direct loopback request with no forwarded header still cancels without pairing, as today.
- `authorize_sop_cancel` and `client_key_from_request` share one helper for the "is this request local" decision, so they can't drift apart again.
- Tests cover: a forwarded `127.0.0.1` with a loopback peer (refused), a forwarded `127.0.0.1` with a remote peer (refused), and a direct loopback peer with no forwarded header (allowed).

### Likely files or areas

- `crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/api_sop_author.rs`: `authorize_sop_cancel`.
- `crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/lib.rs`: `forwarded_client_ip`, `client_key_from_request`.

### Contributor fit

good first issue candidate

### Mentor, reviewer, or contact

@tidux

### Risk notes

Security-relevant but narrow: it only matters with gateway pairing disabled. Land after #12114, which changes `forwarded_client_ip`.

issues.title: resolve_peer_set applies peer-group `ignore` per group, so outbound sends can reach ignored peers
issues.body:
### Affected component

runtime/daemon

### Severity

S2 - degraded behavior

### Current behavior

`resolve_peer_set` (`crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/peers.rs`) walks `config.peer_groups`, a `HashMap`, and for each group inserts its `external_peers` and then removes that group's own `ignore` entries from the set for that group's `channel` string. A deny therefore only removes peers that were inserted earlier, under the same channel key, as the same literal string:

1. **Order-dependent.** If one group lists a peer and another group on the same channel ignores it, the peer stays known whenever the ignoring group is visited first.
2. **Bare type vs. dotted alias.** An `ignore` in a group on `discord` never removes a peer listed by a group on `discord.main`. They are separate keys, and `is_known_peer` checks the dotted key first.
3. **Wildcard.** `ignore = ["*"]` removes only a literal `"*"` entry, so it denies nobody.

The resolved set is the outbound gate in `send_message_to_peer` (`is_known_peer`). It also feeds the peer map rendered for the agent (`render_sender_peer_map_for_channel`) and the `send_message_to_peer` target suggestions (`param_options::peer_targets`). In these cases an ignored peer can be messaged, and is advertised to the agent.

### Expected behavior

As documented in `docs/book/src/channels/peer-groups.md` ("Resolution"), `ignore` wins over a grant, including a wildcard, across every group matching the channel type or dotted alias, independent of group order. `ignore = ["*"]` denies everyone.

### Steps to reproduce

```toml
[agents.assistant]
channels = ["discord.main"]

[peer_groups.allow]
channel = "discord.main"
agents = ["assistant"]
external_peers = ["alice"]

[peer_groups.deny]
channel = "discord.main"     # also try "discord", or ignore = ["*"]
agents = ["assistant"]
ignore = ["alice"]
```

`resolve_peer_set(&config, "assistant").is_known_peer("discord.main", "alice")` should be false. I built this config 1,000 times in a throwaway unit test, with a fresh `Config`, and so fresh `HashMap` ordering, each time. `peers.rs` was unchanged from master `a66cc98a4`.

| `deny` group | known | unknown |
|---|---|---|
| `channel = "discord.main"`, `ignore = ["alice"]` | 424 | 576 |
| `channel = "discord"`, `ignore = ["alice"]` | 1000 | 0 |
| `channel = "discord.main"`, `ignore = ["*"]` | 1000 | 0 |

Expected: 0 known in every row.

### Impact

An operator's per-group blocklist does not reliably stop an agent from sending to that peer with `send_message_to_peer`, or from seeing it as a target. For the same-channel case, the outcome can change from one process start to the next. Inbound authorization is applied by the channel and is not covered here. This came up while testing #12271, whose Discord route lookup excludes peers ignored by any in-scope group on its own.

### Possible direction

Collect grants and denies across all of the agent's groups that match the channel type or dotted alias, then apply denies after the union, with the documented normalization (case-insensitive, leading `@`, `*` denies all), so that `is_known_peer` and the derived lists agree with the channel-side rule.

### ZeroClaw version

master `a66cc98a4`

### Operating system

Linux aarch64 (unit-level reproduction; not OS-specific)

### Regression?

Unknown

### Pre-flight checks

- [x] I reproduced this on the latest master branch or latest release.
- [x] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content.

issues.title: perf(runtime): system prompt is rebuilt from disk every turn, so a personality-file edit busts the prompt cache for all live sessions

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: runtime
labels.description: Auto scope: src/runtime/** changed.

labels.name: agent:prompt
labels.description: Manual prompt, context, and response guidance across agent/channel/memory/provider/runtime.

issues.body:
**Affected component:** runtime/daemon (also zerocode/tui and gateway/api, which share the `Agent` turn path)
**Severity:** S2 - degraded behavior (cost)

### Current behavior

Every new turn of an `Agent` re-reads the agent's workspace personality files from disk and writes the result into the system message. If any of those files changed since the previous turn, the system prompt changes. The system prompt is the head of the cached prefix, so the provider prompt cache misses for the whole conversation. This happens on the next turn of **every live session** of that agent, not only the session that edited the file.

Code path, checked on `origin/master` @ `f12da7462a0f`:

- `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/agent/agent.rs:Agent::turn` and `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/agent/agent.rs:Agent::turn_streamed_with_steering_state` both call `rebuild_system_prompt_for_dispatcher` at turn start. The ACP server (`crates/zeroclaw-channels/src/orchestrator/acp_server.rs`) and gateway WS (`crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/ws.rs`) drive `turn_streamed_with_steering_state`.
- `agent.rs:Agent::rebuild_system_prompt_for_dispatcher` -> `build_system_prompt_with_dispatcher` -> `build_system_prompt_with_dispatcher_and_cap` -> `SystemPromptBuilder::build_with_approval_policy`, then it overwrites `history[0].content` with the new text.
- `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/agent/prompt.rs:IdentitySection::build` -> `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/agent/personality.rs:load_personality_files`, which does `std::fs::read_to_string` on each of `PERSONALITY_FILES`: `SOUL.md`, `IDENTITY.md`, `USER.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `TOOLS.md`, `HEARTBEAT.md`, `BOOTSTRAP.md`, `MEMORY.md`. `MEMORY.md` is skipped when memory isn't injected (`personality_files_without_memory`).

Agents are often told to keep their own notes in these files (the default templates do this), so mid-session edits are routine, not an edge case.

Other inputs to the same builder that can vary between turns, from reading the code:

- **Deferred tool section:** `build_system_prompt_with_dispatcher_and_cap` appends `ToolSearchTool::deferred_prompt_section()` (`crates/zeroclaw-tools/src/tool_search.rs`). That list excludes tools already activated, so activating a tool through `tool_search` also changes the system prompt on the next turn.
- **Date:** not a factor on this path. `SystemPromptBuilder::with_defaults` leaves out `DateTimeSection` on purpose, and a comment there explains it's for cache stability. The `## Current Date` block (`chrono::Local::now()`, formatted to the day) lives in the other builder, `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/agent/system_prompt.rs:build_system_prompt_with_mode_and_effective_tools`. The `loop_::run` CLI path uses that builder through `build_system_prompt_for_turn`, which is rebuilt inside its loop, so that path also changes its system prompt at local midnight. The channel orchestrator builds its prompt once at startup (`system_prompt: Arc::new(...)`, `#8174`) and isn't affected.

### Observed (ZeroCode ACP, `custom` OpenAI-compatible gateway in front of Claude Opus, 2026-10-13)

- A long ZeroCode Code session normally got about 99% cached input: around 155-160k input tokens and about $0.04-0.05 per request.
- Two requests in that session came back with `cached_input_tokens` null: 159,794 tokens for $1.29 and 161,107 for $1.30, one minute apart. Each was the first request of a new turn, and in the turn just before it the agent had edited its own `AGENTS.md`. Every following request in the same turn was cached again.
- Those two came 55 s and 51 s after the previous request, so idle cache expiry doesn't explain them. (A third miss a minute earlier followed a 7.5-minute idle gap and may just be TTL expiry.) A steered message that joined a running turn never missed (no new turn, so no rebuild).
- Other live sessions of the same agent missed in the same minutes after an edit. In one 8-minute window there were four misses across two other sessions, $0.54-$2.10 each.
- Over 9.5 hours of that agent's sessions, 63 of 591 requests (10.7%) that came under 300 s after the previous request missed the cache completely, costing $19.58. Not every one of those is proven to follow an edit. The edit-then-miss pattern is the one we could tie to a cause.

### Expected behavior

Editing a workspace file shouldn't silently re-bill the whole conversation prefix for every live session. A bootstrap file change should either be deferred, or applied knowingly, with the cost visible.

### Steps to reproduce

```bash
# 1. Start a session against a provider that reports cached input tokens; run a few turns
#    until cached_input_tokens is ~= input_tokens on each request.
# 2. Open a second session of the same agent and do the same.
# 3. Append one line to <agent workspace>/AGENTS.md (any byte change).
# 4. Send a new message in each session.
# 5. In the cost ledger, the first request of the new turn in BOTH sessions shows
#    cached_input_tokens null/0 and is billed at the full input rate; later requests are cached again.
```

### Options (not choosing one here; trade-offs listed)

1. **Snapshot per session.** Read the personality files once at session start or rehydrate and reuse that text every turn. This gives no mid-session misses. The cost: edits only take effect in new sessions, or after an explicit refresh. Today an agent that edits its own rules sees them on its next turn; this option changes that, and the staleness is silent.
2. **Rebuild only on change.** Keep the rebuild but skip it unless a file's mtime, size or hash changed since the last build. This saves the rereads, but the cache behavior stays the same: still one full miss per edit per live session. It doesn't reduce the misses above.
3. **Option 1 plus a visible signal.** For example a notice ("AGENTS.md changed; applies to new sessions") or a `/reload-context` action that rebuilds on purpose and pays the one miss knowingly. This keeps the cost predictable without hiding that the session runs on older rules.

Whichever fix is chosen should also cover the `tool_search` deferred section above, or document it as an accepted per-activation miss.

### Impact

- Affected: any long-lived `Agent` session (ZeroCode, gateway WS) whose agent edits, or has someone else edit, its workspace personality files mid-session. It's worse with several concurrent sessions per agent and long contexts.
- Frequency: deterministic, on every edit.
- Consequence: about 25x the normal per-request cost on the turn after each edit, multiplied by the number of live sessions.

Related: #8321 (cache policy for volatile runtime context), #10777 (request config flips rewrite the cached history). #9005 touches the same prompt sections but isn't this bug.

### ZeroClaw version

Seen on an experiment build based on dogfood [`dogfood/zerocode-builds/20261008T194402Z-0341618f9d69`](https://github.com/Audacity88/zeroclaw/tree/dogfood/zerocode-builds/20261008T194402Z-0341618f9d69) ([commit](https://github.com/Audacity88/zeroclaw/commit/0341618f9d69e31bf38300d134ba86e98491d49d)). issues.body:
When ZeroClaw runs behind a reverse proxy, operators turn on a setting so the gateway reads the real client address from the X-Forwarded-For header. The gateway takes the first address in that header, but a client can write that header itself and most proxies simply add the real address after it. A client that writes 127.0.0.1 there is treated as the local machine, which every login limiter trusts, so it skips the pairing lockout, the sign-in budgets and the flow caps.

### Affected component

gateway/api

### Severity

S0 - data loss / security risk

### Current behavior

`forwarded_client_ip` in `crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/lib.rs:625-638` returns the first entry of `X-Forwarded-For` that parses as an address, and `client_key_from_request` (lines 640-652) uses it as the client key whenever `gateway.trust_forwarded_headers` is on. Every auth limiter exempts a loopback key: `AuthRateLimiter` skips both the check and the record for it (`crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/auth_rate_limit.rs:63-70`, `:109`, `:120`), and the enrollment relay skips its budget and its per-client flow cap (`crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/api_oidc.rs:150`, `:316`). The docs tell same-host proxy operators to enable the setting so the per-client limits apply (`docs/book/src/security/authentication.md:311-315`), and a standard appending proxy keeps the client-supplied first entry in place.

### Expected behavior

The client key should come from the proxy's own addition, which is the rightmost entry when the proxy appends, or from a single header the proxy sets rather than forwards. A forwarded address should never be treated as loopback, because the real loopback caller never arrives through the proxy with a forwarded header. The pairing lockout, the enrollment budget and the flow caps should hold for every remote client regardless of what it sends.

### Steps to reproduce

```text
1. Run the gateway behind nginx with proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
   (the usual appending form) and set [gateway] trust_forwarded_headers = true.
2. From a remote host send POST /pair with a wrong X-Pairing-Code more than ten times in a minute,
   each request carrying the header X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1.
3. No 429 lockout appears, because the gateway keys every attempt as 127.0.0.1 and the limiter
   exempts loopback; the same header lifts the enrollment budget and the per-client flow cap.
Source-traced at master 5d4b18d335; not executed.
```

### Impact

The brute-force lockout on pairing codes and webhook authentication, and the per-client budgets on the OIDC enrollment relay, can all be switched off by a remote client with one header. The default pairing code is 32 alphanumeric characters, so guessing it stays impractical, but the numeric compatibility charset at the minimum length of six becomes guessable, and the flow-store denial in #12049 then needs only one host. #12047 and #12049 assume the per-client keys hold, so this weakens both; related tracker #8289.

### Logs / stack traces

_No response_

### ZeroClaw version

master 5d4b18d335 (v0.8.7)

### Rust version

n/a (source review); CI pins 1.98.0

### Operating system

Any; reviewed in source on macOS

### Regression?

No, first-time setup

### Pre-flight checks

- [ ] I reproduced this on the latest master branch or latest release.
Source-traced at master 5d4b18d335; no runtime reproduction was run.
- [X] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content.

### Recommended action

Pick the client address from the right-hand end of `X-Forwarded-For`, skipping a configured list of trusted proxy addresses, or read only one header the proxy overwrites such as `X-Real-IP`. Never grant the loopback exemption to a forwarded address, and add a test that a request carrying `X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1` through a trusted proxy is still rate limited. Document the proxy directive operators should use so the gateway sees exactly one hop.
